Steel Crown Historical Fencing

Historical European Martial Arts · Charlotte, NC

About the Club

Steel Crown Historical Fencing is a HEMA organization in Charlotte, North Carolina dedicated to the serious study and practice of historical fencing. We train longsword and other weapons drawn from primary historical sources, with an emphasis on disciplined technique, honest instruction, and a culture where every member is both a student and a contributor.

Whether you are new to HEMA or an experienced practitioner, you will find a training environment built on mutual respect, open knowledge, and long-term development.

docs.title: Mission Statement
docs.text: Steel Crown Historical Fencing is a Historical European Martial Arts (HEMA) organization dedicated to the study, practice, and advancement of historical fencing through disciplined training, integrity, and shared growth. We foster a culture where every member, regardless of experience, is both a student and a contributor, united by sportsmanship, mutual respect, and the pursuit of continual improvement. Through instruction, competition, historical study, and community engagement, we aim to develop skilled fencers, responsible training partners, and strong communities built on trust and accountability.

docs.title: Vision Statement
docs.text: We envision a club where excellence and community reinforce one another, and where rigorous training, historical study, and genuine camaraderie exist side by side. Steel Crown Historical Fencing strives to build an environment in which every student is challenged, supported, and valued, and where knowledge is shared openly across all levels of experience. We measure success not only through individual achievement, but through the strength, character, and development of the club as a whole. Our goal is to build a lasting institution that develops exceptional fencers, respectful competitors, dedicated contributors, and people of character.

docs.title: Core Organizational Principles
docs.text:
• Student-Centered Growth

    We believe every member is responsible for learning and contributing, and that growth is a shared responsibility.

  • Integrity in Instruction

    We value honesty, integrity, and transparency in how we teach, train, and represent the art.

  • Excellence Through Discipline

    We believe that skill is built through consistency, accountability, and purposeful training.

  • Safety and Responsibility

    We are responsible for creating and maintaining a safe and inclusive training environment that allows for integrity, trust, and long-term development.

  • Respect

    We treat everyone, including ourselves, with kindness and respect.

  • Sportsmanship

    We claim victory with humility and accept defeat with dignity.

  • Community Over Ego

    We believe having a strong sense of community is more important than any individual status, recognition, or organizational politics.

  • Open Knowledge

    We believe that knowledge should be shared freely and carried forward for the benefit of the entire club.

  • Long-Term Development

    We aim to build not only skilled competitors, but capable leaders and ambassadors for HEMA.

docs.title: Choose the Right Answer I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | LIECHTENAUER & MEYER LENS

The class develops choice among four broad defensive families. It is an assessment and decision lesson, not a test of named techniques.

CENTRAL QUESTION: When an opponent attacks, how do I choose among counterattacking, parry-riposte, evading, or withdrawing?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students recognize attack commitment, distance, line, and available time, then select a response that removes the threat and produces a clean outcome rather than forcing a preferred answer.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: The Liechtenauer tradition's Before, After, and Indes, paired with Meyer's warning that even a good technique fails when used without the right opportunity.

The target behavior counts only when all four observable conditions are present.

REQUIREMENT OBSERVABLE STANDARD Recognition The student identifies the attack early enough to perceive distance, line, and commitment. Selection The response fits the available time and geometry: intercept, parry-answer, evade, or withdraw. Execution The chosen response genuinely removes or avoids the incoming threat. Adaptation The student changes or abandons the answer when the attack changes and avoids the double.

NO DOUBLE: A result that leaves both fencers validly hit does not satisfy the lesson, even if one blade arrived first.

C | BLOCK 1 | 0:00-0:05

Students understand the problem, success test, and class arc.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Tonight we are solving one problem: When an opponent attacks, how do I choose among counterattacking, parry-riposte, evading, or withdrawing?"

SUCCESS DEFINITION: State the four-part success test in plain language and make clear that a double is a failed solution.

CLASS ARC: Experience the problem first; compare what worked; examine one historical lens; increase choice and pressure; test transfer in open fencing.

DO NOT: Teach the complete historical solution before the first game. Students should possess the problem before receiving the model.

C | BLOCK 2 | 0:05-0:20

React in four directions and arrive balanced enough to continue, rather than making one maximal movement.

WHAT THIS BLOCK IS: A short movement lesson, not conditioning. Demonstrate each exercise once, keep the volume low, and stop or regress when posture or landing quality deteriorates.

TARGET QUALITY: React in four directions and arrive balanced enough to continue, rather than making one maximal movement.

Use the checklist to distinguish learning from mere scoring.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Recognition Sees line, distance, and commitment Reacts only when blade is close Selection Choice fits time and geometry Forces favorite defense Defense Threat is removed or avoided Relies on scoring first Complexity Uses simplest adequate response Adds unnecessary actions Adaptation Changes answer as attack changes Finishes preplanned script Outcome Clean resolution; doubles decline Counts doubles as partial success Transfer Chooses freely without bonuses Needs instructor to name response

docs.title: Choose the Right Answer I
docs.text:
When an opponent attacks, how do I choose among counterattacking, parry-riposte, evading, or withdrawing?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | July 2026 | Version 1.0

docs.title: Primary functional model
docs.text:
Use the simplest response that solves the present attack. More ambitious actions require earlier information and better geometry; when those are absent, choose a larger safety margin.

Preserve the sequence. If time is lost, compress explanation before removing open sparring or reflection.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival & orientation Define choose the right answer i and its success test Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Athletic development React in four directions and arrive balanced enough to continue, rather than making one maximal movement. Movement readiness 0:20-0:40 Problem exposure Game 1: Four Answers Experience the problem 0:40-0:55 Guided coaching Debrief; one useful intervention; variable rehearsal Small intervention 0:55-1:05 Historical integration The Liechtenauer tradition's Before, After, and Indes, paired with Meyer's warning that even a good technique fails when used without the right opportunity. Historical model 1:05-1:30 Progressive constraints Game 2: Distance Changes the Answer; Game 3: Decision Under Uncertainty More choice and pressure 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Five 4-minute rounds; normal fencing Transfer 1:55-2:00 Reflection & close Name cues, choices, failures, and next action Consolidation

TIME CHECK: 5 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 5 = 120 minutes.

TRANSITION PLAN: Students gear before the opening. Pair by compatible control and size. Keep masks and gloves on from problem exposure through sparring. Use one audible timer and announce rotations before each interval ends.

IF RUNNING LATE: Shorten the guided discussion or historical explanation by 2-3 minutes and reduce Game 2 by one role interval. Preserve at least one open-sparring round and the reflection.

docs.title: Instructor hypothesis
docs.text: Students will force their favorite response, label the choice only after the fact, or treat retreat as failure even when it is the safest solution.

docs.title: Exercise sequence
docs.text:
EXERCISE DOSE COACHING FOCUS MOVEMENT PURPOSE Four-direction stance step 2 x 4 each direction Short travel; feet do not tangle; eyes forward Prepare multiple defensive movement options Drop-step and recover 2 x 4 each lead Move center first; recover under control Rehearse creating emergency distance without falling backward Lateral bound or step-and- stick 2 x 3 each side Quiet landing; stable knee; usable posture Prepare evasive displacement Four-choice partner reaction 3 x 20 seconds each Name cue after moving; no guessing Connect visual information to different movement families

Preserve the information and decision while reducing uncertainty, speed, distance, or impact.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE First-time student Use a known attack or response, longer preparation time, controlled partner, and score safe resolution as success. Mixed experience Give beginners less uncertainty; give experienced students more choice or rhythm variation, not greater impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. Observer applies the four-part success test, then roles rotate. Limited space Use narrow lanes; prohibit passing and large leaps; emphasize compact footwork and controlled stops. Injury / low impact Replace bounds with steps; reduce speed and contact; permit observer or limited-role participation. Large attendance Create lanes, assign a senior student to each cluster, and synchronize changes with one timer. Game breaks down Remove one variable, increase distance, slow the action, or return to a known starting state. Time loss Compress explanation and one role interval; preserve open transfer and reflection.

docs.title: How to perform the exercises
docs.text:
GAME CARD 3

Test whether choices survive a more representative attack environment.

STARTING STATE: Free onset; designated attacker initiates within eight seconds and may use one feint.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender solves the attack with any safe family and continues only while the opportunity remains.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Normal movement; continue to clean hit, double, or safe separation; no bonus for a named technique.

SCORING: Clean defensive solution 2; safe withdrawal/reset 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Change attacker every 3 minutes; final minute reset.

COACH OBSERVES: Early information, changing decisions, simplest adequate answer, and double reduction.

PROGRESSION: Remove designated attacker and scoring categories.

REGRESSION: Remove feint and restrict attack to one side.

docs.title: 1. FOUR-DIRECTION STANCE STEP
docs.text:
From fencing stance, take one short step forward, back, left-diagonal, or right-diagonal, returning to center after each. Keep the feet from crossing and finish every step ready to move again. Cue: 'One step, one stable shape.'

C | BLOCK 6 | 1:05-1:30

Increase uncertainty while preserving the lesson's central information-action relationship.

GAME CARD 2

Show that the same attack may require a different solution at a different distance.

STARTING STATE: Attacker secretly chooses close edge, normal edge, or stretched entry before a committed high cut.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender selects a response suited to actual distance and remains safe.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Either side high cut; no feints; exchange may continue through one immediate answer.

SCORING: Appropriate clean solution 2; safe disengagement 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes transition.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether distance changes selection and whether students can explain the cue before seeing the result.

PROGRESSION: Let attacker change distance during preparation.

REGRESSION: Instructor announces near or far before each attempt.

docs.title: 2. DROP-STEP AND RECOVER
docs.text:
From a comfortable stance, let the rear foot move backward first while the hips travel with it, then bring the front foot back enough to restore stance. Do not lean the shoulders behind the hips. Pause, then advance back to start. Cue: 'Move the center, then rebuild the stance.'

C | BLOCK 4 | 0:40-0:55

Use the first game's evidence to provide the smallest intervention that improves the class.

C | BLOCK 5 | 0:55-1:05

Connect the experienced tactical problem to a documented historical principle without claiming that the source prescribes the modern game.

SOURCE IDENTIFICATION: The Liechtenauer tradition's Before, After, and Indes, paired with Meyer's warning that even a good technique fails when used without the right opportunity.

VERIFIED HISTORICAL CLAIM: The Liechtenauer gloss tradition treats Before and After as foundational and uses Indes to regain initiative while responding. Meyer likewise emphasizes that no sequence, however good, is useful without the proper opportunity. [1][2]

MODERN TRAINING INTERPRETATION: Show the same high cut at four distances and timings. Early, clear commitment may permit a covered counterattack; moderate time supports parry-riposte; a line that can be cleared supports evasion; late recognition or poor geometry favors withdrawal. The four-family decision tool is modern, while the historical lens concerns initiative, timely response, and opportunity.

DEMONSTRATION: Show three slow examples: one successful application, one common failure, and one case in which the action should be declined. Let students rehearse briefly, then return to live choice.

EVIDENCE LINE: Historical text supplies the cited principle or action. The success test, games, scoring, cues, and safety adaptations are modern coaching design.

docs.title: 3. LATERAL BOUND OR STEP-AND-STICK
docs.text:
Push gently from one leg and travel a small distance sideways to land on the opposite leg, holding for two seconds. Students who should not jump use a quick lateral step and the same hold. Knee tracks over toes; chest stays controlled. Cue: 'Move enough to clear the line, then own the landing.'

C | BLOCK 3 | 0:20-0:40

Make response selection visible without requiring open-sparring complexity.

STARTING STATE: Attacker begins at variable but controlled distance and may deliver one committed high cut.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender chooses counterattack, parry-riposte, evade-and-hit, or withdrawal. Attacker recovers honestly.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Attacker varies side, distance, and rhythm but no feints. Defender is never required to score if safe withdrawal is appropriate.

SCORING: Clean threat removal plus appropriate score 2; safe no-hit resolution 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partners and repeat.

INSTRUCTOR OBSERVES: Favorite-answer bias, response too ambitious for timing, retreat without posture, and after-the-fact rationalization.

COACH POSTURE: Observe across the room before intervening. Record common patterns and let several exchanges occur before deciding what the class needs.

docs.title: 4. FOUR-CHOICE PARTNER REACTION
docs.text:
Partners face each other without swords. Leader shows one of four clear cues: straight hand forward, diagonal hand left, diagonal hand right, or both hands advancing. Mover responds with a short intercepting step, parry-shaped hand action, lateral evade, or withdrawal step respectively. After moving, the student names the cue they saw. Keep speed moderate. Cue: 'See, choose, arrive balanced.'

REGRESSION AND STOP RULE: Reduce speed, distance, or impact; replace jumps with controlled steps. Stop for pain, dizziness, repeated loss of balance, loud uncontrolled landings, or a student who cannot maintain the described posture.

docs.title: Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. What information made one answer safer than another?

  2. Which answer required the earliest decision?

  3. When did withdrawal preserve a better future opportunity?

  4. What caused a technically correct action to fail?

PRIMARY INTERVENTION: Build a simple decision hierarchy: can you intercept with cover? If not, can you parry and answer? If the line is avoidable, can you evade while staying ready? If information is late or geometry poor, create distance. Cue: 'Solve the threat you actually have.'

VARIABLE REHEARSAL: Partners re-test the target problem at approximately 60-70% intensity. Keep at least one meaningful variable - side, rhythm, distance, pressure, or response - rather than feeding identical repetitions.

FEEDBACK PLAN: Use one cue at a time. Correct immediate danger at once; otherwise give feedback between sets of three attempts. Ask the student to identify the information that shaped the action.

AVOID: Turning the block into a long lecture or adding several fixes before students can test the first one.

docs.title: Game 2 - Distance Changes the Answer | 12 minutes
docs.text:
Show that the same attack may require a different solution at a different distance.

  • Attacker secretly chooses close edge, normal edge, or stretched entry before a committed high cut.
  • Defender selects a response suited to actual distance and remains safe.
  • Either side high cut; no feints; exchange may continue through one immediate answer.
  • Appropriate clean solution 2; safe disengagement 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0.
  • 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes transition.

C | BLOCK 7 | 1:30-1:55

Test whether the behavior appears without forced actions or bonus scoring.

FORMAT: Five 4-minute rounds with approximately 1 minute between rounds for rotation and brief feedback. Use normal open-fencing rules and the club's usual intensity agreement.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. Do not hunt a particular defense. Notice the attack's line, distance, and commitment, then use the least complicated answer that genuinely keeps you safe."

PAIRING PLAN: Use compatible control and size, then rotate across different rhythms and preferences. Supervise novice pairings and avoid a large mismatch solely to complete the rotation.

C | BLOCK 8 | 1:55-2:00

Students consolidate one usable cue and one testable next action.

GAME CARD 1

Make response selection visible without requiring open-sparring complexity.

STARTING STATE: Attacker begins at variable but controlled distance and may deliver one committed high cut.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender chooses counterattack, parry-riposte, evade-and-hit, or withdrawal. Attacker recovers honestly.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Attacker varies side, distance, and rhythm but no feints. Defender is never required to score if safe withdrawal is appropriate.

SCORING: Clean threat removal plus appropriate score 2; safe no-hit resolution 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partners and repeat.

COACH OBSERVES: Favorite-answer bias, response too ambitious for timing, retreat without posture, and after-the-fact rationalization.

PROGRESSION: Add a low-line attack or one false preparation.

REGRESSION: Use two attack types and two response families only.

docs.title: Game 3 - Decision Under Uncertainty | 13 minutes
docs.text:
Test whether choices survive a more representative attack environment.

  • Free onset; designated attacker initiates within eight seconds and may use one feint.
  • Defender solves the attack with any safe family and continues only while the opportunity remains.
  • Normal movement; continue to clean hit, double, or safe separation; no bonus for a named technique.
  • Clean defensive solution 2; safe withdrawal/reset 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0.
  • Change attacker every 3 minutes; final minute reset.

PROGRESSION TRIGGER: Remove designated attacker and scoring categories.

REGRESSION TRIGGER: Remove feint and restrict attack to one side.

docs.title: Coach records
docs.text:
• Sees line, distance, and commitment
  • Choice fits time and geometry
  • Threat is removed or avoided
  • Uses simplest adequate response
  • Changes answer as attack changes
  • Clean resolution; doubles decline
  • Chooses freely without bonuses

FEEDBACK: Observe during rounds and coach mainly between them. Open sparring is not another constrained game.

docs.title: Whole-group questions
docs.text:
1. Which cue most influenced your choice?

  2. Which answer did you overuse?

  3. When did a safe withdrawal create a better next exchange?

INDIVIDUAL NEXT ACTION: Each student states one small, observable action they will test the next time this problem appears.

INSTRUCTOR CLOSE: Restate the functional success test, not a technique name. Record any safety issue, equipment problem, or student who needs a lower-intensity follow-up.

END ON TIME: Do not let the final sparring round consume reflection. The class is incomplete until students name the information that shaped their decision.

docs.title: Plan modifications before the room forces them
What to watch without interrupting every exchange
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what information the student perceived, offer one change, and let the next round test it.

SOURCES AND FINAL GATE

Historical claims are kept narrower than the modern class design. Representative games preserve opponent information and live decisions, but no source proves that this exact lesson is uniquely optimal.

[1] Pseudo-Peter von Danzig. Cod. 44.A.8, gloss on Before, After, Weak, Strong, and Indes. Wiktenauer concordance and translations

[2] Meyer, Joachim. Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part One: Longsword, Chapter 8, fols. I.24v.1-I.24v.3. Wiktenauer transcription and Garber-Chidester translation

[3] Meyer, Joachim. The Art of Combat, 2nd ed., trans. Jeffrey L. Forgeng. Frontline Books, 2015.

[4] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araújo. "Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport." Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33, no. 1 (2011): 146-155. doi:10.1123/jsep.33.1.146. PubMed record

[5] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. "A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play." Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24, no. 2 (2019): 103-116. doi:10.1080/17408989.2018.1552676. DOI

TERMS: Historical terminology and English renderings vary by manuscript and translation. This plan paraphrases short claims and identifies modern coaching labels as modern.

READY: Read the attack, choose the simplest adequate response, remove the threat, and refuse the double.

docs.title: Class-level success evidence
docs.text:
• Cleaner solutions and fewer doubles from Game 1 to Game 3.
  • Students can name at least one reliable cue.
  • The target behavior appears selectively in open fencing.
  • Students can explain why an unsafe score does not satisfy the lesson.
  • Beginners show safer structure even when they do not score.

docs.title: Compact Cutting I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW

Compact cutting is the skill of finishing one credible cut in a position that can immediately threaten, cover, redirect, or leave.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I keep producing credible threats at close measure without withdrawing the sword to reset?

WORKING PRINCIPLE: Cut at the target. Finish useful. Attack the next opening from where you already are.

STUDENT CUE: Cut. Finish useful. Read the opening. Recycle or leave.

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: The first cut has edge alignment, a legible cutting plane, and body support. Any follow-up begins from the real endpoint, answers an opening or pressure that actually appeared, and leaves the fencer able to stop, cover, or exit.

COMMON NON-EXAMPLE: A loose wrist tap, a large withdrawal to reload, a memorized Zwerch chain thrown regardless of the defender, or a frantic sequence that ends in a double.

RESEARCH POSTURE: This is an experimental acquisition lesson. Meyer supplies historical clues; the crossed-hand, uncrossed- hand, and hip-turn mechanics are modern hypotheses to test rather than settled universal answers.

WARM-UP | 0:00-0:15

Prepare elastic feet, quiet landings, quick changes of direction, and recovery without stiffness. This is preparation, not conditioning.

TIME MOVEMENT COACHING FOCUS 0:00-0:05 Pogo hops in place, then small forward, backward, and lateral hops Stay tall; spring through the ankles; land quietly; stop while quality is high 0:05-0:10 Low boxes: two-foot on and off, alternating single-foot, then lateral on and off Use a height everyone owns; knees track cleanly; stabilize before changing direction 0:10-0:15 Short sprints of 5-10 meters, controlled braking, then a slow walk back Sharp first steps; balanced deceleration; the return walk is recovery

WHY THIS WARM-UP: Compact cutting uses the same broad rhythm: accelerate, arrest motion without collapsing, and redirect from the position actually reached. The warm-up previews that quality without pretending to reproduce sword mechanics.

ADAPTATION: Use steps instead of jumps for anyone managing impact or balance limitations. Reduce the box height before reducing control, and keep sprint lanes short enough that braking remains clean.

TRANSITION: Mask and glove up and move directly into controlled cutting before the room cools down.

TECHNICAL EXPLORATION | 0:15-0:30

Show the contrast, then let students feel it. The goal is a shorter reusable action, not the smallest possible action and not one mandatory body mechanic.

EXAMPLE WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE WHAT IT TEACHES Large reset The sword withdraws or loops before every new line Credible, but too much dead travel for the available time Loose tap The hands flick while edge and body connection disappear Short is not automatically meaningful contact Compact cut The blade reaches a target, finishes under control, and remains available Speed comes from a shorter path and a useful endpoint

PARTNER EXPLORATION: In masks and gloves, one partner presents an upper opening. The cutter makes one controlled diagonal or horizontal action, holds the endpoint for one beat, then names what that position can do next: threaten, cover, redirect, or leave. Alternate every three cuts.

CROSSED-HAND FAMILY: Test whether uncrossing can carry a short-edge or Zwerch-like action to a real new line without a withdrawal.

UNCROSSED-HAND FAMILY: Test whether a modest hip and torso turn can cross or redirect the blade while preserving balance, cover, and a visible cutting plane.

MODERN COACHING PHRASE: In HEMA, we cut at things, not through things. Use the phrase to remove unnecessary follow-through, not to excuse contact that has no cutting quality.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:30-0:45

Use the historical source to sharpen the problem while keeping the evidence separate from the specific mechanics this class is testing.

MEYER, 1570: As soon as you have touched, do not tarry any longer, but instead let it fly quickly away from one opening to another.

WHAT THE SOURCE SUPPORTS: After contact, Meyer expects the sword to move promptly from one opening to another rather than remain idle. He presents the Zwerch as especially useful inside and under the opponent's sword, where broad long cuts may be unavailable, and he describes actions supported by the whole body.

WHAT THE SOURCE DOES NOT SETTLE: Meyer does not give us one universal compact-cutting method, one correct hip rotation, or a tournament-validity test for every modern ruleset. The passage does not justify throwing a memorized Zwerch whenever the hands cross.

HISTORICAL CLUE CLASSROOM HYPOTHESIS Move quickly opening to opening Reuse the first cut's endpoint instead of withdrawing to rebuild the attack Zwerch works in constrained inside lines Crossing and uncrossing may create short credible routes when distance collapses The body supports the action Small hip and torso changes may redirect the blade without demanding a large swing

SOURCE NOTE: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Longsword, fol. I.55r; English translation by Rebecca L. R. Garber and transcription by Michael Chidester, via Wiktenauer. The Zwerch summary follows Meyer's 1570 longsword material.

GAME 1 | 0:45-1:05

Make the first cut credible, experience its endpoint, and launch no more than one follow-up without withdrawing or making an oversized reset.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The technical exploration was cooperative. This adds an honest defensive action while keeping the next line readable enough for students to discover a usable route.

STARTING STATE: Full gear. Begin at close striking measure. The defender presents either upper opening. The attacker makes a controlled credible cut. Once that cut has launched, the defender closes the attacked side and may leave the opposite upper line available.

ATTACKER: Deliver the first cut at the target. If the cover creates a real second opening, attack it directly from the endpoint. If the route jams or the line is not present, cover or leave.

DEFENDER: Give an honest cover that stops the first action without becoming a theatrical sweep. Remain responsible after the cover so a weak follow-up can be answered.

STUDENT RULES: Maximum two cuts. The first must matter; the second must come from where the first actually finished. Reset on a clean hit, double, loss of balance, weak contact, or a large withdrawal to restart the sword.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Use 90-second roles, then switch. Change partners after both roles. No points.

COACH WATCHES: Pausing after the first cut, preloading the second before the cover occurs, or shrinking the follow-up until it becomes a tap.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Let the defender vary the timing and depth of the cover or decline to leave the expected second line.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Use one known cover and one known second opening until the endpoint can be recycled without a reset.

GAME 2 | 1:05-1:25

Use crossed or uncrossed hand positions as information, not as commands to complete a memorized combination.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Game 1 established a clean recycle. Now the defender can produce different blade relationships, forcing the attacker to choose a Zwerch-like line change, a body-supported redirection, or an exit.

STARTING STATE: Full gear. The attacker begins with one controlled cut from close measure. The defender may cover from either side and may give light pressure, yield, or keep the line firm. Contact stays at drilling intensity.

ATTACKER: If the hands are crossed and a line exists, test an uncrossing action. If the hands are uncrossed, test a modest hip and torso turn and the shortest supported route. If the defender owns the center or no target is open, cover and leave.

DEFENDER: Make one honest defense, remain capable of an immediate return, and answer a stalled or structurally weak second action with controlled contact. Do not feed a predetermined solution.

STUDENT RULES: The attacker gets one possible follow-up, never a third cut, and must be able to name the opening that caused it. The defender may answer after the follow-up or as soon as the attacker stalls, forces through control, or withdraws to reload.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Use 90-second roles and change partners after a full cycle. Keep each phrase short enough that the starting relationship remains visible.

COACH WATCHES: Whether the second cut answers the defender's actual pressure and opening; whether the sword stays supported; and whether leaving remains available.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Vary pressure, distance, and whether the expected opening appears.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Limit the defender to two named covers and slow the first exchange until the hand relationship is visible.

GAME 3 | 1:25-1:40

Remove the promised follow-up. The attacker decides whether a second cut is actually better than recovering or leaving measure.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The previous games taught a route. This game tests whether students can decline that route when the defender's cover, pressure, or distance makes it wrong.

STARTING STATE: Full gear. Begin just outside close striking measure. The designated attacker enters with one compact cut. After that action begins, both fencers may defend, reposition, and answer normally within the constraints.

ATTACKER: Create one credible first threat. Then choose: finish the hit, make one immediate line change, or recover and leave.

DEFENDER: Use any safe defense or evasion. Answer immediately when the attacker repeats blindly, pauses, or loses cover.

STUDENT RULES: The designated attacker is limited to two cuts before recovering or exiting. The phrase ends on a clean hit, a double, clear control, or full separation. Reset without debating points.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Use 90-second roles and change partners after both roles. Change first cuts and starting guards so the endpoint cannot become a memorized pattern.

COACH WATCHES: A recognizable second cut with no visible re-chamber; a decision that changes with the defender; and an exit that remains covered and balanced.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Remove the designated attacker and let either fencer recognize the close-measure moment.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Return to one known first cut and two possible defensive answers: one that allows the follow-up and one that requires leaving.

OPEN SPARRING | 1:40-2:00

Return to normal fencing. Compact follow-ups should appear only when measure and blade relationship make them useful.

FORMAT: Fence normal Steel Crown rounds of 3-4 minutes and rotate partners. Use the room's ordinary scoring and intensity agreements. Add no bonus points for compact cutting.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: Notice when distance closes and a conventional reset would be too slow. If a credible line change is present, use it. If not, defend, work within the club's current close-play rules, or separate safely.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the first cut genuinely required a defense; whether the next action begins from the real endpoint; whether the second opening actually appeared; and whether the fencer can stop after one action, remain covered after two, and avoid the double.

FEEDBACK RHYTHM: Watch several phrases without interrupting. Between rounds, give one cue or ask one question. Do not turn live fencing into a hunt for the featured technique.

TRANSFER CUE: When the space gets small: cut at the target, finish useful, and let the exchange decide whether you recycle or leave.

OPTIONAL CLOSE: Ask: Which endpoint gave you the cleanest next action, and when should you have left instead? Take two fast answers and stop.

COACH REFERENCE

Protect the distinction between efficient movement and meaningless contact. More cuts are not the outcome; better decisions from useful positions are.

IF YOU SEE... TRY... Tiny wrist taps or flat contact Restore a visible target and cutting plane; slow down until edge and body support return Hands collapsed into the torso Give the hands room to work and recover structure before asking for speed Huge hip turn or exposed back Reduce rotation and keep both the opponent and the exit available Preset Zwerch chain Let the defender decline the expected opening and require the attacker to name what changed Second cut through firm control Make leaving a successful answer; reward recognition rather than stubborn continuation Frantic multi-cutting Reinstate the two-cut limit and a one-beat endpoint check

QUESTIONS THAT PRESERVE DISCOVERY: Did the first cut need to be defended? What actual opening or pressure caused the follow-up? Where did the first cut leave the hands, point, hips, and balance? Could the fencer stop, cover, or leave from that same position?

RECORD FOR THE NEXT CLASS: Note which endpoints produced credible actions, which routes jammed, what measure made compact cutting necessary, and what contact standard students could reproduce. Let those findings shape Compact Cutting II rather than forcing the hypothesis to survive contrary evidence.

ADAPTATIONS: Newer fencers receive a fixed side and known cover. Advanced fencers vary pressure, rhythm, and whether the expected line appears. Odd groups use an observer who names the endpoint, the opening, and the final decision.

SUPPORTING REFERENCES: Meyer (1570), Longsword, via Wiktenauer; Southern California Swordfight 2024 General Tournament Rules; FightCamp 2026 Tournament Rules; Merkert, biomechanical analysis of longsword striking (2019). Full citations and interpretive limits appear in the companion Compact Cutting Research Brief.

Use this page for observations, adjustments, and ideas for Compact Cutting II.

docs.title: Make the next threat from where the sword finishes
What makes a compact cut matter
Move from one opening to another
Compact Cutting II
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW

Part I built useful endpoints. Part II tests whether the fencer can read the opponent's real response and continue only while continuing remains safe.

CENTRAL QUESTION: After my first action, can I immediately recognize whether to cut again, defend, follow, or leave?

WORKING PRINCIPLE: Fast enough to exploit the opening. Controlled enough to abandon the chain.

STUDENT CUE: Finish. Read. Continue or protect.

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: The fencer makes a credible compact first cut, recognizes whether the blade is free or controlled, and chooses an immediate follow-up, defensive action, pursuit, or exit without pausing to reset the weapon.

PART I CONNECTION: Use the position the first action created: crossed or uncrossed hands, point near the target, and hips still available. Do not withdraw simply to recreate a familiar guard.

COMMON NON-EXAMPLE: Three fast cuts thrown because three cuts were planned. Speed does not rescue an invented opening, a blade already under control, or a follow-up that produces a double.

EXPERIMENTAL STANDARD: The class is testing which endpoints make rapid decisions possible. Keep the mechanics that remain credible under pressure and discard the ones that require the defender to cooperate.

WARM-UP | 0:00-0:15

Repeat the approved plyometric sequence. The goal is elastic movement, clean braking, and the ability to change direction without losing posture.

TIME MOVEMENT COACHING FOCUS 0:00-0:05 Pogo hops in place, then small forward, backward, and lateral hops Stay tall; spring through the ankles; land quietly; stop while quality is high 0:05-0:10 Low boxes: two-foot on and off, alternating single-foot, then lateral on and off Use a height everyone owns; knees track cleanly; stabilize before redirecting 0:10-0:15 Short sprints of 5-10 meters, controlled braking, then a slow walk back Sharp first steps; balanced deceleration; the return walk is recovery

WHY THIS WARM-UP: Rapid close work depends on acceleration that can be stopped or redirected. The athlete must be able to change the decision without the body continuing blindly in the old direction.

ADAPTATION: Use steps instead of jumps for anyone managing impact or balance limitations. Lower the box before sacrificing landing control, and shorten sprint lanes if braking becomes sloppy.

TRANSITION: Mask and glove up. Begin with controlled endpoints before adding pressure or choice.

TECHNICAL REVIEW | 0:15-0:30

Review Part I quickly, then attach one clear decision to each common outcome. The purpose is recognition, not rehearsing a long combination.

AFTER THE FIRST ACTION USEFUL FIRST DECISION WARNING A new line is open and the sword is free Cut directly from the endpoint Do not withdraw to reload The blade is caught or the return is already coming Cover, counter-parry, disengage, or leave Do not force a second cut through control The opponent retreats but measure remains Follow with the feet and keep the cut compact Do not chase with the arms alone The opponent crashes closer or the hands collapse Create working space, cover, or separate Do not windmill from a trapped position

PARTNER EXPLORATION: In full gear at drilling intensity, make one compact cut and freeze at its endpoint. The partner gives one of the four outcomes above. Resume for one decision only, then reset. Change roles every three repetitions.

MECHANICS TO REVISIT: Crossed hands may uncross into a Zwerch-like route. Uncrossed hands may use a modest hip and torso turn to change line. Both are options, not automatic answers.

CONTACT STANDARD: In HEMA, we cut at things, not through things. Reach the target with a legible cutting plane, structure, and control, then use the endpoint instead of manufacturing extra follow-through.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:30-0:45

Meyer supports prompt movement from one opening to another. The classroom problem is deciding whether that next opening actually exists under pressure.

MEYER, 1570: As soon as you have touched, do not tarry any longer, but instead let it fly quickly away from one opening to another.

WHAT THE SOURCE SUPPORTS: After touching or making contact, the sword should not remain idle. Meyer repeatedly uses connected actions, opening-to-opening attacks, crossed-hand positions, and Zwerch actions in constrained lines.

WHAT PART II ADDS: Modern training can isolate the perception beneath that flow: Is the blade free? Did a new target appear? Is a return already arriving? Did distance expand or collapse?

HISTORICAL CLUE PART II TRAINING QUESTION Do not tarry after touching Can the fencer recognize the next decision without pausing to reset? Move from one opening to another Did the defender actually create a new opening? Zwerch and body-supported actions work in constrained lines Can the fencer change line while staying able to stop, cover, or leave?

INTERPRETIVE LIMIT: This is not evidence for a mandatory three-cut chain. Meyer provides historical direction; the game's free-or-controlled distinction and decision branches are modern coaching tools.

SOURCE NOTE: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Longsword, fol. I.55r; English translation by Rebecca L. R. Garber and transcription by Michael Chidester, via Wiktenauer.

GAME 1 | 0:45-1:05

Make the fastest useful distinction in close fencing: continue when the sword is free, and protect yourself when the opponent has gained control or begun the return.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Part I taught students to recycle an endpoint. This game prevents that useful habit from becoming an automatic second cut.

STARTING STATE: Full gear. Begin at close striking measure. The attacker makes one known compact cut to an upper opening. The defender chooses between two coached answers: a cover that leaves the attacker's blade free and another line open, or a controlling parry with an immediate measured riposte.

ATTACKER: If the blade remains free and a target appears, make one immediate compact follow-up. If the blade is controlled or the riposte begins, abandon the chain and defend, disengage, or leave.

DEFENDER: Make both answers honest but readable. A free cover should stop the first target without pretending to own the blade. A controlling parry should close the line and begin a safe return without waiting for permission.

STUDENT RULES: Maximum two attacks. A follow-up through clear control fails even if it lands. A successful defense or exit is a correct answer, not a lost attacking turn. Reset on a clean hit, double, firm control, or separation.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Use 90-second roles, then switch. Change partners after both roles. Begin with the two answers alternating, then let the defender choose freely.

COACH WATCHES: Whether the attacker reads pressure and the beginning of the riposte rather than merely noticing blade contact; whether the follow-up begins without a withdrawal; and whether stopping remains possible.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Let the defender vary the firmness and timing of contact so the distinction becomes less visually obvious.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Announce 'free' or 'controlled' after the parry and slow the exchange until the attacker's choice consistently matches the state.

GAME 2 | 1:05-1:25

Chain compact attacks only as long as the defender keeps creating a real new line and the attacker's sword remains available.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Game 1 established the stop condition. Now the defender can close successive openings, allowing the attacker to practice rapid crossed-to-uncrossed and hip-driven changes without memorizing the chain length.

STARTING STATE: Full gear. Begin at close measure. The attacker launches one credible compact cut. The defender may leave it open, cover once, or cover twice. Covers may redirect the blade but should not deliberately trap it during the first acquisition rounds.

ATTACKER: Finish immediately if the current target remains open. Change line only when an actual cover removes it. Use the endpoint already reached and stop the chain if structure, measure, or blade freedom disappears.

DEFENDER: Make each cover late enough that the preceding threat was real. Sometimes stop after zero or one cover so the attacker cannot safely perform a memorized three-action sequence.

STUDENT RULES: The attacker may change line no more than twice: three credible threats total. Every continuation must answer a defense that occurred. The phrase ends on a hit, double, clear blade control, loss of balance, or full separation.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Use 90-second roles and change partners after both roles. Give many short phrases rather than one prolonged exchange.

COACH WATCHES: A first threat that genuinely demands defense; compact travel between targets; an immediate finish when no new cover appears; and the ability to stop before the third action when the situation changes.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Allow a controlling parry or immediate counterattack at any point. The attacker must protect instead of completing the planned chain.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Use one known three-threat route for several repetitions, then restore the defender's ability to stop covering after the first or second threat.

GAME 3 | 1:25-1:40

Apply compact follow-ups inside a short live phrase where the opponent may cover, counterattack, retreat, crash closer, or establish control.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The first two games isolated blade freedom and opening recognition. This game adds the changing measure and immediate danger that determine whether rapid follow-ups survive in fencing.

STARTING STATE: Full gear. Begin just outside close striking measure. The designated attacker enters with one credible action. After it launches, both fencers may move and answer normally within the short-phrase limits.

ATTACKER: Use the first endpoint to choose one response: cut a real opening, cover the return, follow a manageable retreat, create space from a crash, or leave. Continue only while the blade, balance, and target all support it.

DEFENDER: Defend naturally. You may cover, riposte, retreat, step closer, or establish blade control. Punish blind continuation with controlled contact, but do not turn the game into prolonged wrestling.

STUDENT RULES: The designated attacker gets no more than three attacking actions. Either fencer may end the phrase sooner with a clean hit, clear control, safe separation, or a double. Reset immediately and preserve decision volume.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Use 90-second roles and rotate partners after both roles. Change starting guards and first actions so the same endpoint does not solve every phrase.

COACH WATCHES: Whether the attacker recognizes when the problem has changed from offense to defense; whether pursuit uses the feet; whether close pressure collapses the hands; and whether exits remain balanced and covered.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Remove the designated attacker and let either fencer recognize the close-measure moment, while retaining the three-attack cap.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Limit the defender to three announced possibilities: cover and open a line, controlling parry and riposte, or retreat.

OPEN SPARRING | 1:40-2:00

Return to normal fencing. The goal is not to produce more cuts; it is to make a better decision sooner when the exchange compresses.

FORMAT: Fence normal Steel Crown rounds of 3-4 minutes and rotate partners. Use ordinary scoring and intensity agreements. Give no bonus points for compact cutting or multi-hit sequences.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: When distance closes, recognize the first useful endpoint. Continue only if the blade is free, the opening is real, and the next action does not ignore an immediate return.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the first attack was credible; whether a follow-up was caused by the defender; whether the fencer notices control before striking through it; and whether retreats, crashes, and counterattacks change the decision.

FEEDBACK RHYTHM: Watch several complete phrases before intervening. Between rounds, use one short question: What told you to continue, and what told you to stop?

TRANSFER CUE: Finish. Read. Continue or protect.

OPTIONAL CLOSE: Ask each pair for one endpoint that supported a clean follow-up and one situation where abandoning the chain was clearly better.

COACH REFERENCE

Protect the lesson's real outcome: rapid decisions from compact positions, not rapid cutting for its own sake.

IF YOU SEE... TRY... Every phrase becomes three cuts Have the defender sometimes leave the first target open or gain control immediately Attacker continues through the riposte Make the return immediate and reward the counter-parry, cover, or exit as the correct solution Follow-ups require a large reload Freeze the first endpoint and find the shortest credible route before restoring speed Retreat is chased with reaching arms Require the feet to recover measure before the blade continues Hands collapse during a crash Slow the entry, preserve working space, and make separation a successful answer Students stop after every first cut Use a cooperative cover that clearly exposes the next line, then restore choice

QUESTIONS THAT PRESERVE DISCOVERY: Was the sword free or controlled? What real opening caused the next cut? Did the opponent's feet change measure? When did the exchange become defensive? Could the fencer have abandoned the chain one action sooner?

RELATION TO EARLIER LESSONS: Compound Attacks changes line because a defense is forming before blade control. Second Intention prepares for the opponent's answering action after the defense. Compact Cutting II begins from the compressed endpoint and asks which of those problems - or an exit - now exists.

RECORD AFTER CLASS: Note which endpoints survived live pressure, which cues helped students recognize control, how often follow-ups became doubles, and whether the three-action cap improved or distorted decisions.

ADAPTATIONS: Newer fencers receive named responses and fixed targets. Advanced fencers vary pressure, timing, measure, and whether the expected line appears. Odd groups use an observer who names the endpoint, opponent response, and chosen decision.

Record what remained credible under pressure, where students lost the ability to stop, and what should change before teaching the block again.

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | October 2026 | Version 1.0

docs.title: Make the next decision before the moment disappears
Read the position the first cut created
Move quickly without inventing the next opening
Compound Attacks I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW | 0:00-0:05

Students chain credible threats through one or two defensive reactions, finishing as soon as a line remains open and stopping when the defender gains control.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I chain credible attacks as defenses appear without falling into a memorized combination?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students threaten a real opening. If it remains open, they finish. If the defender commits to a parry, they evade before control and make the next opening into another credible threat. They may repeat this once more when a second real parry appears. If the defender controls the blade, distance is lost, or no safe opening remains, the attacker defends, recovers, or leaves.

THE CUE: Threaten. Read. Change. Repeat only if needed.

SUCCESS EVIDENCE

LOOK FOR OBSERVABLE STANDARD Every link threatens The first, second, and possible third action could each land if the defender stopped answering. Real information Every change follows a parry that actually begins; the attacker does not perform the full chain from memory. Compact redirection Each change clears before blade control and travels by the smallest useful path. Correct chain length The attacker finishes as soon as an opening stays open and uses no more than two changes. Clean outcome The attacker remains covered and does not accept a double as proof the attack worked.

BOUNDARY: The chain continues only while the attack remains free. Once the defender truly controls the blade, the compound attack is over and the attacker must manage the riposte.

WARM-UP | 0:05-0:20

Use the familiar plyometric block to prepare quick acceleration and controlled changes without turning the warm-up into conditioning.

SECTION MOVEMENT OPTIONS COACHING FOCUS Low-box jumps Two-foot on/off; single-foot variations; lateral on/off Quiet landings; stable knees; own the box and the floor Pogo hops Quick, low contacts in place or over a short distance Tall posture; elastic ankles; stop before rhythm gets heavy Short sprints Brief accelerations followed by slow walks back Sharp start; controlled braking; the walk is recovery

PURPOSE FOR THIS LESSON: Every link in the chain needs a real acceleration, followed by enough balance to brake and redirect again. The warm-up prepares repeated intent and recovery without rehearsing a fixed sword combination.

SUGGESTED RHYTHM: Move continuously through the three sections for about five minutes each. Keep demonstrations brief. Students select a box height and contact variation they can land quietly and repeat cleanly.

LOAD CONTROL: Stop before landings become noisy, posture collapses, or sprint speed meaningfully drops. Reduce box height, use step variations, shorten the lane, or replace jumping with controlled footwork when needed.

CLASS CUE: Spring. Brake. Redirect. Be ready again.

GAME 1 | 0:20-0:30

Build repeated finish-or-change decisions with soft gloves before adding sword speed, blade contact, or technical vocabulary.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The attacker experiences a chain as several small decisions: finish when a target stays open, or redirect when the defender truly covers it. The defender learns not to manufacture reactions for weak threats.

STARTING STATE: No swords or protective gear. Partners wear or hold soft gloves. Begin at a comfortable step-and-touch distance. The shoulders and outside of the knees are targets.

FENCER A: Make a genuine touch attempt to one target. If it stays open, finish. If B covers it, redirect to another target. If B covers again, redirect once more and finish the third threat.

FENCER B: Cover only touches that can actually arrive. After the first cover, remain active and decide whether the new target also requires a cover. Do not wave, chase A's hand, or follow a rehearsed pattern.

STUDENT RULES: A may change no more than twice. Every link must be able to touch if ignored. B does not counterattack. Reset after a touch, miss, loss of balance, early change, or third defense. No scorekeeping.

ROTATION: Use 90-second fixed roles, switch immediately, then change partner after one complete A/B cycle.

SAY TO STUDENTS: Keep asking real questions. The moment one is not answered, finish it.

GAME 2 | 0:30-0:45

Use two known parries so students can build three connected threats and feel where each change must happen before blade control.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The defensive route is temporarily known so students can develop economical changes, stable footwork, and a second and third threat that do not fade into gestures.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Agree on a three-line route, such as A threatening upper left, then upper right, then a lower opening. B attempts the matching parry against each of the first two threats.

FENCER A: Threaten the first opening with enough extension and measure to land. As B commits, clear the parry and immediately threaten the second opening. When B commits again, clear it and finish the third opening.

FENCER B: Begin from a neutral guard. Build each parry only after its threat becomes real. Make the second defensive decision from A's new attack rather than moving through two rehearsed guard positions automatically.

RULES: B does not counterattack yet. If either parry controls A's blade, pause and reset. Every threat must reach if B stops defending. Use exactly two changes for acquisition, then mirror the route. No points.

ROTATION: Use 90-second roles. Switch immediately; change partners after the A/B cycle when time allows.

SUCCESS: Three credible threats arrive as one continuous attack, each change clears before control, and the final cut needs no extra windup.

GUIDED COACHING | 0:45-0:55

Use the known chain to distinguish responsive chaining from a rehearsed combination that continues regardless of the defender.

ASK BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN: Could every threat in the chain have landed if the defender stopped moving? What actual movement caused the first change? What caused the second? Did the middle action become a real attack, or only a bridge to the planned finish? Did either change begin after the defender had already controlled the blade? When should the chain have ended earlier?

SHOW THREE CONTRASTS

EXAMPLE WHAT HAPPENS COACHING MEANING Memorized combination A performs all three cuts whether B defends or not. The sequence has replaced perception. Responsive chain Each credible threat draws a new parry; A changes only when that parry begins. Every link is both a possible finish and the start of the next decision. Parried, then continued The defender finds and controls the blade before A changes. The compound attack failed. A must manage the riposte, not force the planned finish.

FEEDBACK RHYTHM: Watch several exchanges. Name one observable event, ask what caused each continuation, give one cue, and let the next exchange test it. Correct a weak middle threat before asking for more speed.

KEY PHRASE: Threaten. Read. Change. Repeat only if another defense actually appears.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:55-1:10

Meyer's changing actions give a historical lens for threatening one opening and redirecting when the opponent moves to meet the attack.

LESSON CONNECTIONS

Compound attacks, second intention, and parry-riposte can appear in the same exchange, but they describe different jobs and different moments.

CONCEPT WHAT IT DESCRIBES IN THIS CURRICULUM Compound attack - today The attacker makes one continuous attack. Each forming parry causes a new credible threat; the chain ends when an opening stays open or after two changes. Second intention - last week The attacker expects a complete parry-riposte. The first attack may be successfully parried; the attacker reads the actual riposte, counter-parries it, and answers. Parry-riposte The defender stops or controls the incoming attack with a parry, then immediately attacks back from the position created by that defense. No feint or deception is required.

THE DECISION POINT

WHAT B DOES WHAT A SHOULD DO WHAT THE PHRASE BECOMES Does not close the first line Finish the original attack. A simple direct finish; no compound action was needed. Begins a parry but has not controlled the blade Change and make the next opening a real threat; repeat once only if another parry forms. Today's compound-attack chain. Finds and controls A's blade Stop forcing the attack; defend B's immediate answer. B now has a parry-riposte. Controls the blade, ripostes, and A was prepared for it A reads the real riposte, counter-parries, and answers. Last week's second-intention problem.

HOW THEY RELATE: Both lessons begin with a credible attack and demand quick decisions from real information. The difference is what the attacker intends to defeat. Today, A may defeat one or two parries while they are forming. In Second Intention I, A allows the parry to succeed and defeats the riposte that follows.

WHY THE DISTINCTION MATTERS: If A changes after the blade is already controlled, that is not a successful compound attack. If B merely starts moving toward the first line but never stops the blade, B has not yet earned a parry-riposte.

QUICK CUE: Before control: change and threaten again. After control: defend. If you planned for the riposte, confirm its line before answering.

GAME 3 | 1:10-1:20

The defender may answer zero, one, or two threats. The attacker must discover the correct chain length instead of completing the known route.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Students know how a three-threat chain feels. Now they must end after the first, second, or third threat according to B's actual choices.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. A begins with the same agreed first attack. B privately chooses to defend zero, one, or two credible threats.

FENCER A: Finish the current threat whenever B leaves it open. When B begins a parry, clear it and make the next opening into another attack. Continue once more only when a second parry genuinely begins.

FENCER B: Choose the chain length independently each repetition. Never announce it. Once you decide not to parry a threat, let it finish safely rather than adding a late defense.

RULES: B does not counterattack yet. A may change no more than twice. Reset after the hit, miss, unnecessary continuation, blade control, loss of balance, or a third defensive action. No points.

ROTATION: Use 90-second roles, then change partners after a complete A/B cycle. Keep resets quick so each student receives many short decisions.

COACH WATCHES: Does every link remain credible? Can A stop after any threat, or does the body keep performing the remembered three-cut route?

GAME 4 | 1:20-1:30

The attacker chooses the first line. The defender protects openings naturally and may riposte whenever a parry gains real control.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The final constrained game removes the preset route. A must choose each new opening from B's real defense while recognizing when the chain has ended.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. A may begin a controlled attack to any agreed opening. B defends naturally and may use an immediate controlled riposte after a successful parry.

FENCER A: Threaten the chosen line. Finish if it stays open. Each time B commits a parry, change to an opening that action creates and make it credible. Use no more than two changes. If B controls the blade, defend or leave.

FENCER B: Parry each threat naturally, but do not chase a blade that has already cleared. If any parry gains control, riposte immediately so A learns that the compound chain has ended.

RULES: One offensive phrase, then reset after a hit, clean separation, B's riposte, or A's second change. No extended scrambling, no simultaneous counterattack, and no points.

ROTATION: Use 90-second roles. Change partners after a complete A/B cycle so the decision is tested against different defensive habits.

LESSON TEST: Every new threat asks a real question. Stop when one is unanswered, when the blade is controlled, or after two changes.

EXAMPLES LIBRARY

The route may change, but each link must remain a possible finish and every continuation must answer a defense that actually happened.

ACTION STRUCTURE COACHING NOTE Upper - upper - lower Threaten one upper opening; clear its parry; threaten the other; clear again; finish below. Today's known-chain example. High - low - high Draw a high closure; redirect below; if B drops to defend, return to the newly opened high line. Same two-change decision with a vertical route. Thrust - disengage - return Threaten with the point; pass around the first search; threaten again; return around a second search. Same structure with thrusts. Shorter chain Begin any route, but finish after the first or second threat when the defender stops closing lines. This is correct, not incomplete.

TERMS THAT SHOULD NOT BLUR TOGETHER

TERM PLAIN-LANGUAGE DISTINCTION Simple attack One direct final action with no feint. Compound attack One continuous attack containing one or more feints, the defensive reactions they draw, and a final action. Second intention A tactical plan to provoke an expected response so a later action can defeat it; the response may include a riposte. Renewal A new offensive effort after the original attack missed, fell short, or was parried.

TODAY'S BOUNDARY: Allow no more than two changes. The goal is a responsive chain, not the longest possible combination.

OPEN SPARRING | 1:30-2:00

Students fence normally and chain compound attacks only while an opponent continues closing threatened lines without gaining blade control.

FORMAT: Use normal Steel Crown fencing, intensity agreements, and pairings. Aim for five four-minute rounds with short partner changes, then use the remaining time for gear transition and individual feedback. Adapt freely to the room.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. Make every threat real. Finish when a line stays open; change when a parry forms; repeat once only if another real parry appears."

COACH BEHAVIOR: Watch several exchanges before speaking. Give one individual adjustment between rounds. Open sparring is the transfer test, not another constrained game.

TRANSFER EVIDENCE: The fencer uses the tactic against an opponent who repeatedly commits to parries. Every threat reaches a distance and line that must be respected. Each continuation is selected from the parry that actually occurs. The chain ends immediately when an opening stays open; it never runs automatically to three actions. After two changes or real blade control, the fencer finishes, defends, recovers, or leaves.

OPTIONAL CLOSE: Ask one question if it helps: What caused each link in your longest successful chain, and where could it have ended earlier?

STEEL CROWN STANDARD: A priority rule may help classify the phrase, but a double still fails the lesson. The goal is a clean tactical solution.

SAFETY AND COACHING

Reduce speed, uncertainty, or movement volume while preserving the relationship between threat, parry, and change.

SAFETY AND ADAPTATION

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE No-gear game Light touches to shoulders and outside of knees only. No face, head, throat, hard slaps, diving, or collisions. Mixed experience Give newer students a known parry. Let experienced students vary line and timing rather than increasing impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. The observer names what caused each change and where the chain ended before rotating. Limited space or injury Shorten lanes, lower or remove jumps, reduce sword speed, or use controlled steps. Keep the decision intact.

COACH TROUBLESHOOTING

IF YOU SEE... DO THIS Empty feints Let B ignore them. Require the first line to arrive safely if no defense occurs. Memorized three-cut sequence Vary chain length. Require A to stop the instant B leaves any threat unanswered. Weak middle threat Let B ignore it. Require every link to reach and become a possible finish before adding speed. Change begins too early Delay or withhold B's parry. Ask A to name the movement that caused each change. Blade is already controlled Let B riposte. Teach A to accept the failed attack and defend instead of forcing the plan. Chain grows past two changes Reset after the second change. More actions are not useful when perception and structure decay. Doubles increase Reduce speed and defender choice. Require A to survive for the final hit to count as learning.

FEEDBACK: Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Preserve the decision even when the movement is simplified.

Record how long the chains became, whether every link remained credible, what caused each change, and where students should have stopped.

SOURCES

Meyer supplies the historical actions. Modern fencing terminology and skill-acquisition research support the contemporary class design.

FROM MEYER'S 1560s LONGSWORD MATERIAL - ENGLISH
docs.text:
"When you note that he wants to meet your oncoming strike, then jerk and cut to the other side." [1]

CHANGING: Meyer explains that this is useful against fencers who cut toward the incoming sword rather than the body. The attacker notices the attempt to meet the strike, withdraws from that meeting, and cuts to the other side. [1]

DECEIVING: In the same handwork list, Meyer describes showing an intention toward one opening and striking elsewhere. He links this to working quickly against opponents who eagerly set off or cut away attacks. [1]

WHAT THIS SUPPORTS: The source supports the lesson's core relationship: present a believable line, perceive the defender moving to close it, and redirect to the opening that movement creates. The same relationship can repeat when the new threat draws another defense.

MODERN TERMINOLOGY: Meyer does not label this a 'compound attack.' Modern fencing uses that term for an attack containing one or more feints before the final action. Modern rules also treat a blade found during a feint as a successful parry, which is why today's lesson insists on changing before control. [2]

HISTORICAL BOUNDARY: The source actions are historical; the two-change cap, soft-glove game, 90-second roles, target constraints, timing, and success tests are modern coaching design. They make repeated changing easier to perceive and practice safely.

DEMONSTRA TION: Show one threat finished immediately, one changed once, one changed twice, and one stopped because the defender gained blade control.
