docs.title: Control the Measure I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW

Students learn to move in and out of danger, test an opponent's reach, enter behind a real threat, and recover before the easy return.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I enter striking distance, create a real threat, and leave without giving my opponent an easy hit?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students stay light and balanced while probing the edge of reach; recognize how a planted opponent and an opponent with an available lunge create different danger zones; and enter and leave without surrendering a simple return.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: Meyer's account of opportunity in the Onset, Middle, and Withdrawal, supported by his instruction that the step and strike occur together and that a poor ending can undo an otherwise good exchange.

THE CUE: Harass the edge. Enter with purpose. Leave clean.

CLASS DESIGN: Start with springy movement and an unarmed glove game. Repeat the same task with swords, then expand the defender's reach through an anchored lunge. Boxing supplies a useful movement analogy; Meyer remains the historical source.

LEARNING OUTCOMES

Look for active distance control: repeated safe approaches, an intentional entry, and a recovery that denies the return.

LOOK FOR WHAT IT MEANS Active measure The mobile fencer tests the edge repeatedly and updates the safe distance from the opponent's available reach. Movement quality Small, quiet steps preserve a useful fighting shape and the ability to enter, stop, retreat, or reverse. Protected entry The glove or sword threatens as the feet close; the body does not drift into range before the action is ready. Opponent awareness The student distinguishes a defender with planted feet from one who can suddenly extend through a lunge. Clean finish After touching or discovering that the opening is gone, the student recovers without accepting the easy counter or double.

CLASS SCHEDULE

A physical warm-up leads into one repeated distance problem: first with gloves, then with swords, and finally against an opponent who can lunge.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival and frame Define changing measure and the success test Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Movement warm-up Low boxes, pogo hops, and short sprints Spring, brake, recover 0:20-0:30 Soft-glove range game Fixed defender; mobile attacker; no swords Feel the safe edge 0:30-0:45 Game 1: Fixed Base Repeat the glove game in full gear with swords Find sword measure 0:45-0:55 Guided coaching Compare the two tasks; give one intervention One useful adjustment 0:55-1:10 Meyer source study Opportunity, three phases, steps, and withdrawal Historical frame 1:10-1:30 Game 2: Anchored Lunge Defender may lunge while the rear foot stays fixed Respect expanding reach 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Normal fencing with one transfer objective Selective transfer 1:55-2:00 Gear and feedback Individual feedback; optional one-question close Next cue

IF TIME IS TIGHT: Reduce one role interval or shorten the discussion. Keep the glove game, both sword constraints, a meaningful sparring block, and a calm gear transition.

ROTATION STANDARD: Use 90-second fixed roles, then switch immediately. Change partners after a complete A/B cycle. Keep explanations short enough to preserve live repetitions.

OPENING | 0:00-0:05

Explain that measure depends on what the opponent can do, not only on the visible gap between two bodies.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Today we are going to live at the edge of somebody else's reach: move in, move out, bother them, learn what they can hit, and choose the moment to enter without handing them a free answer."

SUCCESS DEFINITION: Stay mobile and balanced, identify the opponent's real danger zone, touch when an opportunity is present, and leave before the easy return.

CLASS ARC: Prepare the feet; solve the problem with soft gloves; repeat it with swords; study Meyer; then change the defender's reach by allowing an anchored lunge.

KEY DISTINCTION: A planted opponent and an opponent who can lunge do not own the same amount of space, even if their feet start in the same place.

WARM-UP | 0:05-0:20

Use low boxes, pogo hops, and short sprints to prepare the legs and feet for repeated changes of range.

TIME WARM-UP SECTION MOVEMENT OPTIONS COACH'S JOB 0:05-0:10 Low-box jumps Two-foot on/off; single-foot variations; lateral on/off Use stable low boxes; demand quiet, balanced landings 0:10-0:15 Pogo hops Short, springy hops in place or over a small distance Keep contacts quick, posture tall, and volume controlled 0:15-0:20 Short sprints Short accelerations followed by slow walks back Use room-length lanes; stop before form or braking breaks down

BOX VARIATIONS: Use both-feet jumps on and off, single-foot variations when appropriate, and lateral movements on or across the box. Keep the box low enough for clean, confident landings.

POGO GUIDANCE: Use short sets of quick, low hops. Keep the torso organized, the contacts light, and the movement springy rather than deep or exhausting.

SPRINT GUIDANCE: Accelerate over a short lane, decelerate under control, and walk slowly back before the next effort. The walk is recovery, not another conditioning interval.

LOAD CONTROL: Stop before landings become noisy, posture breaks down, or speed drops. Step down or use lower-impact variations when ankles, knees, fatigue, or experience call for it. [5-6]

GLOVE RANGE GAME | 0:20-0:30

Introduce the tactical problem with soft gloves before adding equipment, blade length, or additional rules.

STARTING STATE: No protective gear and no swords. Fencer A adopts a fighting stance and keeps both feet planted. Fencer B faces A in a straight lane. Each holds or wears one soft glove.

FENCER A: Protect the space from the fixed stance. Tag B lightly when B enters reachable distance, but do not step, lunge, or slide either foot.

FENCER B: Move forward and backward as often as needed. Probe, change rhythm, draw a reaction, and touch A without receiving the immediate return.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Get close enough to bother them, leave before they can punish you, and touch when the opening is real."

ROTATION: 90 seconds as the planted fencer, 90 seconds as the moving fencer, then change partner after a full A/B cycle.

COACH WATCHES: Whether B stays light and balanced; whether the motion changes distance instead of traveling straight upward; how A's glove defines the edge; and whether B exits after the touch.

NO-GEAR SAFETY: Use light glove taps to an agreed arm, shoulder, or torso target only. No face, head, throat, hard swings, collisions, or competitive scorekeeping.

GAME 1 | 0:30-0:45

Repeat the glove game in full gear so students discover how blade length, guard, and recovery change the moving edge.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The learner already understands the relationship. Adding swords changes the reach and consequences without changing the basic problem.

STARTING STATE: Both fencers wear full protective equipment and use swords. Fencer A takes a fighting stance and keeps both feet planted. Fencer B moves only forward and backward in the lane.

FENCER A: Protect the space and answer with controlled sword actions from the planted stance. Adjust the guard or blade as needed, but do not step or lunge.

FENCER B: Move in and out, test the guard, apply credible pressure, and enter only when the sword can threaten or protect. Leave before A can land the immediate return.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "It is the glove game with a sword: bother the edge, enter behind your blade, and get back out clean."

RULES AND ROTATION: Linear movement for B; both of A's feet stay fixed. Use controlled contact, no points, and 90-second roles. Reset after a touch, double, or clearly unsafe entry.

COACH QUESTION: What changed when the defender's glove became a sword? Do not answer for the students until they have felt the difference.

GUIDED COACHING | 0:45-0:55

Use the room's own exchanges to identify effective probing, compact footwork, protected entry, and responsible recovery.

COACH TROUBLESHOOTING

The most useful intervention changes what the student can perceive without turning the exercise into a scripted technique.

IF YOU SEE... DO THIS The mobile fencer bounces straight up Lower the bounce and shorten the steps. Ask for quiet feet and a stance that can reverse direction immediately. The mobile fencer reaches from too far Let the fixed fencer punish the reach with one controlled touch. Re-test with feet and glove or sword arriving together. The fixed fencer becomes a dead target Remind Fencer A to protect the space and answer credible entries while obeying the foot constraint. Students rush after one probe Allow several in-and-out passes before committing. Success is a useful entry and clean exit, not maximum attempts. The lunge catches everyone by surprise Slow Fencer A's lunge and make the starting shape readable. Ask what changed in hips, shoulders, lead foot, or reach. The rear foot slides off its mark Use a visible tape spot and reset immediately. Shorten the lunge until the rear foot and recovery stay controlled. Box jumps become a conditioning test Reduce box height, contacts, or speed. Step down, recover, and keep the warm-up sharp rather than exhausting.

CLASS STANDARD: Use one adjustment at a time: quieter feet, a clearer threat, a shorter step, or a cleaner exit. Let the partner's response show whether it helped.

OBSERVATION AND FEEDBACK

Use these cues to recognize improvement from the glove game to the anchored lunge and open sparring.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Rhythm Small, quiet changes of pace and direction Large vertical hops or predictable bouncing Perception Tests reach and notices the opponent's available action Treats safety as one fixed distance Shape Keeps a usable stance while moving in and out Crosses feet, stands tall, or loses balance Entry Glove or sword threatens as the feet close Body or face arrives before the threat Reaction Reads the planted reach or anchored lunge Commits before seeing the counter Exit Leaves under control or a protective sword Admires the touch and accepts the return Transfer Probes selectively during ordinary fencing Bounces constantly or forces every entry

GAME CARD 1

Learn to harass and measure the edge before adding swords or protective equipment.

STARTING STATE: No gear or swords. Fencer A stands in fighting stance with both feet planted; Fencer B moves linearly. Each has a soft glove.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Get close enough to bother them, touch when it is there, and leave before they can answer."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role. Switch immediately and change partner after a full A/B cycle.

COACH WATCHES: Light below-neck touches; purposeful in-and-out footwork; stance quality; changing rhythm; and the exit after contact.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Let the planted fencer vary glove height, timing, and stance while keeping both feet fixed.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Slow both fencers, choose a clear arm or shoulder target, and allow wider starting distance.

GAME CARD 2

Repeat the glove-distance problem with blade length, guard, full equipment, and real recovery demands.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Fencer A keeps both feet planted in fighting stance; Fencer B moves forward and backward in a lane.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Bother the edge, enter behind your blade, and get back out clean."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role; switch immediately; reset after a touch, double, or unsafe entry.

COACH WATCHES: Whether the sword changes the edge; whether the body arrives first; whether A remains live; and whether B can leave under cover.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Allow A to vary guard and timing while both feet remain planted.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Return to soft gloves or require one clear, controlled sword action before the reset.

GAME CARD 3

Teach the moving fencer to respect the extra distance created by a defender's available lunge.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Fencer A's rear foot stays on a tape mark; the lead foot may lunge. Fencer B moves linearly.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Find the new edge, make them show it, and get in and out clean."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role. Change partner after a full A/B cycle and reset if the rear foot leaves its mark.

COACH WATCHES: Lunge cues, expanded reach, controlled recoveries, rear-foot discipline, protected entry, and the immediate return.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Let A vary lunge timing and depth while preserving rear-foot contact and safe control.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Slow the lunge, shorten its depth, or return to the fully planted defender.

SOURCES

Meyer provides the historical material. Boxing and strength-and-conditioning references inform the modern movement and coaching choices.

[1] Meyer, Joachim. Gründtliche Beschreibung der freyen Ritterlichen unnd Adelichen kunst des Fechtens (1570), Longsword Book, Chapters 6-8: Withdrawal, Steps, and Before/After/Simultaneous/Indes. 1570 transcription and translation

[2] Meyer, Joachim. The Art of Combat, 2nd ed., translated by Jeffrey L. Forgeng. Frontline Books, 2015.

[3] England Boxing. Shadow Boxing Drills - Week Five: range, shape, tempo, balance, in-and-out movement, and defense after the attack. England Boxing coaching drills

[4] England Boxing. Shadow Boxing Drills - Week Eight: lead-hand range control, footwork, and occupying an opponent with credible actions. England Boxing range-control drills

[5] National Strength and Conditioning Association. Plyometric Exercises, excerpt from Developing Power: purposeful, low-volume jumping and stretch-shortening work. NSCA plyometric guidance

[6] National Strength and Conditioning Association. Agility and Quickness Test: Box Step-Off Landing Assessment: controlled landing, stability, and athlete readiness. NSCA landing assessment

[7] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araujo. 'Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport.' Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33 (2011): 146-155. DOI

[8] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. 'A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play.' Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24 (2019): 103- 116. DOI

docs.title: Control the Measure I
docs.text:
How can I enter striking distance, create a real threat, and leave without giving my opponent an easy hit?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | August 2026 | Version 3.0

docs.title: Own the moving edge of measure
The lesson spine
docs.text:
QUESTION: How close can I get while remaining able to hit and leave?

EVIDENCE: I can test the edge more than once, recognize what the defender can reach, enter without overcommitting, and recover safely.

COMMON NON-EXAMPLE: I bounced without purpose, leaned into range, or treated a stationary opponent's current reach as their only possible reach.

docs.title: Build spring, acceleration, and controlled recovery
Fixed Base - the same problem with swords
Connect the glove game to sword measure
Ask before you explain
docs.text:
• What told you the planted fencer could reach you?
  • How did the edge change when the glove became a sword?
  • Which movements let you reverse direction without standing up or crossing your feet?
  • What happened when your body entered before your blade?
  • Did the touch still count as a good solution if you could not get out?

SAFETY AND ADAPTATION

Keep contact, movement volume, uncertainty, and floor conditions appropriate to the people in the room.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE No-gear glove game Use soft gloves and light touches to agreed below-neck targets. Stop face contact, hard swings, collisions, or chasing. Jumping or sprint limitations Lower the box, step up or down, reduce pogo contacts, shorten the sprint, or substitute brisk controlled steps. First-time or overwhelmed student Start with a slower planted partner and a clear reachable target; count a safe entry and exit as success. Mixed experience Vary defender timing, rhythm, and lunge depth rather than raising impact or removing protective equipment. Odd attendance Use planted/anchored defender, moving attacker, and observer. The observer identifies the safe edge before rotating. Limited space Set short, non-slip linear lanes; keep boxes stable; prevent passing; and use floor tape rather than a physical wall. Game breaks down Return to soft gloves or the planted-foot version, reduce speed, and restore one clear success condition.

docs.title: Show three useful contrasts
docs.text:
OPEN SPARRING | 1:30-1:55

Students fence normally and use active range testing when it helps them find or deny a real opportunity.

FORMAT: Five four-minute rounds with short rotation and water breaks. Use normal Steel Crown intensity agreements and pair by compatible control and size.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. Test the edge, notice what your opponent can reach, and enter or leave while you still control your feet."

COACH BEHAVIOR: Watch several exchanges before speaking. Give one individual adjustment between rounds rather than a checklist the fencer must carry during the exchange.

TRANSFER EVIDENCE: A student moves into and out of measure with purpose, notices the difference between current reach and possible reach, and denies the easy immediate return.

FINISH | 1:55-2:00: Use the final minutes for gear transition and individual feedback. If a whole-group close helps, ask: 'What told you their real reach was longer than you first thought?'

docs.title: 1. EMPTY BOUNCE
docs.text:
The feet move, but the rhythm is predictable or the body travels upward instead of changing the usable distance.

BOXING COACHING LENS

England Boxing coaching materials use in-and-out movement, range control, balance, lead-hand occupation, and defense after the attack. Those ideas transfer cleanly to this fencing problem. [3-4]

IN AND OUT: The moving fencer repeatedly approaches and exits the edge instead of making one long, hopeful commitment.

MAINTAIN SHAPE: The feet remain under a usable fighting stance. The fencer can stop, reverse, defend, or enter without crossing the feet or standing upright.

OCCUPY THE OPPONENT: Presence, rhythm, glove threat, or sword position keeps the defender solving a problem while the moving fencer gathers information.

DRAW THE ANSWER: A small approach can reveal the defender's reach or trigger the anchored lunge. The reaction changes the next decision.

DEFEND AFTER THE TOUCH: Landing is not the finish. The same movement that creates the entry must also support an exit or protective recovery.

TRANSFER BOUNDARY: Do not copy boxing head movement, punching posture, or a boxing guard into sword range. The transferable idea is control of space, timing, balance, and the immediate return.

docs.title: 2. BODY-FIRST REACH
docs.text:
The head, hands, or torso drift into range before the glove or sword presents a problem. The planted fencer can answer easily.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:55-1:10

Meyer places timing and opportunity in the approach, the handwork, and the withdrawal - not only in the moment of the first hit.

MEYER TACTICAL MODEL

Use Meyer's discussion of steps and withdrawal to interpret what students experienced at the moving edge of measure.

ONSET / APPROACH: Recognize an opportunity to come to the opponent. Do not cross merely because a familiar distance appears; cross when the action, timing, and opponent make the entry workable.

MIDDLE / HANDWORK: Once contact or pressure exists, continue only while the relationship remains favorable. The next action is selected from the bind, opening, movement, or threat that actually appears.

WITHDRAWAL: The exchange is not complete at the first touch. Recover before the opponent, after them, or with them, but do not remain available for a simple return.

GAME 2 | 1:10-1:30

Keep the original game intact while giving the fixed fencer one new option: a controlled lunge with the rear foot anchored.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Place a visible tape mark or floor spot under Fencer A's rear foot. Fencer B moves forward and backward in the same straight lane.

FENCER A: Protect the space and may now lunge with the front foot, provided the rear foot remains planted on its marked spot. Recover under control before attempting another action.

FENCER B: Probe the edge, invite or read the lunge, and adjust the safe distance before committing. Enter only when the available threat and recovery support it.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Their feet start in the same place, but their reach is bigger now. Find the new edge, make them show it, and get in and out clean."

RULES: A's rear foot cannot lift, slide, or hop off the mark. B stays in the linear lane. Use controlled lunges, normal safety equipment, no scorekeeping, and a clean reset after each exchange.

ROTATION: 90 seconds as the anchored fencer, 90 seconds as the moving fencer, then change partner after the A/B cycle.

COACH WATCHES: Whether B recognizes the expanded danger zone; whether A telegraphs through hips, shoulders, or front-foot pressure; whether both recover their shape; and whether the rear foot stays fixed.

SAFETY DETAIL: Use a tape spot or floor marker, not an actual wall. A wall behind a lunging fencer can interfere with recovery and create a collision risk.

docs.title: 3. USEFUL HARASSMENT
docs.text:
Small steps test the edge; rhythm changes make the defender react; the entry arrives behind the glove or sword; the feet immediately recover.

ONE CUE FOR THE RE-TEST: Harass the edge. Enter with purpose. Leave clean.

docs.title: Chapter 8 - English rendering for this lesson
docs.text:
TIMING: Because the opponent may know the same instruction and meet everything you do, you must know what opportunity lets you approach. Experience shows how much depends on opportunity in fencing: no device, however good, is useful unless applied at the proper time.

ORIGINAL GERMAN: Dieweil aber dein gegenpart gleichfals disen bericht haben mag ... so ist von nöten das du zuvor wissest mit was gelegenheit du ime zukommen mögest ... kein stuck es sey wie gut es immer wölle, wol mag nützlich gefochten werden, wo es nit angewendet wirt zu gelgner zeit.

THE THREE PARTS: Therefore attend in all three parts of every device: in the approach or attack, in the middle or handwork, and afterward in the withdrawal - and within them to the Before, Simultaneous, After, and Indes.

ORIGINAL GERMAN: So hab nun derwegen acht in allen dreyen theilen eines jeden stucks, nemlich im zufechten oder angreiffen, im mittel oder handtarbeit, und hernach volgendt im abziehen auff das Vor, Gleich, Nach, und Indes.

SOURCE NOTE: The English above is our classroom rendering of Meyer's 1570 German, I.24v, Chapter 8, shown beside the original to keep historical text distinct from modern lesson language. [1]

docs.title: Enter, work, and leave as one complete action
Two supporting passages - English renderings
docs.text:
STEP + STRIKE: Each strike must have its own step, and the step should happen with the strike. A step made too early or too late ruins the device and brings the cut to nothing.

ORIGINAL GERMAN: Derwegen ein jeder streich sein eigen Trit muß haben, welcher zugleich mit dem streich soll geschehen, ... Trittestu zu frü oder zu spat, so ist es umb dein stuck geschehen.

THE EXIT: Attack and safe handwork are not enough unless a good withdrawal is made as the third action; a bad ending can undo what was previously done well.

ORIGINAL GERMAN: Dieweil aber solches nit gnug wo nit zum dritten ein guter abzug gemacht wirt ... ein böses endt alles, so zuvor wol und gut gemacht, zu nicht machen und verderben.

MODERN COACHING LABEL: Outside / edge / inside is a modern teaching shorthand, not Meyer's terminology. The historical claim is the need to recognize opportunity and complete the whole fencing action. [1]

docs.title: Anchored Lunge - the edge gets longer
Borrow the movement problem, not the boxing technique
Transfer the moving edge to ordinary fencing
Adjust the task without losing the distance problem
Correct the pattern, then return to the game
What to watch during live fencing
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what the fencer noticed, offer one change, and let the next exchange test it.

CLASS-LEVEL SUCCESS EVIDENCE: Movement becomes quieter and more purposeful; entries arrive behind the glove or sword; students adjust when the defender gains a lunge; and clean exits appear in open fencing.

docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW

Students learn to make an opponent answer a credible first action, read the response, and choose the next action from the information they receive.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I make an opponent reveal or commit to a response before I risk my decisive attack?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students make a first action that could land if ignored, notice the opponent's actual response, and either take the opening, continue safely, or recover without forcing a pre-planned second action.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: Meyer's Provoker, Taker, and Hitter framework: an action can draw an opponent out of advantage, manage the response that arrives, and exploit the opening the response creates.

THE CUE: Make them answer. Then follow the answer.

DESIGN CHOICE: The cognitive load stays low in the room: one problem, one cue, and one or two rules at a time. The plan itself stays detailed so the coach can recognize what is happening and decide what to change.

LEARNING OUTCOMES

Look for a clear relationship between the first action, the opponent's response, and the fencer's next choice.

LOOK FOR WHAT IT MEANS Honest first action The first action could touch safely if the opponent ignores it; it is not a gesture made from too far away. Attention The student sees a real response before choosing the continuation. Flexible choice The student takes, continues, recovers, or leaves based on what appeared - not a memorized second target. Survival The student stays able to cover or abort; a double is feedback that the solution was not yet safe.

CLASS SCHEDULE

The class moves from preparation and guided discovery to historical study, progressive games, and open sparring.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival and frame Define an honest threat and the success test Clear problem 0:05-0:15 Warm-up General, fencing-specific, then partnered preparation Ready to enter and recover 0:15-0:35 Game 1: Make Me Answer Honest first action; natural response; fast roles Experience the problem 0:35-0:50 Guided coaching Use the room's evidence; give one intervention One useful adjustment 0:50-1:05 Meyer source study Source text, tactical gloss, and three demonstrations Historical frame 1:05-1:30 Progressive games Three Honest Answers, then Provoke From the Onset Read and choose 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Normal fencing with one transfer objective Selective transfer 1:55-2:00 Gear and feedback Individual feedback; optional one-question close Next cue

IF TIME IS TIGHT: Shorten the historical discussion or one progressive-game role interval. Preserve the warm-up, a freer game, open sparring, and an unhurried gear transition.

ROTATION STANDARD: Use a clear 90-second timer whenever roles are fixed. Switch immediately, then change partner after a complete A/B cycle. Nobody should wait four minutes to experience the other side of the problem.

OPENING | 0:00-0:05

Frame the central question and give students a clear picture of the behavior they will explore.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Tonight, your first action is allowed to be the thing that makes the next action possible. Make it real enough that they have to answer it - then let their answer tell you what comes next."

SUCCESS DEFINITION: The first action is credible. The second choice follows evidence. The fencer can still cover, leave, or recover if the answer is not the one they expected.

CLASS ARC: Experience the problem; compare what happened; study a historical model; add choice; then test the behavior in ordinary fencing.

DO NOT: Teach the complete historical model before Game 1. Students should first possess the problem that the source helps explain.

WARM-UP | 0:05-0:15

Use a short progression from general movement to fencing-specific and partnered preparation.

TIME WARM-UP SECTION PURPOSE COACH'S JOB 0:05-0:08 General movement Raise temperature; mobilize; find relaxed balance Choose movements that fit the room and the day 0:08-0:12 Fencing preparation Footwork, cuts, and recoveries at solo range Keep it familiar and light; do not introduce the lesson yet 0:12-0:15 Partnered preparation Find measure; make a controlled threat; recover Check control, distance, and equipment before Game 1

WARM-UP GUIDANCE: Use familiar movements and choose them for the actual room: available space, temperature, attendance, injuries, and the day's training load. Keep the volume low enough that everyone arrives fresh for the fencing.

TODAY, LISTEN FOR: Can each person enter, stop, cover, and leave in balance? Are masks, gloves, distance, and partner control ready before the first game?

Instructor preparation: Choose the warm-up before class using the guidance above.

GAME 1 | 0:15-0:35

Explore the difference between a credible provocation and movement the opponent can ignore.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Before students learn labels or combinations, they need to feel when an action actually changes the opponent's options. The responder is allowed to act naturally so the information stays real.

STARTING STATE: Both begin just outside measure. One fencer is the provoker; the other responds naturally. Begin slowly enough that both can make a clean choice.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Make one action that could touch if I ignored it. Then fence what actually happens. If there is no opening, you are allowed to recover."

RULES: The first action must be capable of landing safely if ignored. After that, both fence the actual exchange. There is no point system, bonus target, or required second hit.

ROTATION: 90 seconds as provoker, 90 seconds as responder, then change partner after one complete A/B cycle. Repeat until the coach has seen enough examples. Keep the changes quick.

COACH WATCHES: Threats from too far away; a second action chosen before evidence; oversized first actions; unsafe pursuit; and useful small cues being missed - head tilt, guard lift, shoulder turn, weight shift, a step, or stillness.

IMPORTANT: Small movement is information, not an automatic target. Continue only when it produces a usable opening.

GUIDED COACHING | 0:35-0:50

Use evidence from the first game to help students distinguish an empty gesture, an honest threat, and an unexpected answer.

SOURCES

Meyer's texts provide the historical foundation; the class structure and coaching methods are modern instructional choices.

[1] Meyer, Joachim. Gründtliche Beschreibung der freyen Ritterlichen unnd Adelichen kunst des Fechtens (1570), Dusack Book, Chapter 6, especially the statement that the first, second, or third cut can be a Reitzer, Nemer, or Treffer. Transcription and translation hosted by Wiktenauer. 1570 text and transcription

[2] Meyer, Joachim. Lund manuscript (1560s), 2.7, on the Provoker, Taker, and Hitter. This related long- sword passage gives the fuller explanation used in the source-study section. Transcription and translation hosted by Wiktenauer. manuscript comparison

[3] Meyer, Joachim. The Art of Combat, 2nd ed., trans. Jeffrey L. Forgeng. Frontline Books, 2015.

[4] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araujo. 'Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport.' Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33, no. 1 (2011): 146-155. doi:10.1123/jsep.33.1.146. DOI

[5] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. 'A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play.' Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24, no. 2 (2019): 103-116. doi:10.1080/17408989.2018.1552676. DOI

docs.title: Create Commitment I
docs.text:
How can I make an opponent reveal or commit to a response before I risk my decisive attack?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | August 2026 | Version 2.2

docs.title: Create commitment through an honest threat
The lesson spine
docs.text:
QUESTION: What did your first action make them do?

EVIDENCE: I can describe the response before I claim the continuation was available.

COMMON NON-EXAMPLE: I planned a second hit, noticed a small movement, and chased it even though it did not create access.

WHAT THIS IS NOT: Not a requirement to feint every exchange, not a fixed two-hit combination, and not a contest to track points while the action is new.

docs.title: Prepare to enter, threaten, and recover
Name the response and re-test the action
Ask before you explain
docs.text:
• What did they have to do because of your first action?
  • What did you actually see before you chose the next action?
  • What happened when they did not give the response you expected?

GAME CARD 3

Make provocation compete with direct attack and safe disengagement in a freer context.

STARTING STATE: Free onset from outside measure. Either fencer may choose to attack directly, provoke, or leave.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Fence normally. If you provoke, make it honest and let their response choose your continuation."

DOSE AND ROTATION: Three-minute rounds, then change partner. Coach between rounds rather than after every exchange.

COACH WATCHES: Selective use, credibility, reading, safe abortion, and whether opponent adaptation changes the choice.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Remove the designated initiator and allow either fencer to begin when the room is ready.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Return to a fixed initial threat and two defender choices.

docs.title: Show three outcomes
docs.text:
GAME CARD 2

Force the attacker to read rather than assume the opponent's reaction.

STARTING STATE: The defender privately chooses hold, parry/cover, or withdrawal before the exchange. The attacker begins outside measure.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Make them answer. Before you continue, know which answer they gave you."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role; then change partner. Keep speed controlled until the response is readable.

COACH WATCHES: Whether the attacker waits for evidence, whether the first action remains safe, and whether recovery is accepted as a valid choice.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Let the defender choose during the exchange or offer a smaller partial response.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Use only hold or full parry. Increase distance and slow the action.

docs.title: 1. EMPTY GESTURE
docs.text:
The opponent can hold position because it could not reach. No information was created.

OBSERVATION AND FEEDBACK

Use these cues to recognize progress, diagnose common failures, and give focused feedback between rounds.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Credibility First action can land and demands respect Decorative movement outside measure Perception Waits for and names the response Second action begins before information Structure Can take, cover, or abort Fake leaves hands or body exposed Choice Target follows created opening Always attacks the same second target Timing Redirects during the opponent's response Pauses after a successful provocation Transfer Uses provocation selectively Tries to feint every exchange

GAME CARD 1

Expose the difference between a credible provocation and an empty feint.

STARTING STATE: Both begin just outside measure. One is the provoker; the other responds naturally.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Make one action that could touch if I ignored it. Then fence what actually happens. If there is no opening, recover."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role. Switch roles immediately; change partner after a complete A/B cycle.

COACH WATCHES: Distance, credibility, pre-selected second targets, unsafe pursuit, and missed information.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Allow the responder to give smaller or more varied responses while the attacker remains responsible for proving that an opening exists.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Use a known opening and one or two clear defender responses. Slow the exchange.

docs.title: 2. HONEST THREAT
docs.text:
The opponent must parry, shift, withdraw, or counter. Now there is something to read.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:50-1:05

Read Meyer's language in context and connect the three tactical functions to the fencing problem students have experienced.

COACH TROUBLESHOOTING

Use the pattern you observe to choose one practical adjustment, then return students to the task.

IF YOU SEE... DO THIS Students freeze or overthink Return to one honest threat and two defender answers. Ask only: 'What did they do?' Students pre-plan the second hit Have the defender change response more clearly. The attacker may recover instead of forcing a finish. The first action is decorative Increase distance clarity; make the defender ignore it until it could genuinely land. Students chase tiny motions Remind them: a head tilt or guard shift is information, not an automatic target. Continue only if it creates usable access. The room is overloaded Remove a rule, remove a choice, and remove all scorekeeping. Keep the opponent and the honest threat.

CLASS STANDARD: For new material, do not combine a new action, several rules, and scorekeeping. Keep the opponent information real, then add complexity only after students can attend to it.

docs.title: 3. DIFFERENT ANSWER
docs.text:
The opponent answers in an unexpected way. The attacker covers, recovers, or leaves rather than forcing a planned finish.

ONE CUE FOR THE RE-TEST: Make them answer. Then follow the answer.

FEEDBACK RHYTHM: Observe a few exchanges -> name what happened -> ask what they saw -> give one cue -> let the next round test it.

docs.title: Directly from the 1570 print
docs.text:
ENGLISH - DUSACK 6: ...sometimes the first, now the second, then the third becomes a Provoker, Taker, or Hitter.

ORIGINAL GERMAN: ...das bißweilen der erst, jetzt der ander, dann der dritt ein Reitzer, Nemer, oder Treffer wirdt.

COACHING INTERPRETATION: The first, second, or third cut can serve as the Provoker, Taker, or Hitter. Meyer is marking a cut's job in the exchange, not assigning it a permanent place in a three-beat sequence. [1]

MEYER TACTICAL MODEL

Use the historical text to sharpen attention to the opponent and clarify the tactical purpose of each action.

PROVOKER: A credible action that changes the opponent's situation. It may be a cut, threat, invitation, or pressure, but it must be real enough that ignoring it has a consequence.

TAKER: The work that manages the response that comes back: take it away, close it, redirect it, or otherwise keep it from deciding the exchange against you.

HITTER: The action to the opening that the exchange actually produced. It is not owed to the fencer; if the opening did not appear, recover or leave.

PROGRESSIVE GAMES | 1:05-1:30

The next two games add response variety and freer initiative while keeping the tactical problem clear.

SAFETY AND ADAPTATION

Use these options to match uncertainty, speed, distance, and impact to the needs of the room.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE First-time or overwhelmed student Use a known attack or response, longer preparation time, controlled partner, and safe recovery as success. Mixed experience Give newer fencers less uncertainty; give experienced fencers more timing or rhythm variation, not greater impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. Observer names the first action and response, then roles rotate. Limited space Use narrow lanes; prohibit passing and large leaps; emphasize compact footwork and controlled stops. Injury or low-impact day Replace bounds with steps; reduce speed and contact; permit limited-role or observation participation. Game breaks down Remove one variable, increase distance, slow the action, or return to a known starting state. Time loss Compress explanation and one role interval; preserve open transfer and a calm finish.

docs.title: Related long-sword explanation
docs.text:
ENGLISH - LUND 2.7: ...not because you desire to hit, but rather provoke him to strike out from his position of advantage...

ORIGINAL GERMAN: ...nit das du begerst zutreffenn, sonder ihn reitzest, auß seinem vortheil zuschlagen...

COACHING INTERPRETATION: Enter with a high or low cut not simply to hit, but to draw the opponent out of advantage into a counteraction. Take that incoming action away; the taking can expose them; then strike the opening. [2]

TERMINOLOGY NOTE: The original terms are Reitzer, Nemer, and Treffer. This plan uses the common English labels Provoker, Taker, and Hitter. Translations and spellings vary by edition.

docs.title: Three demonstration cases
docs.text:
DIRECT ATTACK IS THERE: Hit directly. Do not manufacture a provocation when the line is already open.

OPPONENT DEFENDS HARD: Give an honest high threat. If they rise or turn to defend, manage their blade or movement and take the line they created.

OPPONENT EXITS OR COUNTERATTACKS: Do not force the Hitter. Cover, recover, or leave. The exchange still gave you valid information.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Threaten them with a real action. Let their defense make your next choice clearer. If it does not, leave safely and try again later."

docs.title: Read the answer and choose the continuation
Game 2 - Three Honest Answers | 12 minutes
docs.text:
WHY THIS GAME NOW: The attacker must read a real answer instead of assuming every threat earns the same continuation.

SETUP: The defender privately chooses to hold, parry/cover, or withdraw. The attacker begins outside measure with one credible high-line threat.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Make them answer. Then tell me which answer you saw before you take, continue, or recover."

RULES: One honest threat. One defender answer. One honest continuation or recovery. Reset. No announced answer and no points.

ROTATION: 90 seconds each role; then change partner. Increase speed only when both fencers can identify the response without guessing.

OPEN SPARRING | 1:30-1:55

Students fence freely and use provocation selectively when it helps them create and recognize an opening.

FORMAT: Five four-minute rounds with short rotation and water breaks. Use normal Steel Crown intensity agreements and pair by compatible control and size.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. When the direct attack is uncertain, make them answer; then follow the answer. If they give you nothing, do not invent an opening."

COACH BEHAVIOR: Watch several exchanges before speaking. Give individual feedback between rounds, not a checklist students must carry while fencing.

TRANSFER EVIDENCE: A student uses provocation selectively, sees the answer before continuing, and can decline the continuation when the exchange is no longer safe.

FINISH | 1:55-2:00: No formal reflection is required. Use the time for gear transition and individual feedback. If a whole-group close helps, ask only: 'What did you see that changed your choice?'

docs.title: Game 3 - Provoke From the Onset | 13 minutes
docs.text:
WHY THIS GAME NOW: Provocation now competes with direct attack and safe disengagement. It should become a useful option, not a behavior students force every exchange.

SETUP AND RULE: Free onset from outside measure. Either fencer may attack directly, provoke, or leave. If someone chooses a provocation, its first action must be honest and the continuation must follow the opponent's actual response.

ROTATION: Three-minute rounds; then switch partners. Save feedback for the breaks unless an immediate safety correction is necessary.

docs.title: Transfer the behavior to ordinary fencing
Adjust difficulty while preserving the problem
Adjust the task when learning stalls
What to watch during live fencing
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what information the student perceived, offer one change, and let the next round test it.

CLASS-LEVEL SUCCESS EVIDENCE: Cleaner solutions and fewer doubles from Game 1 to Game 3; students can name a reliable cue; and the target behavior appears selectively in open fencing.

docs.title: Decisive Action I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MODERN PERFORMANCE LESSON

A decision lesson that helps students make timely, trained choices against a live opponent. It does not ask them to react randomly or to chase an imaginary perfect answer.

Doing Something Is Better Than Nothing

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I recognize a meaningful cue, choose from a small prepared menu, and act before the window closes?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students identify a real invitation to act, commit to one safe prepared answer without waiting for complete certainty, then recover or exit rather than freezing or flailing.

PRIMARY COACHING IDEA: Fast decisions are not random decisions. Strong fencers pick up useful information sooner, narrow the menu, and act from a practiced answer.

SOURCE NOTE: Deliberately modern. Pair it with the current technical curriculum rather than attaching a historical source where one does not belong.

SAFETY BOUNDARY: A decision must remain controlled, structurally sound, and appropriate to the partner. Panic swings, reckless entries, and continuing after a clear failure are not successes.

The useful evidence is about choice load, sport-specific information, and transfer. It does not show that a faster first motion or more technical options will solve the problem.

docs.title: Decisive Action I
docs.text:
How can I see a real opening, choose a safe plausible answer, and commit before I lose the moment searching for certainty?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | July 2026 | Version 1.2

docs.title: What the fencing evidence actually supports
Study 1 - choice load in quasi-realistic fencing
docs.text:
Milic and colleagues compared 10 beginners with 10 experienced national-team fencers. Participants saw fencing-specific video stimuli and made simple, two-choice, or four-choice offensive/defensive responses. Reaction time rose as the number of stimulus-response alternatives rose. Across conditions, beginners were 25.5% to 34.8% slower; their reaction-time increase as options grew was also steeper (35.2% to 55.2%).

WHAT THE STUDY TESTED WHAT IT FOUND WHAT THIS CLASS BORROWS One known response; then 2 and 4 possible response alternatives. 4-choice > 2-choice > simple; beginners were slower in every condition. Start with two practiced answers. Vary timing and distance before adding techniques.

Study result summarized above: Milic et al. (2020), Figure 3 and Figure 4.

Keep the claim human and precise. The point is not to make students think less; it is to give thinking a fast, usable structure.

docs.title: Study 2 - transfer, not trick performance
docs.text:
A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies (45 effect sizes) found perceptual-cognitive training improved controlled laboratory tasks more strongly than real-game performance: ES = 1.51 in the laboratory and ES = 0.65 in real play. The transfer effect was still positive, but materially smaller.

THE TAKEAWAY: Clean drills are the start of the lesson, not proof that the skill transferred. Restore real information quickly: a moving opponent, genuine measure, variable timing, and a consequence for waiting.

docs.title: The conversation to have before fencing
1. Normalize the problem
docs.text: In a zero-sum bout, both people are trying to act before the other does. Freezing while searching for the perfect answer is a normal combat-sport problem, not evidence that someone lacks courage or talent.

docs.title: 2. Define the goal
docs.text: We are not trying to make you swing faster. We are trying to help you recognize a real cue, choose a practiced answer, and commit while the action is still available.

docs.title: 3. Give the rule
docs.text:
When you see a real cue, choose one safe, plausible response from the menu. A technically acceptable answer on time is worth more than a perfect plan that arrives after the exchange is over.

E | BLOCK 1 | 0:10-0:20

Before anyone chooses a fencing action, their feet must be free to move. This block does not teach the two sword answers yet. It teaches the simpler habit underneath them: wait for something real, then move with balance.

THE POINT IN PLAIN ENGLISH: Do not decide while nothing is happening. Stay balanced until your partner actually changes the distance. If they take space toward you, leave or make room. If they give space away, take space under control. The exact sword actions come in the next block.

H | BLOCK 5 | 1:10-1:30

Increase one variable at a time. If quality collapses, return to the last version that still looked like fencing.

docs.title: 4. Protect safety
docs.text:
This does not authorize panic. If the cue is not real, keep measure. If the answer fails, recover or leave. The standard is controlled commitment, not blind aggression.

The lesson progresses from known answers to real choice, then releases the behavior into score pressure and open fencing.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:10 Talk + orientation Name the decision problem; set the two-answer menu and safety boundary. Shared language 0:10-0:20 Decision-ready movement Enter, brake, and leave measure on a real visual cue. Usable body positions 0:20-0:35 Known-answer rehearsal Build two familiar, safe answers before forcing selection. Both answers available 0:35-0:50 Cue-and-commit Read one of two distinct entries and act before the feeder completes it. Cue linked to action 0:50-1:10 Constraint game I Give delay a cost while protecting cue quality and recovery. Timely, controlled choices 1:10-1:30 Constraint game II Vary measure, preparation, and recovery without enlarging the technical menu. Transfer under uncertainty 1:30-1:45 Scenario bouts Apply score pressure without rewarding panic or random attacks. Composure under pressure 1:45-1:55 Open fencing Notice whether the class behavior appears without bonus scoring. Real transfer 1:55-2:00 Debrief Name a useful cue and the next small decision menu. Next action

TIME CHECK: 10 + 10 + 15 + 15 + 20 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 5 = 120 minutes.

TRANSITION PLAN: Students gear before the opening. Pair by compatible control and size. Keep masks and gloves on from cue-and-commit through open fencing. Use one audible timer and announce rotations before each interval ends.

docs.title: 5. Explain today’s score
docs.text:
A point can count even if the hit does not land when the student saw the cue and made a clean, appropriate decision before freezing. Open fencing later tests whether that behavior survives.

REPEAT ALL CLASS: See something real. Pick one answer. Commit cleanly. Recover if it is wrong.

docs.title: 1. PARTNER MIRROR: ENTER, BRAKE, LEAVE (4 MIN)
docs.text:
One fencer leads with small advances, retreats, and angle changes. The follower mirrors while staying in a fenced posture. On the leader's hand signal, both stop and hold their balance for one beat. Switch at 2:00. This is the warm-up for seeing movement without guessing.

G | BLOCK 3 | 0:35-0:50

The opponent owns the cue. The actor does not know which answer is appropriate until meaningful information appears.

SETUP: Begin at a range where either partner can make a composed, one-exchange action. The feeder may use two honest entries: one clearly calling for Answer A and one clearly inviting Answer B. Make them visually distinct at first.

REPETITION: The feeder moves naturally, chooses an entry, and commits enough to make the cue readable. The actor recognizes, selects A or B, completes the action, and exits. Reset each exchange. Switch after 8-10 repetitions.

SUCCESS STANDARD: The actor gets the repetition for a safe, appropriate choice before the feeder completes the entry - even if the final hit is imperfect. No credit for pre-empting a non-cue, changing answers halfway through, or freezing until contact.

GAME CARD 1

Give delay a real cost without asking anyone to charge forward. The game rewards timely commitment and recovery, not merely who lands first.

STARTING STATE: Fencers begin in measure. One is the initiator and one is the responder. The initiator may use genuine preparation, then chooses either class picture. The responder’s job is to recognize and use A or B. After 30 seconds, switch roles and rotate partners often.

PLAYER GOALS: The responder identifies an honest cue and makes a safe class answer before the initiator finishes a committed action.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Responder scores 2 for a timely, safe answer with clean exit or recovery. Initiator scores 1 if the responder freezes through a clear cue or chooses an unsafe/nonsensical action. No point for fake/noncommittal pictures, pre-emption before an honest cue, or loss of control.

SCORING: Score the class behavior separately from the hit. The goal is an informed answer on time, not random first motion.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Two 4-minute role blocks, one partner change, and 2 minutes to reset rules and debrief.

COACH OBSERVES: Waiting through an honest cue, early guessing, switching answers halfway through, forgotten exits, and any action that becomes unsafe under speed.

PROGRESSION: Let the initiator change preparation tempo or delay the moment of commitment.

REGRESSION: Return to unmistakable entries and slightly slower speed; retain the same two answers.

docs.title: 2. TAKE SPACE OR LEAVE SPACE (6 MIN)
docs.text:
Stay at sword-safe distance with no cuts. The leader chooses one honest movement: step forward to close distance, or step back to give distance. The follower waits for the step, then makes one matching answer: angle out and reset when space closes, or take one small forward step when space opens. Reset after every repetition; switch at 3:00.

F | BLOCK 2 | 0:20-0:35

This is the whole decision menu for Decisive Action I - not a list of every good longsword answer. Students rehearse two familiar answers so the later decision is between two usable actions, not every possibility they know.

ANSWER A - COVER AND EXIT: Use this when the opponent is already entering with a committed, threatening line. The immediate job is to protect yourself, remove the line, and leave at an angle. Success is not a pretty counter; it is ending the exchange safe and balanced.

ANSWER B - TAKE THE OPENING: Use this when the opponent has given a real opening before their action is fully established. Enter with one simple, controlled action, then recover or exit. Success is acting on the opening without staying in front of their return.

WHY ONLY TWO? A small menu makes the lesson about recognition and commitment. Later classes can add more actions. Today, adding options would only make it harder to see whether the student recognized the cue or simply got lost choosing.

KNOWN-CUE REHEARSAL: In pairs, the feeder gives the same committed entry each time. The actor performs A five times, then B five times. The feeder keeps the picture honest and safe; the actor finishes every answer with posture and an exit.

HOLD HERE: This block confirms that both answers are actually usable before asking a student to recognize when either one belongs.

docs.title: A successful repetition looks like this
docs.text:
• The follower waits for an actual change in distance rather than moving on a guess.
  • The first step fits what the partner did: make room when they close, take space when they give it.
  • Both fencers finish balanced enough to stop, change direction, or add a sword action next.

PARTNER RULE: The leader may wait as long as they like before making a real step. Do not fake cues. The follower resets if they move before the step or remain frozen after it.

docs.title: Build two answers before demanding a choice
Coach prompts
docs.text:
• Which cue did you see?
  • Which answer fit it?
  • Were you still safe at that measure?
  • Did you leave after the decision?

NEXT STEP: Once both choices are clean, give the feeder a neutral preparation before either entry. The actor must now wait for information without becoming passive.

docs.title: Level 1 - Clear entries
docs.text:
The feeder’s two choices are deliberately distinct. The actor learns what each cue feels like.

L | FAILURE MODES

The distinction matters. Decisive action is a trainable information-action link, not an excuse for panic or a demand to move before the opponent gives anything real.

docs.title: Level 2 - Variable preparation
docs.text:
The feeder may change tempo, take a small step, or wait longer before either entry. The actor may not launch early.

J | BLOCK 7 | 1:45-1:55

The final portion is the test, not the whole lesson. Students may use any safe, appropriate fencing; watch whether the class behavior survives without game rules.

OPEN FENCING: Run normal short bouts. Before each bout, each fencer names one personal cue they intend to recognize: for example, committed high entry, opponent freezing after a feint, or opponent giving ground with extended hands. They do not need to force it; they are responsible for noticing it.

K | COACHING LANGUAGE

This lesson can accidentally reward two bad outcomes: acting before information, or rewarding any action simply because it was fast. Keep feedback tied to cue, choice, structure, and recovery.

WHEN YOU SEE SAY OR ASK NEXT COACHING MOVE Freeze after an honest cue What did you see? Which of the two answers was available? Return to the clear-entry version; make the cue unmistakable before restoring speed. Early action before a cue That was a guess. What information would make that answer appropriate? Let the feeder delay longer. Reward waiting for the cue, not guessing faster. Half-committed action You chose, then changed your mind halfway. Was the menu too big or was the answer not ready? Reduce to one cue/two answers; rehearse physical exit again. Reckless action Speed is not the goal. Can you make that same decision with structure and partner control? Slow down and rebuild quality. Do not award the repetition. Clean on-time miss Good decision. What adjustment would make the finish better? Award the decision separately from the technical finish; run it again with a tighter constraint.

docs.title: Level 3 - Variable measure
docs.text:
Start one step farther or closer. The same answer must now be scaled to the distance actually present.

I | BLOCK 6 | 1:30-1:45

Scenario pressure restores the reason people hesitate: score, consequence, and the feeling that one decision matters. Keep it short enough that the class behavior remains visible.

SCENARIO CONSTRAINT WHAT YOU ARE WATCHING Down 3-1 Responder has 45 seconds to create or take one honest decision window. They may not turtle indefinitely. Do they act from information or force an action from anxiety? Protecting a lead Initiator is up 3-1 but cannot retreat out of all range. They must remain able to give or take a real cue. Does score pressure make the fencer passive, early, or still composed? One clean exchange Each fencer receives one meaningful exchange. A clean, timely choice counts even without a perfect hit. Can they preserve the class behavior when the moment feels scarce? COACH RESPONSE Do not punish missed decisions with extra conditioning or public criticism. Name the information, name the available answer, and run the situation again. This is decision training, not shame training.

docs.title: Level 4 - Honest counterpressure
docs.text:
After the actor’s response, the feeder may recover or defend safely. The actor exits or recovers rather than expecting the exchange to stop.

COACH DECISION: Do not add feints, lower-line work, or three new technical answers just because the drill becomes easy. This is Decisive Action I. Complexity comes from timing, distance, and an opponent - not an unlimited decision tree.

docs.title: Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Where did you see a real cue and act before you had full certainty?

  2. Where did you wait for the perfect answer and lose the moment?

  3. What should the next lesson do: make the cue clearer, make the answer cleaner, or add one new

branch?

CLOSE: Decisive does not mean reckless. It means your preparation lets you make a controlled answer while there is still time.

docs.title: Doing something becomes random aggression
docs.text: Correct the phrase: a safe, plausible, trained response is better than freezing. Require an honest cue and a controlled recovery.

docs.title: Students wait for a verbal prompt
docs.text: Use the opponent’s body, weapon, timing, and measure as information. The coach may freeze or replay, but should not become the source of every decision.

docs.title: The feeder is too cooperative
docs.text:
If every cue is huge and every response lands, the actor is memorizing. Give the feeder real preparation and an honest recovery without turning it into uncontrolled free fencing too soon.

docs.title: Score pressure creates panic
docs.text:
Reduce consequence while preserving the cue. Ask for one clean exchange rather than five points, then reintroduce score pressure gradually.

VERSION 1.2 CHOICE: Keep the first lesson narrow. We are building a habit of committed, informed action - not a library of clever answers.

docs.title: Defend and Answer I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW

Students solve a committed attack with a genuine parry, then immediately answer the opening that the defense creates.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I stop a committed attack and regain the initiative before the attacker safely recovers?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students recognize when the opponent owns the attacking turn, remove the incoming sword with a compact parry, and riposte before the opponent can recover or renew. They select a real opening and finish without accepting a double.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: Meyer's instruction to meet an incoming cut actively and early, weaken it through displacement, and follow immediately to the arm or the next opening.

THE CUE: Make it safe. Take your turn. Answer clean.

CLASS BOUNDARY: This lesson is parry followed by riposte. A simultaneous strike, stop-hit, or counterattack into the opponent's ongoing attack is a different solution and does not satisfy today's objective.

LEARNING OUTCOMES

The sequence succeeds only when the incoming attack is actually removed before the defender begins an effective answer.

LOOK FOR WHAT IT MEANS The original attack The opponent makes a credible, committed action that must be addressed rather than ignored or raced. A genuine parry The defending blade prevents the original attack from arriving; incidental blade contact is not enough. A useful finish The parry stays compact enough that hands, point, edge, balance, and vision can support an immediate answer. A real riposte The defender's attack begins after the parry has done its job and reaches an opening that is actually available. A clean outcome The initial attack does not land, the defender does not reset unnecessarily, and the exchange does not become a double.

CLASS SCHEDULE

A movement warm-up leads into one turn-taking problem: first without equipment, then with progressively less predictable sword exchanges.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival and frame Separate parry-riposte from counterattacking Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Movement warm-up Low boxes, pogo hops, and short sprints Spring, brake, recover 0:20-0:30 Shoulders and Knees No-gear touch game; answer after the attack Respect the turn 0:30-0:45 Game 1: Defend, Then Answer Known high cut; real parry and immediate riposte Clean sequence 0:45-0:55 Guided coaching Compare the games; remove the reset or early hit One useful change 0:55-1:10 Meyer source study Active displacement, after-cuts, and the opening Historical frame 1:10-1:20 Game 2: Opening Changes Either high side; attacker varies the recovery Read the opening 1:20-1:30 Game 3: Take Back Initiative Freer onset; genuine attack, parry, and answer Own the phrase 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Normal fencing with one transfer objective Selective transfer 1:55-2:00 Gear and feedback Individual feedback; optional one-question close Next cue

IF TIME IS TIGHT: Shorten one role interval or the discussion. Preserve the no-gear game, the first sword problem, one variable-recovery progression, open sparring, and a calm finish.

ROTATION STANDARD: Use 90-second fixed roles, switch immediately, and change partners after a complete A/B cycle. Keep the game explanation short enough to preserve meaningful live attempts.

OPENING | 0:00-0:05

A committed incoming attack must be defended before the other fencer earns a genuine parry-riposte.

OPENING SENTENCE: "If somebody attacks you, you do not win this problem by trying to hit at the same time. You solve their attack, and the instant it is safe, you take your turn back."

SUCCESS DEFINITION: A real incoming attack is removed with a parry; the defender answers immediately from that position; the opening exists; and neither fencer receives an unnecessary return.

CLASS ARC: Prepare the feet; learn attack-and-answer timing without gear; add swords; examine Meyer; then vary the attacker's recovery and release the problem into freer fencing.

KEY DISTINCTION: A parry-riposte is a defensive action followed by an offensive action. A hit made during the opponent's attack is a counterattack, even if it lands first.

WARM-UP | 0:05-0:20

Use the established Steel Crown movement warm-up: low boxes, pogo hops, and short sprints with easy walking recovery.

TIME WARM-UP SECTION MOVEMENT OPTIONS COACH'S JOB 0:05-0:10 Low-box jumps Two-foot on/off; single-foot variations; lateral on/off Use stable low boxes; demand quiet, balanced landings 0:10-0:15 Pogo hops Short, springy hops in place or over a small distance Keep contacts quick, posture tall, and volume controlled 0:15-0:20 Short sprints Short accelerations followed by slow walks back Use room-length lanes; stop before form or braking breaks down

BOX VARIATIONS: Use both-feet jumps on and off, single-foot variations when appropriate, and lateral movements on or across the box. Keep the box low enough for clean, confident landings.

POGO GUIDANCE: Use short sets of quick, low hops. Keep the torso organized, the contacts light, and the movement springy rather than deep or exhausting.

SPRINT GUIDANCE: Accelerate over a short lane, decelerate under control, and walk slowly back before the next effort. The walk is recovery, not another conditioning interval.

LOAD CONTROL: Stop before landings become noisy, posture breaks down, or speed drops. Step down or use lower-impact variations when ankles, knees, fatigue, or experience call for it. [6-7]

NO-GEAR GAME | 0:20-0:30

Practice seeing an attack finish before answering, without swords, masks, fencing jackets, or impact.

STARTING STATE: No protective gear and no swords. Partners face one another at light-touch distance. Use open hands or soft gloves; legal touch targets are the shoulders and the outside knee area.

FENCER A: Initiate one clear, light touch attempt to a shoulder or outside knee area, then recover honestly. Do not chain attacks together or crash into your partner.

FENCER B: Avoid, move away, or lightly redirect the incoming hand. You may touch A only after the original attack has finished or has been clearly displaced and no longer threatens.

WHAT ENDS THE ATTACK: The attack is over when it lands, clearly misses, or is redirected out of the target line. If it lands, reset; the defender does not earn a return after accepting the first touch.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Do not hit while their attack is still happening. Make it miss, let their turn end, and touch the opening they leave."

ROTATION: 90 seconds as attacker, 90 seconds as defender, then change partner after a complete A/B cycle. Use no points or scorekeeping.

NO-GEAR SAFETY: Use light fingertip or soft-glove touches only. No head, face, throat, hard slaps, grabbing, direct pressure on the kneecap, diving, or twisting the knee.

GAME 1 | 0:30-0:45

Transfer the no-gear turn-taking problem into a genuine parry followed by a clean, immediate riposte.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Students already understand that their answer cannot begin during the opponent's attacking turn. Swords add the requirement that the defending blade actually removes the threat.

STARTING STATE: Both fencers wear full protective equipment and use swords. Fencer A begins at workable measure and delivers one committed, controlled high cut from an agreed side.

FENCER A: Make the initial attack credible. After it is parried, recover honestly and defend or make one controlled renewal only if the defender leaves you time.

FENCER B: Meet and displace the incoming sword, then immediately answer the nearest available opening from the position your parry creates. Do not counterattack into the original cut.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "They attack first. Stop the sword first. Then take your turn before they recover."

RULES AND ROTATION: The attack and riposte must be distinct actions. A landed initial attack, an early counterattack, or a double ends the exchange without success. Use 90-second roles and no scorekeeping.

COACH QUESTION: Could someone watching clearly see the first attack, the completed parry, and the answer - in that order?

GUIDED COACHING | 0:45-0:55

Use the room's own exchanges to distinguish early counterattacks, passive blocks, unnecessary resets, and real parry-ripostes.

GAME CARD 4

Release the parry-riposte into a freer fencing phrase with a genuine attack and possible renewal.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Fencers move freely; A owns the first committed high-line attack; B owns the defensive role.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Let them start. Stop what comes. Take your turn back before they can start again."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role; reset after a clean answer, an unsafe double, or a clearly resolved exchange.

COACH WATCHES: Recognition of preparation versus attack; a genuine parry; answer timing; the renewed attack; and protected recovery.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Vary the initial side, approach rhythm, or recovery while keeping the attacker/defender roles clear.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Return to a known high cut, slower entry, and one obvious recovery opening.

SOURCES

Meyer supplies the historical material. Published rules clarify the fencing phrase; movement and learning sources support modern coaching choices.

[1] Meyer, Joachim. Grundtliche Beschreibung der freyen Ritterlichen unnd Adelichen kunst des Fechtens (1570), Dusack Book, Chapters 5-6: openings, active displacement, and following cuts. 1570 transcription and English translation

[2] Meyer, Joachim. Manuscript Comparison, MS A.4o.2, fol. 31r.3: displacement followed by a short-edge cut to the arm or next opening. Meyer manuscript concordance

[3] Meyer, Joachim. The Art of Combat, 2nd ed., translated by Jeffrey L. Forgeng. Frontline Books, 2015.

[4] Iron Gate Exhibition. Longsword Tournament Rules: tactical priority, including Parry-Riposte > Renewed Attack. Official HEMA event rules

[5] International Fencing Federation. Technical Rules, August 2026, articles t.9-t.14: attack, parry, riposte, counterattack, and renewed actions. Official FIE competition rules

[6] National Strength and Conditioning Association. Plyometric Exercises: purposeful, low-volume jumping and stretch-shortening work. NSCA plyometric guidance

[7] National Strength and Conditioning Association. Agility and Quickness Test: Box Step-Off Landing Assessment: controlled landing, stability, and readiness. NSCA landing assessment

[8] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araujo. 'Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport.' Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33 (2011): 146-155. DOI

[9] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. 'A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play.' Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24 (2019): 103- 116. DOI
