docs.title: Defend and Answer I
docs.text:
How can I stop a committed attack and regain the initiative before the attacker safely recovers?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | August 2026 | Version 2.0

docs.title: Defend their turn, then take yours
What a real parry-riposte looks like
The lesson spine
docs.text:
QUESTION: Did I stop their attack before I started mine?

EVIDENCE: The original strike is genuinely removed; the answer starts from the parry's finishing position; and the target is still open.

COMMON NON-EXAMPLE: I hit into the attack, allowed the first hit to land, made an oversized block, or returned to guard before choosing an answer.

docs.title: Build spring, acceleration, and controlled recovery
Shoulders and Knees - wait for your turn
Defend, Then Answer - add the swords
Make the defense useful, then remove the pause
Ask before you explain
docs.text:
• Did the original attack actually stop before the answer began?
  • Where did your hands and sword finish after the parry?
  • Could you reach an opening from that exact position?
  • What did the attacker's recovery reveal or close?
  • If both fencers were hit, did the solution meet the class objective?

GAME CARD 3

Prevent a memorized riposte by changing the attacker's side and recovery position.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Fencer A cuts high from either side, then recovers into one of two different lines.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Stop the attack. See what the recovery leaves open. Answer that opening."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per fixed role; change partners after a full A/B cycle when time allows.

COACH WATCHES: Real removal of the attack; useful parry finish; eyes on the opponent; target selection; and an answer without a separate reset.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Allow the attacker to withdraw, close a line sooner, or vary the timing of the initial cut.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Return to a known-side attack and announce the recovery position before each exchange.

docs.title: Show three useful contrasts
docs.text:
GAME CARD 2

Transfer the no-gear turn-taking problem into a genuine parry followed by an immediate riposte.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Fencer A makes one controlled high cut from an agreed side; Fencer B must remove the attack first.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "They attack. Stop the sword. Then take your turn before they recover."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per role; switch immediately; reset after a landed first attack, early counterattack, double, or clean answer.

COACH WATCHES: Clear attack-parry-riposte order; compact defensive structure; immediate answer; nearest opening; and safe recovery.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Allow the attacker to vary rhythm or defend honestly after the first attack has been parried.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Announce the attack side, reduce speed, and briefly hold the recovery so the defender can recognize the opening.

docs.title: 1. EARLY COUNTERATTACK
docs.text:
The defender tries to hit while the original attack remains threatening. Even a first hit is not today's solution.

OBSERVATION AND FEEDBACK

Track whether students respect the attacking turn, create a real defensive stop, and answer before the opportunity disappears.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Turn Recognizes that the attack belongs to the opponent first Answers into the attack and calls it a riposte Defense Removes a credible incoming threat before attacking Touches first while the original attack remains live Structure Finishes the parry with useful hands, point, and balance Oversized block creates a separate reset Timing Answers as soon as the defense has done its job Admires the block or waits until recovery is complete Target Chooses the nearest opening the opponent actually gives Repeats a memorized target against a closed line Outcome Completes the phrase without a double or easy return Uses priority language to excuse unsafe fencing Transfer Finds a real parry-riposte during normal fencing Forces the pattern against every preparation

GAME CARD 1

Recognize when an incoming attack has finished before taking the answering turn.

STARTING STATE: No gear or swords. Partners use open hands or soft gloves to attempt light touches to shoulders and the outside knee area.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Make their attack miss or finish. Only then take your turn and touch the opening they leave."

DOSE AND ROTATION: 90 seconds per fixed role. Switch immediately and change partner after a full A/B cycle.

COACH WATCHES: The initial attack; whether the defender answers too soon; safe knee-area touches; balance; and an immediate answer after the threat ends.

IF THE ROOM IS READY: Vary the target, attacking rhythm, and recovery direction while keeping the original one-attack rule.

IF THE ROOM NEEDS LESS: Use shoulder targets only, slow the touch attempt, and make the end of the attacking action unmistakable.

docs.title: 2. PASSIVE BLOCK AND RESET
docs.text:
The sword stops the attack but the hands travel too far, the fencer admires the block, or a fresh guard replaces the available answer.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:55-1:10

Read Meyer in English: remove the opponent's attack with purpose, then strike the opening the defense creates.

COACH TROUBLESHOOTING

The most useful intervention makes the original attack, the completed defense, and the available answer easier to perceive.

IF YOU SEE... DO THIS The defender hits during the attack Reset the exchange. Slow the feed and ask the defender to show a completed defense before starting the answer. The defender accepts the first touch Do not reward the late return. Reduce speed and restore the rule: if the original attack lands, the exchange ends. The parry becomes a huge swing Make the attack slower and clearer. Ask for the smallest displacement that genuinely removes the threat and leaves the hands useful. The defender resets before answering Freeze immediately after a successful parry. Ask what opening can be reached from that exact position. The answer ignores the new opening Vary the attacker's recovery shape. Let the wrong target close and require the defender to notice what actually remains open. The attacker never recovers honestly Require a genuine initial attack followed by a controlled, realistic recovery or one renewed action; no frozen targets or machine-gun cuts. Priority becomes an excuse for doubles State that event rules may award a priority exchange, but the class standard remains a defended first attack and a clean, protected answer. Box jumps become a conditioning test Reduce box height, contacts, or speed. Step down, recover, and keep the warm-up sharp rather than exhausting.

CLASS STANDARD: Use one adjustment at a time: a clearer attack, a smaller parry, an earlier answer, or a better target. Let the next live exchange test the change.

docs.title: 3. USEFUL PARRY-RIPOSTE
docs.text:
The attack is actively removed, the defending position remains organized, and the next action reaches the opening before recovery.

ONE CUE FOR THE RE-TEST: Make it safe. Take your turn. Answer clean.

docs.title: 1570 Dusack, Chapter 6 - classroom English rendering
docs.text:
ACTIVE PARRY: Do not hold your weapon still and simply allow the opponent to strike it. Meet the incoming high cut actively. Receiving the attack earlier and higher weakens it and makes the following cut more useful and safer to complete.

WHAT MEYER IS SOLVING: A passive block may stop the immediate blow but leave the defender late, crowded, or unable to answer. An active displacement changes the incoming blade while preserving the position needed for the next action. [1]

MEYER TACTICAL MODEL

The historical pattern is sequential: a real threat is displaced, then the nearest workable opening receives the answer.

SAFETY AND ADAPTATION

Keep touching, sword contact, movement volume, uncertainty, and partner behavior appropriate to the people in the room.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE No-gear touch game Use light touches to shoulders and the outside knee area only. No head contact, hard slaps, kneecap pressure, diving, or collisions. Jumping or sprint limitations Lower the box, step up or down, reduce pogo contacts, shorten the sprint, or substitute brisk controlled steps. First-time or overwhelmed student Use one known high attack, slower speed, a visible recovery, and a clearly open target. Count a genuine defense as progress. Mixed experience Change attack timing, attack side, or recovery shape rather than raising impact or asking students to accept doubles. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. The observer identifies attack, parry, answer, and any unsafe return before roles rotate. Limited space Use short lanes, stable boxes, compact entries, controlled braking, and partners who do not pass or collide. Game breaks down Return to the no-gear turn-taking rule or the known-side sword attack. Slow the action and restore one clear defensive success condition.

docs.title: 1570 Dusack, Chapter 5 - classroom English rendering
docs.text:
THE OPENING: Notice the side from which the opponent begins the cut. Remove that cut without being struck, then answer promptly toward the opening their action exposes. Often, the line the attack came through becomes the available opening.

READING NOTE: These are modern classroom English renderings of Meyer's original material, not a claim that the 1570 text describes this exact game or a modern tournament rule. [1]

docs.title: Displace first; strike from what remains
Meyer manuscript comparison, folio 31r.3 - English
docs.text:
AFTER THE PARRY: When you displace from your right toward the opponent's left, answer from below with the short edge toward the arm. When the displacement goes the other direction, reverse the answer and continue toward the next available opening.

OPEN SPARRING | 1:30-1:55

Students fence normally and use sequential parry-riposte when a real committed attack creates the opportunity.

FORMAT: Five four-minute rounds with short rotation and water breaks. Use normal Steel Crown intensity agreements and pair by compatible control and size.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. When they genuinely attack you, stop the attack first and answer from the position your defense creates."

COACH BEHAVIOR: Watch several exchanges before speaking. Offer one individual cue between rounds rather than turning open fencing into another constrained game.

TRANSFER EVIDENCE: The fencer recognizes a committed attack, performs a real parry, answers before the opponent safely recovers, and declines the riposte when the opening is gone.

FINISH | 1:55-2:00: Use the final minutes for gear transition and individual feedback. If a whole-group close helps, ask: 'What told you their attack was over and your answer could begin?'

docs.title: 1. RECOGNIZE
docs.text:
The opponent begins a credible, committed attack. Do not confuse preparatory movement with a completed attack, and do not race the attack with your own hit.

COMPETITION AND PRIORITY

Published HEMA and modern fencing rules distinguish an original attack, a genuine parry-riposte, and an attacker's renewed action.

ORIGINAL ATTACK: The fencer who initiates a credible offensive action creates the problem that the opponent must first solve. A stop-hit into that live action is a counterattack, not this lesson's parry-riposte.

PARRY: The defending weapon must actually prevent the original attack from arriving. A brief, incidental blade touch does not automatically mean the attack was removed.

RIPOSTE: The defender's offensive action comes after the parry. It may be direct or indirect, but it must grow out of the completed defensive action rather than racing the incoming blade.

RENEWED ATTACK: The original attacker may try to attack again after being parried. If the defender gives away time, the renewal becomes a live tactical problem.

EXAMPLE HEMA CONVENTION: Iron Gate Exhibition's published longsword rules explicitly list Parry-Riposte > Renewed Attack in their tactical-priority hierarchy. Treat that as one event-specific example, not a universal HEMA rule. [4]

MODERN FENCING TERMINOLOGY: The FIE defines a riposte as the offensive action made by the fencer who has parried an attack and distinguishes it from a counterattack made during the opponent's action. [5]

STEEL CROWN STANDARD: An event may award priority in a double, but this class still aims to remove the attack and finish clean. Right of way explains the fencing phrase; it does not make being hit a good outcome.

docs.title: 2. DISPLACE
docs.text:
Meet and remove the incoming sword with a compact action. Preserve a usable fighting shape, awareness of the opponent, and a blade position that still threatens.

GAME 3 | 1:20-1:30

Add a freer onset and an honest renewed attack without changing the sequence: attack, parry, riposte.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Partners begin outside measure and move naturally. Fencer A owns the first genuine high-line attack; Fencer B owns the defensive role.

FENCER A: Choose when to commit the initial attack. After it is defended, recover, close the line, or attempt one controlled renewed attack if the defender hesitates.

FENCER B: Read the real attack rather than every preparation. Parry it, take the initiative with an immediate riposte, and stay protected against the possible renewal.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Let them start. Stop what actually comes. Take your turn back before they can start again."

RULES: The target behavior remains sequential parry-riposte only. If the initial attack lands, the defender counterattacks early, or both are hit, reset without awarding success.

ROTATION: 90 seconds as initial attacker, then 90 seconds as defender. Keep explanations short and preserve continuous, controlled attempts.

PROGRESS OR REGRESS: If the group is ready, vary entry rhythm and initial attack side. If the task breaks down, return to the agreed high cut and one obvious recovery line.

docs.title: 3. ANSWER
docs.text:
When the attack is genuinely stopped, cut or thrust to the nearest real opening from the position the parry created. The riposte is a second action, not a simultaneous counterattack.

GAME 2 | 1:10-1:20

Keep the parry-riposte requirement while allowing the attacker's cut and recovery to reveal different answers.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. Fencer A may initiate a controlled high cut from either side and recovers into one of two clearly different blade positions.

FENCER A: Attack with genuine commitment, then recover naturally into either a high/closed line or a lower/opposite-side line. Defend the first recovery honestly.

FENCER B: Parry the actual incoming attack, notice which line is exposed, and riposte into the nearest available opening. If the expected opening closes, choose the other one or reset safely.

SAY TO STUDENTS: "Do not decide the answer before the attack. Stop their sword, see what they leave open, and hit that."

RULES: No simultaneous counterattack, no preset target, and no points. The defender must genuinely stop the first attack before beginning the riposte.

ROTATION: Use 90-second fixed roles. Change partner after a full attacker/defender cycle when time allows.

COACH WATCHES: Look for students who memorize one return, chase a closed line, or reset to guard instead of answering from the parry's finish.

docs.title: 4. FINISH
docs.text:
Stay protected through the hit and recovery. If the opening has closed or the original threat was never removed, defend again or leave rather than forcing the answer.

HISTORICAL BOUNDARY: The named passages come from Meyer's dusack material and manuscript comparison. Applying their active displacement and following-cut relationship to this longsword lesson is a modern coaching interpretation. [1-2]

docs.title: Take Back Initiative - release the phrase
Understand the phrase without excusing the double
Transfer the answer to ordinary fencing
Adjust the task without losing the defensive problem
Correct the sequence, then return to the game
What to watch during live fencing
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what the fencer noticed, offer one change, and let the next exchange test it.

CLASS-LEVEL SUCCESS EVIDENCE: Early counterattacks decrease, parries become more compact, unnecessary resets disappear, ripostes follow real openings, and clean defensive answers appear in open fencing.

docs.title: Efficient Cutting I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER + LIECHTENAUER LENS

This class develops compact diagonal cuts to the upper openings: launch from a usable forward position, cut with real edge alignment and body support, then arrest, redirect, cover, or leave without a large reset. It does not reward wrist taps, uncontrolled doubles, or huge cutting combinations.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I make a real cut arrive quickly, stay covered, and leave me ready for the next action?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students make a credible diagonal cut by using only as much path as the target requires. They finish balanced, with the sword still between them and the opponent, and choose a second cut only when the first action actually leaves one available.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: Meyer's quick short-edge continuations and the Liechtenauer glosses' immediate actions after blade contact. The sources support prompt, protected continuation; the lesson's compact-cut mechanics, exercise choices, and tournament success test are modern coaching adaptations.

The target behavior counts only when all four observable conditions are present.

REQUIREMENT OBSERVABLE STANDARD Threat If the opponent leaves the upper opening open, the cut can land cleanly with recognizable edge alignment and safe control. Economy The sword starts from a usable forward relationship and reaches the target without a large backward windup, shoulder-driven loop, or excessive travel beyond the opening. Readiness The fencer can arrest or redirect the sword while remaining balanced and covered, rather than needing a separate reset before the next decision. Judgment The fencer links a second cut only when it is still available; otherwise they recover, cover, or leave without accepting the return.

NO DOUBLE: A result that leaves both fencers validly hit does not satisfy the lesson, even if one blade arrived first.

C | BLOCK 1 | 0:00-0:05

Students understand the problem, success test, and class arc.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Tonight we are solving one problem: How can I make a real cut arrive quickly, stay covered, and leave me ready for the next action?"

SUCCESS DEFINITION: State the four-part success test in plain language and make clear that a double is a failed solution.

CLASS ARC: Experience the problem first; compare what worked; examine one historical lens; increase choice and pressure; test transfer in open fencing.

DO NOT: Teach the complete historical solution before the first game. Students should possess the problem before receiving the model.

C | BLOCK 2 | 0:05-0:20

Build the ability to accelerate, decelerate, and redirect the sword through a stable shoulder, rotating forearm, controlled grip, and balanced base - without stiffness or fatigue.

WHAT THIS BLOCK IS: A short movement lesson, not conditioning. Demonstrate each exercise once, keep the volume low, and stop or regress when posture or landing quality deteriorates.

TARGET QUALITY: Build the ability to accelerate, decelerate, and redirect the sword through a stable shoulder, rotating forearm, controlled grip, and balanced base - without stiffness or fatigue.

C | BLOCK 2 | CONTINUED

Keep the movements low-volume and precise. The goal is controllable redirection, not fatigue.

docs.title: Efficient Cutting I
docs.text:
How can I make a real cut arrive quickly, stay covered, and leave me ready for the next action?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | August 2026 | Version 1.0

docs.title: Primary functional model
docs.text:
Begin with the sword present enough to threaten. Use the hands and forearms to organize the line, with the torso and feet supporting the action rather than adding a large shoulder windup. The grip firms only enough to control the arrival. Finish with posture, point, and hilt still useful; then either change to the next real opening or recover under cover.

Preserve the sequence. If time is lost, compress explanation before removing open sparring or reflection.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival & orientation Define efficient cutting i and its success test Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Athletic development Build the ability to accelerate, decelerate, and redirect the sword through a stable shoulder, rotating forearm, controlled grip, and balanced base - without stiffness or fatigue. Movement readiness 0:20-0:40 Problem exposure Game 1: Cut and Recover Experience the problem 0:40-0:55 Guided coaching Debrief; one useful intervention; variable rehearsal Small intervention 0:55-1:05 Historical integration Meyer's quick short-edge continuations and the Liechtenauer glosses' immediate actions after blade contact. The sources support prompt, protected continuation; the lesson's compact-cut mechanics, exercise choices, and tournament success test are modern coaching adaptations. Historical model 1:05-1:30 Progressive constraints Game 2: One Cut, Two Windows; Game 3: Cut, Change, or Leave More choice and pressure 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Five 4-minute rounds; normal fencing Transfer 1:55-2:00 Reflection & close Name cues, choices, failures, and next action Consolidation

TIME CHECK: 5 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 5 = 120 minutes.

TRANSITION PLAN: Students gear before the opening. Pair by compatible control and size. Keep masks and gloves on from problem exposure through sparring. Use one audible timer and announce rotations before each interval ends.

IF RUNNING LATE: Shorten the guided discussion or historical explanation by 2-3 minutes and reduce Game 2 by one role interval. Preserve at least one open-sparring round and the reflection.

docs.title: Instructor hypothesis
docs.text: Students will often load behind the body, lead with a tense shoulder, flick loosely at the target, cut so far past it that the sword must travel back before it can defend, or throw a second cut by habit when the opponent has already recovered. Some will mistake frantic speed for sharpness and score an initial touch while accepting the immediate return.

docs.title: Exercise sequence
docs.text: EXERCISE DOSE COACHING FOCUS MOVEMENT PURPOSE Scapular set and reach 2 x 6 Ribs stacked; no shrug Stable, mobile shoulder Forearm rotation map 2 x 6 each side Elbows quiet; wrist neutral Organizes edge and hand position Shadow cut and freeze 2 x 4 each diagonal Short path; balanced finish Acceleration-to-brake pattern Step, cut, and stick 2 x 3 each side One step; controlled finish Entry to usable recovery

docs.title: 1. SCAPULAR SET AND REACH
docs.text:
Stand in fencing stance with empty hands. Let the shoulder blades settle gently down and around the ribs, then reach both hands forward as though presenting the hilt and point. Return without pinching the shoulder blades together or lifting the shoulders to the ears. Cue: 'Long neck; live hands.'

A short 2-3x/week routine for shoulder stability, forearm control, grip balance, trunk control, and controlled solo cutting. This is practice, not a speed test.

Keep every repetition smooth. Begin with no load or a very light object; use a waster or synthetic trainer for solo cutting only in a clear space, never near people, pets, glass, or low ceilings. Stop if wrist, elbow, or shoulder pain increases.

docs.title: 2. FOREARM ROTATION MAP
docs.text:
Hold the elbows comfortably in front of the ribs at about a right angle. Slowly rotate the forearms so the palms travel inward, downward, then outward again, keeping the wrists straight and grip relaxed. The goal is control, not range. Cue: 'Turn the forearm, not the whole shoulder.'

C | BLOCK 4 | 0:40-0:55

Use the first game's evidence to provide the smallest intervention that improves the class.

C | BLOCK 5 | 0:55-1:05

Connect the experienced tactical problem to a documented historical principle without claiming that the source prescribes the modern game.

SOURCE IDENTIFICATION: Meyer's quick short-edge continuations and the Liechtenauer glosses' immediate actions after blade contact. The sources support prompt, protected continuation; the lesson's compact-cut mechanics, exercise choices, and tournament success test are modern coaching adaptations.

VERIFIED HISTORICAL CLAIM: Meyer includes several short-edge continuations to be performed quickly after a prior action, including the After-cut from Below; the Liechtenauer glosses likewise describe striking again immediately from the sword after a clash. Together, these sources support prompt action that remains connected to a threatening line. They do not prescribe the exact modern cut size, speed test, or physical training used here. [1] [2]

MODERN TRAINING INTERPRETATION: Use a slow crosswise-cut or short-edge continuation as the historical example: the hands and cross stay protective while the weapon changes line quickly. Then show the modern lesson translation: a diagonal cut should not need a giant loop before it can threaten again. The goal is not to make every cut small; it is to choose the smallest path that can still produce a real, defensible threat.

DEMONSTRATION: Show three slow examples: one successful application, one common failure, and one case in which the action should be declined. Let students rehearse briefly, then return to live choice.

EVIDENCE LINE: Historical text supplies the cited principle or action. The success test, games, scoring, cues, and safety adaptations are modern coaching design.

docs.title: 3. SHADOW CUT AND FREEZE
docs.text:
Without a sword, trace a diagonal cut from a forward hand position toward an imaginary upper opening. Freeze at arrival for one second with the chest upright and hands still usable, then return by the shortest safe path. Alternate sides. Cue: 'Arrive; do not fall through.'

C | BLOCK 3 | 0:20-0:40

Establish a real but controlled first cut, and reveal whether it leaves the attacker capable of protecting themselves immediately afterward.

STARTING STATE: Partners work in a lane at the edge of one-step cutting distance. The defender begins in a mobile high guard and, on the attacker’s approach, either leaves one upper opening genuinely available for a beat or closes it with a simple high cover. The attacker may make one diagonal cut only.

PLAYER GOALS: Attacker chooses a compact diagonal cut only when the upper line is truly open, lands with controlled structure, then returns to a usable forward cover. Defender gives an honest opening or cover and may make one light return only against an attacker who overtravels or hangs unprotected.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: The attacker gets one approach and one cut. If the defender closes the line in time, the correct answer is to recover or leave - not to strike through the cover. Keep impacts light and stop after the first clean outcome or safe separation.

SCORING: Clean cut to an open line plus usable recovery 2; correct abort or covered exit when the line closes 1; defender return against an overextended finish 1; loose tap, forced cut into cover, double, or accepted return 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partner and repeat on the opposite diagonal. Use the final 2 minutes of the block to compare what made one cut feel ready and another feel stranded.

INSTRUCTOR OBSERVES: Large backward windups, shoulder tension, edge drift, feet arriving after the sword, sword traveling far past the target, and attackers who only learn about their recovery when the defender hits them back.

COACH POSTURE: Observe across the room before intervening. Record common patterns and let several exchanges occur before deciding what the class needs.

docs.title: 4. STEP, CUT, AND STICK
docs.text:
With a trainer and full room awareness, begin just outside a partner's measure. On an agreed opening cue, take one controlled approach step and deliver a light diagonal cut to a legal protected target or a safe target substitute. Freeze for one second in the finish before moving again. Do not chase speed; own the endpoint. Cue: 'One step, one cut, one ready shape.'

REGRESSION AND STOP RULE: Reduce speed, distance, or impact; replace jumps with controlled steps. Stop for pain, dizziness, repeated loss of balance, loud uncontrolled landings, or a student who cannot maintain the described posture.

docs.title: Representative problem exposure: Cut and Recover
Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. Where did your sword start before the cut, and how much of that path was actually necessary?

  2. What made the cut real rather than a loose wrist tap?

  3. Could you protect yourself or change lines from the position where the cut ended?

  4. When the opening closed, what told you to stop rather than force the cut?

  5. Which part of the action made you feel slow: the launch, the arrival, or the recovery?

PRIMARY INTERVENTION: Demonstrate the same diagonal cut three ways: a large shoulder windup, a loose flick, and a compact cut that reaches the target and finishes ready. Keep the language simple: 'Start present. Cut through the opening. Finish useful.' Then show that a second cut is a choice made from the first finish, not a mandatory pattern.

VARIABLE REHEARSAL: Partners re-test the target problem at approximately 60-70% intensity. Keep at least one meaningful variable - side, rhythm, distance, pressure, or response - rather than feeding identical repetitions.

FEEDBACK PLAN: Use one cue at a time. Correct immediate danger at once; otherwise give feedback between sets of three attempts. Ask the student to identify the information that shaped the action.

AVOID: Turning the block into a long lecture or adding several fixes before students can test the first one.

docs.title: Build the mechanics behind the cut
1. SCAPULAR WALL SLIDES - 2 X 8
docs.text: Stand with your back near a wall, ribs down, and slide the arms upward only as far as the shoulders stay comfortable. Do not force the elbows or shrug. This builds a stable overhead/forward shoulder position.

docs.title: 2. LIGHT FOREARM ROTATIONS - 2 X 8 EACH
docs.text:
Hold a light hammer, dowel, or similar object with the elbow by your side. Slowly rotate palm-up to palm-down without bending the wrist. Use so little weight that you can stop anywhere in the path.

Use the checklist to distinguish learning from mere scoring.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Start position Sword begins usable and forward enough to threaten Loads behind body or requires a visible windup Line and edge Diagonal path and edge alignment are clear Wrist tap, vague line, or floppy edge Structure Shoulder stays mobile; torso and feet support the action Tense shrug, shoulder-led loop, or collapsing posture Endpoint Can arrest, cover, or redirect from the finish Sword overtravels and needs a reset Choice Second cut appears only when the defender leaves it available Runs a memorized double-cut regardless of the parry Outcome Clean score survives the immediate return Counts the first touch despite afterblow or double Transfer Uses compactness selectively at appropriate measure Makes all cuts tiny or chases hand taps without threat

docs.title: 3. FINGER-EXTENSOR OPENS - 2 X 12
docs.text:
Put a light rubber band around the fingers and thumb, then open the hand smoothly against it. This balances frequent gripping work and encourages the hands to stay less clenched between cuts.

Preserve the information and decision while reducing uncertainty, speed, distance, or impact.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE First-time student Use a known attack or response, longer preparation time, controlled partner, and score safe resolution as success. Mixed experience Give beginners less uncertainty; give experienced students more choice or rhythm variation, not greater impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. Observer applies the four-part success test, then roles rotate. Limited space Use narrow lanes; prohibit passing and large leaps; emphasize compact footwork and controlled stops. Injury / low impact Replace bounds with steps; reduce speed and contact; permit observer or limited-role participation. Large attendance Create lanes, assign a senior student to each cluster, and synchronize changes with one timer. Game breaks down Remove one variable, increase distance, slow the action, or return to a known starting state. Time loss Compress explanation and one role interval; preserve open transfer and reflection.

docs.title: 4. SPLIT-STANCE ANTI-ROTATION PRESS - 2 X 8 EACH
docs.text:
With a light resistance band at chest height, stand in fencing stance and press straight forward without letting the torso twist. If no band is available, use an isometric palms-together press for 10 seconds. The trunk should support the cut, not spin ahead of it.

GAME CARD 3

A sharp first cut becomes a second only when the defender genuinely leaves the second opening available.

STARTING STATE: Free onset just outside measure. Initiator may cut to either upper opening; defender parries, retreats, or covers and returns once. Initiator may redirect once or leave.

PLAYER GOALS: Initiator makes a real first cut, then reads the result. Change lines only when the opening exists; defender punishes overtravel and scripting.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Maximum two cuts. The second needs a real path; no looped reset. Halt on clean score, double, or safe separation.

SCORING: First cut plus safe finish 2; compact redirection plus finish 3; covered leave 2; defender hit 1; forced second, double, or afterblow 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Change initiator every 3 minutes; release the role in the final minute.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the second cut grows from the first finish, whether students force it after a solid parry, whether the point and hilt keep protecting during the change, and whether either fencer mistakes a frantic double for a good combination.

PROGRESSION: Either fencer may create the compact-cut sequence in normal onset.

REGRESSION: Return to one known side and cover. Add the second cut only after the opening is clear.

docs.title: 5. SOLO CUT-TO-FREEZE - 3 X 4 EACH DIAGONAL
docs.text:
Use empty hands first, then a safe trainer if the space permits. Deliver one diagonal cut at roughly 50- 60% speed and freeze in the end position for one second. Check: balanced feet, no shoulder shrug, sword still able to cover or redirect.

C | BLOCK 6 | 1:05-1:30

Increase uncertainty while preserving the lesson's central information-action relationship.

GAME CARD 2

Make the attacker select a compact cut for the opening that actually appears, while the defender tests whether the cut can be recovered safely.

STARTING STATE: At edge measure, the defender invites one upper line, closes it, or gives ground. The initiator uses footwork, then makes one diagonal cut followed by recovery or cover.

PLAYER GOALS: Initiator takes only a real upper window with no extra windup and survives the response. Defender returns against overtravel or poor recovery.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: One scoring cut only. Defender may use distance or a high cover, but not a pre-frozen parry. Count only a stable forward cover.

SCORING: Selected cut plus covered recovery 2; covered no-cut or exit 1; defender return 1; wrong window, loose tap, double, or accepted return 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes for explanation and reset.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the attacker recognizes the difference between an invitation and a real window, whether the hand path stays economical, and whether recovery happens because it was planned rather than because the blade bounced somewhere useful.

PROGRESSION: Allow the defender to use one small rhythm change or false preparation before choosing the window.

REGRESSION: Announce the upper opening before each exchange and remove the defender return until the attacker can freeze in a usable finish.

docs.title: 6. TWO-CUT FLOW - 2 X 4 EACH DIRECTION
docs.text:
Link one diagonal cut to the opposite upper opening only if the first finish makes it available. Keep the path small and quiet; stop immediately if the sequence becomes a big loop or the grip locks up. Once a week, film two repetitions from the side and look for the reset you are trying to remove.

SIMPLE WEEKLY PLAN: Run items 1-4 as a 10-minute body-prep circuit twice per week. Add items 5-6 for 5-8 minutes on one or two separate days. Speed belongs at the end of a well-controlled progression, never before it.

docs.title: Game 2 - One Cut, Two Windows | 12 minutes
docs.text:
Make the attacker select a compact cut for the opening that actually appears, while the defender tests whether the cut can be recovered safely.

  • At edge measure, the defender invites one upper line, closes it, or gives ground. The initiator uses footwork, then makes one diagonal cut followed by recovery or cover.

  • Initiator takes only a real upper window with no extra windup and survives the response. Defender returns against overtravel or poor recovery.

  • One scoring cut only. Defender may use distance or a high cover, but not a pre-frozen parry. Count only a stable forward cover.

  • Selected cut plus covered recovery 2; covered no-cut or exit 1; defender return 1; wrong window, loose tap, double, or accepted return 0.

  • 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes for explanation and reset.

C | BLOCK 7 | 1:30-1:55

Test whether the behavior appears without forced actions or bonus scoring.

FORMAT: Five 4-minute rounds with approximately 1 minute between rounds for rotation and brief feedback. Use normal open-fencing rules and the club's usual intensity agreement.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. Seek clean upper-opening and hand opportunities, but make each cut only as large as the window needs. A sharp cut is one that can score, keep you covered, and leave you ready to solve the next exchange."

PAIRING PLAN: Use compatible control and size, then rotate across different rhythms and preferences. Supervise novice pairings and avoid a large mismatch solely to complete the rotation.

C | BLOCK 8 | 1:55-2:00

Students consolidate one usable cue and one testable next action.

GAME CARD 1

Establish a real but controlled first cut, and reveal whether it leaves the attacker capable of protecting themselves immediately afterward.

STARTING STATE: Partners work in a lane at the edge of one-step cutting distance. The defender begins in a mobile high guard and, on the attacker’s approach, either leaves one upper opening genuinely available for a beat or closes it with a simple high cover. The attacker may make one diagonal cut only.

PLAYER GOALS: Attacker chooses a compact diagonal cut only when the upper line is truly open, lands with controlled structure, then returns to a usable forward cover. Defender gives an honest opening or cover and may make one light return only against an attacker who overtravels or hangs unprotected.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: The attacker gets one approach and one cut. If the defender closes the line in time, the correct answer is to recover or leave - not to strike through the cover. Keep impacts light and stop after the first clean outcome or safe separation.

SCORING: Clean cut to an open line plus usable recovery 2; correct abort or covered exit when the line closes 1; defender return against an overextended finish 1; loose tap, forced cut into cover, double, or accepted return 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partner and repeat on the opposite diagonal. Use the final 2 minutes of the block to compare what made one cut feel ready and another feel stranded.

COACH OBSERVES: Large backward windups, shoulder tension, edge drift, feet arriving after the sword, sword traveling far past the target, and attackers who only learn about their recovery when the defender hits them back.

PROGRESSION: Let the defender vary which upper opening is available and vary the timing of the closing cover.

REGRESSION: Use one known opening, slower approach speed, and a target substitute. Require the attacker to freeze after the cut before adding a defender return.

docs.title: Game 3 - Cut, Change, or Leave | 13 minutes
docs.text:
A sharp first cut becomes a second only when the defender genuinely leaves the second opening available.

  • Free onset just outside measure. Initiator may cut to either upper opening; defender parries, retreats, or covers and returns once. Initiator may redirect once or leave.

  • Initiator makes a real first cut, then reads the result. Change lines only when the opening exists; defender punishes overtravel and scripting.

  • Maximum two cuts. The second needs a real path; no looped reset. Halt on clean score, double, or safe separation.

  • First cut plus safe finish 2; compact redirection plus finish 3; covered leave 2; defender hit 1; forced second, double, or afterblow 0.

  • Change initiator every 3 minutes; release the role in the final minute.

PROGRESSION TRIGGER: Either fencer may create the compact-cut sequence in normal onset.

REGRESSION TRIGGER: Return to one known side and cover. Add the second cut only after the opening is clear.

docs.title: Coach records
docs.text:
• Sword begins usable and forward enough to threaten
  • Diagonal path and edge alignment are clear
  • Shoulder stays mobile; torso and feet support the action
  • Can arrest, cover, or redirect from the finish
  • Second cut appears only when the defender leaves it available
  • Clean score survives the immediate return
  • Uses compactness selectively at appropriate measure

FEEDBACK: Observe during rounds and coach mainly between them. Open sparring is not another constrained game.

docs.title: Whole-group questions
docs.text:
1. What made a cut feel sharp without making it reckless?

  2. Which part of your body created extra motion that did not help the target?

  3. When did the first cut genuinely leave a second cut available - and when did leaving become the better

answer?

  1. What did the defender do that exposed an overlong or late recovery?

INDIVIDUAL NEXT ACTION: Each student states one small, observable action they will test the next time this problem appears.

INSTRUCTOR CLOSE: Restate the functional success test, not a technique name. Record any safety issue, equipment problem, or student who needs a lower-intensity follow-up.

END ON TIME: Do not let the final sparring round consume reflection. The class is incomplete until students name the information that shaped their decision.

docs.title: Plan modifications before the room forces them
What to watch without interrupting every exchange
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what information the student perceived, offer one change, and let the next round test it.

SOURCES AND FINAL GATE

Historical claims are kept narrower than the modern class design. Representative games preserve opponent information and live decisions, but no source proves that this exact lesson is uniquely optimal.

[1] Meyer, Joachim. Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Longsword: Crosswise Cut and After-cut from Below. The translation describes quick short-edge continuations after a prior action. Wiktenauer transcription and translations

[2] Pseudo-Peter von Danzig. Longsword gloss, plays on striking immediately from the sword after the clash and the Crosswise Cut against descending attacks. Wiktenauer concordance and translations

[3] Meyer, Joachim. Foundational Description of the Art of Fencing: The 1570 Treatise of Joachim Meyer. Trans. Rebecca L. R. Garber. HEMA Bookshelf, 2023. Part I: Longsword. Edition and contents

[4] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araújo. "Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport." Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33, no. 1 (2011): 146-155. doi:10.1123/jsep.33.1.146. PubMed record

[5] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. "A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play." Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24, no. 2 (2019): 103-116. doi:10.1080/17408989.2018.1552676. DOI

TERMS: Historical terminology and English renderings vary by manuscript and translation. This plan paraphrases short claims and identifies modern coaching labels as modern.

READY: Start present, cut through a real window, finish useful, and redirect only when the next opening actually exists.

docs.title: Class-level success evidence
docs.text:
• Cleaner solutions and fewer doubles from Game 1 to Game 3.
  • Students can name at least one reliable cue.
  • The target behavior appears selectively in open fencing.
  • Students can explain why an unsafe score does not satisfy the lesson.
  • Beginners show safer structure even when they do not score.

docs.title: Fencing Actions Quick Reference
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

TERM WHAT IT MEANS LONGSWORD EXAMPLE Attack The initial offensive action intended to hit. Step in and cut to the head. Counterattack An attack made into the opponent's attack, without first completing a parry. Strike the hands while their cut is developing. Stop hit A counterattack intended to land before the opponent completes their attack. Thrust during a large preparation. Parry-riposte First stop or displace the attack; then immediately attack back. Parry the descending cut, then return to the head. Attack in opposition Attack while simultaneously controlling or displacing the opposing weapon. Thrust while carrying their blade safely off line. Compound attack An offensive sequence using one or more feints before the final attack. Feint high, draw the parry, then cut underneath. Second intention Plan the first action to provoke a predicted response that the prepared second action defeats. Attack high expecting the parry, then redirect below it. Remise Immediately renew the attack in the same line without fully recovering. A parried thrust stays forward and thrusts again. Redoublement Immediately renew the attack in a new line without fully returning to guard. A head cut is parried; redirect to the other side. Reprise Begin a new attack after recovering or returning to guard. Recover from the failed attack, then launch again. Countertime Draw or anticipate a counterattack, defeat it, then finish your own offense. Invite the hand shot, parry it, then riposte. Afterblow A retaliatory hit delivered shortly after being struck; especially important in HEMA rulesets. Your head hit lands, but their immediate return hits your arm.

Counterattack: hit during their attack. Parry-riposte: defend, then hit. Compound attack: feint within the attack. Second intention: use the first action to deliberately create the response defeated by the second.

Terminology varies somewhat by fencing tradition and ruleset. In foil and sabre, several labels also carry right-of-way consequences; most HEMA rulesets use the tactical ideas without applying Olympic priority exactly.

Common terms for describing when an action happens and how actions relate within an exchange

REFERENCE | MIXED AUDIENCE

Steel Crown | August 2026 | Version 0.1

docs.title: Guards with a Purpose I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons · Illustrated guard reference

A student can reproduce a guard and still have no useful action from it. Another student may pass through the same position successfully without knowing its name. Tonight connects the name, the position, and the decision: what does this guard let me do, what does it offer my opponent, and when should I leave it?

Main point

A guard is a position of the whole fencer with the sword. Its value depends on the opponent and the distance—not on how closely it resembles a photograph.

Say to the room: “We are not collecting poses tonight. Pick a position for a reason. Know what you can threaten, what you are leaving available, and what you will do if they take it. If the situation changes, the guard can change too.”

Meyer's historical descriptions and movement examples supply the vocabulary. Our competition tests, games, and scoring are modern Steel Crown coaching choices, not exercises prescribed in his book. [S1]

By the end, a student should be able to:

  • Recognize and form Ochs, Pflug, Tag, and Alber; distinguish Longpoint from Hanging Point.
  • Explain one available threat and one exposure from a chosen guard at the current measure.
  • Use that position to attack, defend, invite a response, or leave, without a large unnecessary reset.
  • Change their answer when the expected response does not appear.
  • Finish an exchange balanced and protected, rather than treating the first touch as sufficient.

Success is not using every guard or changing guards constantly. A student who uses one or two positions deliberately and survives the opponent's answer has met the practical aim better than someone who cycles through all twelve without purpose.

Time Block Purpose 0:00–0:05 Introduce the guard problem Connect position, threat, exposure, and next action. 0:05–0:15 Movement preparation Prepare balanced entries, stops, and changes. 0:15–0:35 Guided guard laboratory Learn the four principal guards and two useful connections. 0:35–0:55 Game 1: Make it earn its place Test what a chosen guard actually makes available. 0:55–1:03 Debrief and one intervention Identify the decision or preparation that failed. 1:03–1:10 Change without a reset Connect guard positions through familiar actions. 1:10–1:30 Game 2: Offer, read, leave Use a guard or transition to influence a live opponent. 1:30–1:55 Open fencing Test transfer without requiring named guards. 1:55–2:00 Reflection Link a position to an observed result.

0:05–0:15. In solo lanes, move between low, extended, and high sword positions. Add a short entry, retreat, or change of direction and stop in a position from which another action is immediately available. Compare holding the hands beside the head with extending them in front: what changes about the next cut or cover?

Finish with a partner mirroring changes of measure. Each fencer chooses a starting guard and adjusts it only when the distance or available line gives them a reason. Watch for a separate reload before moving or cutting.

0:15–0:35. Use Meyer’s original guard plates. Demonstrate briefly, let students try, and ask a question before giving another explanation.

First eight minutes: four principal guards. Show Ochs, Pflug, Tag, and Alber using the landmarks in the reference. Have students identify where the hilt and point are, what action is already prepared, and what opening appears available. Show both sides where comfortable. Do not demand that every student make an identical silhouette.

Position First question Practical caution Ochs / Ox Can I threaten or close an upper line without first dropping and reloading? High hands alone do not cover every route to the head or hands. Pflug / Plow Can my low point-forward position affect their approach? Do not let the point float harmlessly outside the relationship. Tag / Day or High Guard Can I make a credible descending cut from here? A prepared cut is not a shield; distance and timing still matter. Alber / Fool Can I recognize the attack this low position makes tempting? An apparent invitation is only useful if I can answer or get out.

Next six minutes: same guard, different distance. Partners take turns presenting a chosen guard. Outside contact range, the other person walks slowly toward a marked limit and points out which target or blade route looks available. Pause before either person can strike. Move the limit farther out or closer and compare the answers. No attacks in this observation task. Ask: “Did the shape change, or did its usefulness change?”

Final six minutes: connect to familiar actions. Show Longpoint as the extended point-forward position and Hanging Point as the high, forward-hand position with the blade descending. Demonstrate one familiar controlled cut into a useful extension, then a familiar hanging cover and exit. Name what appears without claiming every extension is a successful cover or every hanging shape is a successful parry.

Learning check: Ask students to show a named guard, identify one option, and point out one exposure. If they cannot, simplify to two guards before introducing live choice. The full secondary-guard catalogue belongs in the reference, not tonight's memory test.

When two guards look alike: Use the reference's look-alike comparisons. Ask students to identify which side of the body the hands occupy, whether they are beside the head or extended in front, and where the point goes. Use the foreground fencers identified in each plate caption; distinguish the reader’s left/right from the fencer’s own sides. Compare one pair at a time rather than adding every secondary guard to tonight's memory load.

0:35–0:55. The purpose is to discover what a guard can accomplish against a partner who is trying to solve it, rather than feeding its preferred response.

Setup and roles: Use cuts only for this first comparison. A starts just outside a comfortable single-entry cutting distance in one of the four principal guards. B starts in any familiar useful position. A names the guard and tells the observer one threat and one exposure; B does not have to attack that exposure.

The exchange: B initiates with one controlled cutting attack to either of two agreed targets, changes distance, or declines the entry. A may defend and answer, make a covered cut into a genuine opening, or leave. Neither must preserve the original guard. Allow one immediate answer to test the finish, then reset. No extended combinations or pursuit.

How to run it: Use two minutes for demonstration and calibration. Run four four-minute sets, with thirty seconds of feedback between sets and a final short debrief. Within each set, switch A and B after two minutes. In early sets choose between Tag and Alber; then compare Ochs and Pflug. If a student already has a useful familiar guard, allow it as a comparison rather than forcing an unfamiliar position under pressure.

Scoring: A earns one point for a clean touch that survives the permitted answer. B earns one for their own clean touch under the same condition. Doubles and accepted immediate returns score zero for both. A safe exit is a successful defensive decision but does not score a hit. If B declines, A may maintain safe measure and reset; do not chase simply to force a result.

Observer watches: Did the chosen position remove an extra preparation, influence B's entry, or support a safe answer? Was the failure the guard's relationship to the attack, the distance, a late decision, or poor execution? Do not diagnose every failure as “wrong guard.”

Easier: One known attacking line, slower entries, larger starting distance, and only two guard choices. Harder: Both target lines remain live; B may first threaten a blade engagement, but still gets only one committed attack. Raise uncertainty before increasing pace.

0:55–1:03. Ask each pair: “Which option really existed? What did the opponent do that you did not expect? Did you have to reload before answering?”

Choose one recurring problem, demonstrate one change, then retest for several exchanges. Examples: adjust the point so it relates to the opponent; shorten an unnecessary drop before cutting; move the feet so a low invitation is not simply a reachable head; or leave instead of trying to force an unavailable riposte.

Ask for the student’s observation first, then give one cue linked to the guard problem and retest it.

1:03–1:10. In solo lanes, trace Tag → Longpoint → Alber slowly through a descending cut, then Zornhut → Longpoint → Wechsel through a diagonal cut. These are movement relationships Meyer describes, not mandatory finishing routes in a bout. [S1, fols. 9v–10r]

Repeat the cut but stop where the current task requires; do not drive the point into the floor or carry every live cut to the lowest diagram position. Then let a partner show a known high cut. Use a familiar hanging cover and either answer if the line is truly open or leave under cover. No compulsory zwerch or blind riposte.

Question: “Which guard did the action carry you through, and could you act again from the result?” This is the bridge from named positions to continuous fencing. It is not a request to dance through guards in striking range.

1:10–1:30. The purpose is to use a guard as information: suggest an opportunity, see what the opponent actually does, and act without betting everything on a predicted response.

Setup: Keep the short exchanges and one immediate answer from Game 1. Choose cuts-only or the club’s usual thrust-inclusive rules before the set. Start outside immediate reach. Both may use familiar attacks, defenses, and footwork. A chooses a guard or one deliberate guard transition and privately tells the observer what response they hope to invite. B is free to attack, defend, change measure, engage the blade, or wait.

A's task: Make a credible offer while remaining ready. Take the opening if it is real; defend if the opponent attacks differently; reset or leave if nothing useful develops. There is no requirement to change guards after the offer. B's task is to fence successfully, not make A's idea work.

Two starting examples: From a low guard outside reach, invite a high attack and prepare a familiar cover-and-answer or cover-and-exit. From Longpoint at safe measure, invite a blade search and be ready to avoid the search or defend its follow-up. Neither is guaranteed. If they close behind a real threat instead, solve that threat first.

How to run it: Allow three minutes to demonstrate, agree targets, and choose the first intention. Run three four-minute sets with a one-minute debrief after each; switch A/B after two minutes. Use the final two minutes to remove the assigned initiator and let either fencer offer the problem. Rotate partners between sets if space permits.

Scoring and observation: Use the same clean-hit scoring as Game 1. Do not award points for visibly changing guard or making the prediction come true. The observer records whether B gave the expected response and whether A selected an appropriate answer to the response that actually happened. A sound decision that produces no hit can still be good learning; a double cannot be a successful trap.

Easier: Limit B to two genuinely different responses, such as attacking the offered high line or declining. Harder: Remove the declared offer, allow either person to initiate, and vary the starting distance. Discuss how removing thrusts changes the invitation from Ochs, Pflug, or Longpoint: the point’s scoring threat is absent in a cuts-only set.

1:30–1:55. Use five four-minute rounds with one minute of water, partner changes, and brief observation after each round, including the final round before reflection. Use the action rules selected for Game 2, with no bonus scoring or mandatory guards.

Ask students to carry one intention into a round: “I will use my starting position to make the first action simpler,” or “I will stop changing position once the opening is already there.” An observer can name the opening relationship after the exchange, not shout guard names during it.

Look for less unnecessary preparation, fewer freezes after the first action, selective use of invitations, and safer finishes. More guard changes or more touches alone do not demonstrate improvement. Keep score if useful, but compare the quality of decisions, not just totals.

1:55–2:00. Ask each student for one guard they used, one response it actually produced, and one occasion when they changed or abandoned the plan. Then ask: “What would you change if the same opponent simply waited?”

For the next delivery, note whether students could identify the six core positions, which invitations produced the expected response, and whether clean finishes improved from Game 1 to open fencing. Keep naming errors separate from functional failures; both matter, but they need different coaching.

[S1] Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), longsword, chapter 3, fols. 5r–10r: definition and division of guards; individual guard descriptions; transitions and tactical use. Original German with Rebecca L. R. Garber's English translation, accessed November 18, 2026. Historical explanations here are paraphrases; games, scoring, action restrictions, outcome measures, and competition applications are Steel Crown adaptations.

docs.title: What students should leave able to do
Game 1: Make it earn its place
Hanging Parries I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER WITH GLOSS SUPPORT

This is a longsword class for committed descending and diagonal cuts only. Students work both right- and left-side hanging-parry shapes, with modern padded jackets and clamshell gloves in mind. The lesson does not add thrusts, lower-line attacks, feint layers, or extended bind sequences.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I use an opponent's committed high cut to make a protected answer or leave safely, without remaining in a passive hanging parry?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students recognize a catchable committed high or diagonal cut, receive it with an uncrowded two- handed structure that protects the head and body, then immediately either make a clean parry-riposte or leave at an angle under cover. They do not wait in the hanging parry.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part I, Chapter 22, 'Hanging' (fol. I.22r.3), with his Crosswise Cut (fol. I.12v.2); supported by the upper hangings in the Liechtenauer gloss tradition.

The target behavior counts only when all four observable conditions are present.

REQUIREMENT OBSERVABLE STANDARD Recognition The fencer uses the action against a genuinely committed high or diagonal cut, rather than trying to catch an attack that has already passed or a feint that has not committed. Reception The cut lands on a compact, connected blade structure: the head and body remain covered, the hands stay usable in gloves, and the defender does not collapse into a cramped crossed-arm position. Action Immediately after the catch, the defender either lands a clean riposte - commonly a zwerch or cross-cut - or moves out at an angle behind the sword. Outcome The defender neither accepts an afterblow nor remains hanging in place; a double or immediate return hit fails the lesson.

NO DOUBLE: A result that leaves both fencers validly hit does not satisfy the lesson, even if one blade arrived first.

C | BLOCK 1 | 0:00-0:05

Students understand the problem, success test, and class arc.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Tonight we are solving one problem: How can I use an opponent's committed high cut to make a protected answer or leave safely, without remaining in a passive hanging parry?"

SUCCESS DEFINITION: State the four-part success test in plain language and make clear that a double is a failed solution.

CLASS ARC: Experience the problem first; compare what worked; examine one historical lens; increase choice and pressure; test transfer in open fencing.

DO NOT: Teach the complete historical solution before the first game. Students should possess the problem before receiving the model.

C | BLOCK 2 | 0:05-0:20

Reactive lateral stepping and compact upper-line coverage: receive force, change angle, and leave balance available for a cut or exit.

WHAT THIS BLOCK IS: A short movement lesson, not conditioning. Demonstrate each exercise once, keep the volume low, and stop or regress when posture or landing quality deteriorates.

TARGET QUALITY: Reactive lateral stepping and compact upper-line coverage: receive force, change angle, and leave balance available for a cut or exit.

Use the checklist to distinguish learning from mere scoring.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Recognition Selects committed upper-line attacks rather than late or speculative catches Tries to catch every attack or arrives after the line has passed Structure Head protected; flat/strong receives; hands remain usable in gloves Cramps/crosses arms, loses head cover, or collapses into weak contact Both sides Can receive left and right without defaulting to one unsafe shape Only recognizes or reaches one side Timing Moves while the opponent is committed, not after the hit Waits in the parry or catches late Answer Ripostes only when opening remains and stays covered Forces a zwerch/cross-cut into recovery Exit Changes angle with the sword covering the line Backs straight up, stops in range, or lowers the sword Outcome Prevents the return and avoids doubles Counts the first score despite afterblow or double Transfer Uses the action selectively in open fencing Performs only after an announced feed

How can I use an opponent's committed high cut to make a protected answer or leave safely, without remaining in a passive hanging parry?
