docs.title: Primary functional model
docs.text:
Receive a committed upper-line cut on a raised, hanging blade with the hands and cross protecting the head. Use the attacker’s committed line to create time for one immediate answer, or use the blade as cover while stepping diagonally out. The parry is a transition, not a destination.

Preserve the sequence. If time is lost, compress explanation before removing open sparring or reflection.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival & orientation Define hanging parries i and its success test Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Athletic development Reactive lateral stepping and compact upper-line coverage: receive force, change angle, and leave balance available for a cut or exit. Movement readiness 0:20-0:40 Problem exposure Game 1: Catch and Clear Experience the problem 0:40-0:55 Guided coaching Debrief; one useful intervention; variable rehearsal Small intervention 0:55-1:05 Historical integration Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part I, Chapter 22, 'Hanging' (fol. I.22r.3), with his Crosswise Cut (fol. I.12v.2); supported by the upper hangings in the Liechtenauer gloss tradition. Historical model 1:05-1:30 Progressive constraints Game 2: Catch, Answer, or Angle; Game 3: Hit, Cover, Leave More choice and pressure 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Five 4-minute rounds; normal fencing Transfer 1:55-2:00 Reflection & close Name cues, choices, failures, and next action Consolidation

TIME CHECK: 5 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 5 = 120 minutes.

TRANSITION PLAN: Students gear before the opening. Pair by compatible control and size. Keep masks and gloves on from problem exposure through sparring. Use one audible timer and announce rotations before each interval ends.

IF RUNNING LATE: Shorten the guided discussion or historical explanation by 2-3 minutes and reduce Game 2 by one role interval. Preserve at least one open-sparring round and the reflection.

docs.title: Instructor hypothesis
docs.text: Students will often catch too late, leave the blade hanging after contact, over-compress the arms in clamshell gloves, or force a riposte after the attacker has recovered. Others will stop after landing their own first hit and eat the opponent's afterblow rather than use the hanging shape as exit cover.

docs.title: Exercise sequence
docs.text:
EXERCISE DOSE COACHING FOCUS MOVEMENT PURPOSE Fencing stance pulse 2 x 20 seconds Quiet feet; level hips; hands ready to raise Prepare small weight shifts without telegraphing Diagonal load and stick 2 x 4 each side Land softly on an angled step; chest stays tall Build control for a protected diagonal exit Partner high-line cue 3 x 20 seconds each Raise the hands only on the actual cue; keep elbows usable Link visual information to compact upper-line cover Cover, angle, reset 2 x 5 each side Cover the head, take one diagonal step, finish balanced Rehearse leaving immediately instead of freezing in the cover

Preserve the information and decision while reducing uncertainty, speed, distance, or impact.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE First-time student Use a known attack or response, longer preparation time, controlled partner, and score safe resolution as success. Mixed experience Give beginners less uncertainty; give experienced students more choice or rhythm variation, not greater impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. Observer applies the four-part success test, then roles rotate. Limited space Use narrow lanes; prohibit passing and large leaps; emphasize compact footwork and controlled stops. Injury / low impact Replace bounds with steps; reduce speed and contact; permit observer or limited-role participation. Large attendance Create lanes, assign a senior student to each cluster, and synchronize changes with one timer. Game breaks down Remove one variable, increase distance, slow the action, or return to a known starting state. Time loss Compress explanation and one role interval; preserve open transfer and reflection.

docs.title: How to perform the exercises
docs.text:
GAME CARD 3

Train the user’s primary competition application: after landing or threatening a score, use a hanging-parry shape as cover for the opponent’s committed return and leave on your terms.

STARTING STATE: Initiator begins from just outside measure and makes one controlled scoring attack to an upper opening. Responder then gives one committed high or diagonal return at the initiator's upper line. The initiator must recognize the return, cover with the appropriate hanging-parry side, and leave at an angle; roles alternate every exchange.

PLAYER GOALS: Initiator lands or credibly threatens the first action, then turns the opponent's committed return into cover for a safe angled departure. The responder learns to punish a stationary, uncovered finish.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: The initial action can be any safe upper-line attack. The responder's return must be a real committed high/diagonal cut, not a pre-frozen feed. The initiator may riposte only if it is immediately available; otherwise leaving is the correct answer. Halt once safe separation is established.

SCORING: Clean initial score or credible threat plus covered angled exit 2; cover plus clean immediate riposte plus exit 3; initial score followed by a valid return hit 0; double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Rotate initiator/responder every 3 minutes. Use the final minute to remove the announced return and prepare for open fencing.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the first attacker stops after scoring, whether the return is actually committed, whether the cover arrives on the correct side, and whether the exit changes angle rather than simply backing away in the same line.

PROGRESSION: Remove the announced first attacker; either fencer may score first, and the scorer must solve the first committed upper-line return that follows.

REGRESSION: Keep the initiator designated and the return side known for one set, then restore side choice before moving to open sparring.

docs.title: 1. FENCING STANCE PULSE
docs.text:
Stand in a comfortable fencing stance without a sword. Make tiny forward-back weight shifts with the feet in contact with the floor. On an irregular clap, freeze instantly in a balanced stance with the hands ready to rise. Do not bounce or let the head drift. Cue: 'Light feet; quiet eyes.'

C | BLOCK 6 | 1:05-1:30

Increase uncertainty while preserving the lesson's central information-action relationship.

GAME CARD 2

Make the defender choose between a clean parry-riposte and a protected exit instead of forcing a preselected follow-up.

STARTING STATE: Partners begin at high-cut range. Attacker gives one committed high or diagonal cut to either side, then may recover and defend normally. Defender begins mobile and may use either side of the hanging parry.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender catches safely and chooses the best immediate resolution: zwerch/cross-cut riposte if the opening remains, or angled exit if the attacker has recovered or distance closes poorly.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: One defensive reception, then one immediate answer or exit. A riposte must arrive while the defender remains covered; no second chase. Attacker may make one controlled afterblow against a passive or uncovered defender.

SCORING: Clean catch, clean riposte, and no return 2; clean catch and protected exit 2; clean riposte that accepts an afterblow 0; attacker clean hit 1; double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes to explain the change in scoring and transition to the next game.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the student sees the real opening, forces the zwerch after recovery, fails to move the feet, or exits with the weapon no longer between the bodies.

PROGRESSION: Allow the attacker to choose a shallow recovery, full recovery, or immediate controlled afterblow after the cut.

REGRESSION: Have the attacker hold their recovery for one beat. Defenders name 'answer' or 'exit' aloud before acting, then remove the call as reading improves.

docs.title: 2. DIAGONAL LOAD AND STICK
docs.text:
From fencing stance, take one short diagonal step forward and slightly outward, then settle into a stable athletic position for two seconds. Repeat to both sides. The step is not a leap; the knee tracks over the foot and the chest stays tall. Cue: 'Angle, land, own the stop.'

C | BLOCK 4 | 0:40-0:55

Use the first game's evidence to provide the smallest intervention that improves the class.

C | BLOCK 5 | 0:55-1:05

Connect the experienced tactical problem to a documented historical principle without claiming that the source prescribes the modern game.

SOURCE IDENTIFICATION: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part I, Chapter 22, 'Hanging' (fol. I.22r.3), with his Crosswise Cut (fol. I.12v.2); supported by the upper hangings in the Liechtenauer gloss tradition.

VERIFIED HISTORICAL CLAIM: Meyer describes 'Hanging' from Plow as lifting the hilt so the blade hangs somewhat downward, receiving the opponent's cut on the flat of the blade, then working with winding to the nearest opening. His Crosswise Cut is likewise described as countering an upper cut while maintaining the crossguard high over the head and striking at the same time. [1] [2]

MODERN TRAINING INTERPRETATION: Use Meyer's hanging description to show the functional idea of a protected reception that becomes work, and his Zwerch to show an answer that covers while striking. The exact tournament objective here - score, cover the likely return, and take an angled exit - is a modern coaching application. The lesson does not require students to reproduce any cramped crossed-arm shape that is unreliable in padded jackets and clamshell gloves.

DEMONSTRATION: Show three slow examples: one successful application, one common failure, and one case in which the action should be declined. Let students rehearse briefly, then return to live choice.

EVIDENCE LINE: Historical text supplies the cited principle or action. The success test, games, scoring, cues, and safety adaptations are modern coaching design.

docs.title: 3. PARTNER HIGH-LINE CUE
docs.text:
Partners face each other without swords. The feeder gives harmless shoulder or hand noise, then occasionally raises one hand toward the mover's upper line. Only on the real cue, the mover raises both hands into a compact head-cover shape without crushing the forearms together. Reset immediately. Cue: 'See the line; make room for your hands.'

C | BLOCK 3 | 0:20-0:40

Let students discover when a high or diagonal attack is actually catchable, and make an immediate exit the non-negotiable end of the exchange.

STARTING STATE: In a narrow lane, partners begin at a distance where one controlled advance can bring the attacker into high-cut range. Attacker delivers one committed descending or diagonal cut to either upper opening. Defender begins from a neutral, mobile guard.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender recognizes the line, receives it on either hanging-parry side with safe structure, and exits diagonally under cover before the attacker can make a valid return.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Attacker may choose either upper-side cut and may take one controlled return only if the defender remains available. Defender may not stand in a hanging parry before the attack begins and may not remain in it after contact. No riposte is required in this first game.

SCORING: Correct catch plus clearly covered angled exit 2; clean exit without a full catch 1; attacker clean hit 1; passive hang, late catch, afterblow, or double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partner; repeat. Use the last 2 minutes for a short room debrief inside the 20-minute block.

INSTRUCTOR OBSERVES: Early waiting in the hanging shape, catching too late, hands jammed together by gloves, head outside the protection, square exits, and defenders admiring the parry instead of leaving.

COACH POSTURE: Observe across the room before intervening. Record common patterns and let several exchanges occur before deciding what the class needs.

docs.title: 4. COVER, ANGLE, RESET
docs.text:
Start in fencing stance with the hands low. On a partner's high-line cue, bring the hands to a compact head-cover position and take one diagonal step away from the cue. Freeze balanced for one second, then return to guard. Alternate sides. Cue: 'Cover, angle, reset - do not park there.'

REGRESSION AND STOP RULE: Reduce speed, distance, or impact; replace jumps with controlled steps. Stop for pain, dizziness, repeated loss of balance, loud uncontrolled landings, or a student who cannot maintain the described posture.

docs.title: Representative problem exposure: Catch and Clear
Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. What told you the cut was committed enough to catch?

  2. Where did your head sit relative to your hands, cross, and blade?

  3. Could you still use both hands freely in your gloves after the catch?

  4. What changed when you stepped out at an angle instead of backward or straight in?

PRIMARY INTERVENTION: Show a compact right- and left-side hanging receipt against a committed diagonal high cut. Keep the hands apart enough to work in clamshell gloves, get the head behind the sword, and let the feet make the parry functional. Give one cue: 'Catch, answer or angle out.' Demonstrate a common passive hang and why it loses the afterblow.

VARIABLE REHEARSAL: Partners re-test the target problem at approximately 60-70% intensity. Keep at least one meaningful variable - side, rhythm, distance, pressure, or response - rather than feeding identical repetitions.

FEEDBACK PLAN: Use one cue at a time. Correct immediate danger at once; otherwise give feedback between sets of three attempts. Ask the student to identify the information that shaped the action.

AVOID: Turning the block into a long lecture or adding several fixes before students can test the first one.

docs.title: Historical integration: Meyer With Gloss Support
Game 2 - Catch, Answer, or Angle | 12 minutes
docs.text:
Make the defender choose between a clean parry-riposte and a protected exit instead of forcing a preselected follow-up.

  • Partners begin at high-cut range. Attacker gives one committed high or diagonal cut to either side, then may recover and defend normally. Defender begins mobile and may use either side of the hanging parry.

  • Defender catches safely and chooses the best immediate resolution: zwerch/cross-cut riposte if the opening remains, or angled exit if the attacker has recovered or distance closes poorly.

  • One defensive reception, then one immediate answer or exit. A riposte must arrive while the defender remains covered; no second chase. Attacker may make one controlled afterblow against a passive or uncovered defender.

  • Clean catch, clean riposte, and no return 2; clean catch and protected exit 2; clean riposte that accepts an afterblow 0; attacker clean hit 1; double 0-0.

  • 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes to explain the change in scoring and transition to the next game.

C | BLOCK 7 | 1:30-1:55

Test whether the behavior appears without forced actions or bonus scoring.

FORMAT: Five 4-minute rounds with approximately 1 minute between rounds for rotation and brief feedback. Use normal open-fencing rules and the club's usual intensity agreement.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. Use hanging parries only against catchable committed high or diagonal attacks. If you use one, either make the answer immediately or leave at an angle; do not remain hanging in range."

PAIRING PLAN: Use compatible control and size, then rotate across different rhythms and preferences. Supervise novice pairings and avoid a large mismatch solely to complete the rotation.

C | BLOCK 8 | 1:55-2:00

Students consolidate one usable cue and one testable next action.

GAME CARD 1

Let students discover when a high or diagonal attack is actually catchable, and make an immediate exit the non-negotiable end of the exchange.

STARTING STATE: In a narrow lane, partners begin at a distance where one controlled advance can bring the attacker into high-cut range. Attacker delivers one committed descending or diagonal cut to either upper opening. Defender begins from a neutral, mobile guard.

PLAYER GOALS: Defender recognizes the line, receives it on either hanging-parry side with safe structure, and exits diagonally under cover before the attacker can make a valid return.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Attacker may choose either upper-side cut and may take one controlled return only if the defender remains available. Defender may not stand in a hanging parry before the attack begins and may not remain in it after contact. No riposte is required in this first game.

SCORING: Correct catch plus clearly covered angled exit 2; clean exit without a full catch 1; attacker clean hit 1; passive hang, late catch, afterblow, or double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partner; repeat. Use the last 2 minutes for a short room debrief inside the 20-minute block.

COACH OBSERVES: Early waiting in the hanging shape, catching too late, hands jammed together by gloves, head outside the protection, square exits, and defenders admiring the parry instead of leaving.

PROGRESSION: Let the attacker vary onset rhythm and choose either upper opening without signaling.

REGRESSION: Use one known attack side, slow the delivery, and have the attacker hold the sword extended after the cut so the defender can rehearse the exit line.

docs.title: Game 3 - Hit, Cover, Leave | 13 minutes
docs.text:
Train the user’s primary competition application: after landing or threatening a score, use a hanging- parry shape as cover for the opponent’s committed return and leave on your terms.

  • Initiator begins from just outside measure and makes one controlled scoring attack to an upper opening. Responder then gives one committed high or diagonal return at the initiator's upper line. The initiator must recognize the return, cover with the appropriate hanging-parry side, and leave at an angle; roles alternate every exchange.

  • Initiator lands or credibly threatens the first action, then turns the opponent's committed return into cover for a safe angled departure. The responder learns to punish a stationary, uncovered finish.

  • The initial action can be any safe upper-line attack. The responder's return must be a real committed high/diagonal cut, not a pre-frozen feed. The initiator may riposte only if it is immediately available; otherwise leaving is the correct answer. Halt once safe separation is established.

  • Clean initial score or credible threat plus covered angled exit 2; cover plus clean immediate riposte plus exit 3; initial score followed by a valid return hit 0; double 0-0.

  • Rotate initiator/responder every 3 minutes. Use the final minute to remove the announced return and prepare for open fencing.

PROGRESSION TRIGGER: Remove the announced first attacker; either fencer may score first, and the scorer must solve the first committed upper-line return that follows.

REGRESSION TRIGGER: Keep the initiator designated and the return side known for one set, then restore side choice before moving to open sparring.

docs.title: Coach records
docs.text:
• Selects committed upper-line attacks rather than late or speculative catches
  • Head protected; flat/strong receives; hands remain usable in gloves
  • Can receive left and right without defaulting to one unsafe shape
  • Moves while the opponent is committed, not after the hit
  • Ripostes only when opening remains and stays covered
  • Changes angle with the sword covering the line
  • Prevents the return and avoids doubles
  • Uses the action selectively in open fencing

FEEDBACK: Observe during rounds and coach mainly between them. Open sparring is not another constrained game.

docs.title: Whole-group questions
docs.text:
1. Which opponent action made the hanging parry a good choice - and which did not?

  2. When did a zwerch or cross-cut remain clean, and when was exit the smarter answer?

  3. How did your jacket and gloves change the shape you could actually use?

  4. What did you do after a successful score to prevent the return?

INDIVIDUAL NEXT ACTION: Each student states one small, observable action they will test the next time this problem appears.

INSTRUCTOR CLOSE: Restate the functional success test, not a technique name. Record any safety issue, equipment problem, or student who needs a lower-intensity follow-up.

END ON TIME: Do not let the final sparring round consume reflection. The class is incomplete until students name the information that shaped their decision.

docs.title: Plan modifications before the room forces them
What to watch without interrupting every exchange
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what information the student perceived, offer one change, and let the next round test it.

SOURCES AND FINAL GATE

Historical claims are kept narrower than the modern class design. Representative games preserve opponent information and live decisions, but no source proves that this exact lesson is uniquely optimal.

[1] Meyer, Joachim. Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part I: Longsword, Chapter 12, 'Crosswise Cut,' fol. I.12v.2; Chapter 22, 'Hanging,' fol. I.22r.3. Wiktenauer transcription and Garber- Chidester translation

[2] Meyer, Joachim. Foundational Description of the Art of Fencing: The 1570 Treatise of Joachim Meyer. Trans. Rebecca L. R. Garber. HEMA Bookshelf, 2023. Part I, Chapters 12 and 22.

[3] Pseudo-Peter von Danzig. Longsword Gloss, sections 128-133: upper hangings from right and left, windings, stepping, and work to the openings. Wiktenauer transcription and translations

[4] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araújo. "Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport." Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33, no. 1 (2011): 146-155. doi:10.1123/jsep.33.1.146. PubMed record

[5] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. "A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play." Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24, no. 2 (2019): 103-116. doi:10.1080/17408989.2018.1552676. DOI

TERMS: Historical terminology and English renderings vary by manuscript and translation. This plan paraphrases short claims and identifies modern coaching labels as modern.

READY: Recognize the committed upper-line attack, receive it on a usable two-handed structure, then immediately answer or take the angle out - no passive hanging and no accepted afterblow.

docs.title: Class-level success evidence
docs.text:
• Cleaner solutions and fewer doubles from Game 1 to Game 3.
  • Students can name at least one reliable cue.
  • The target behavior appears selectively in open fencing.
  • Students can explain why an unsafe score does not satisfy the lesson.
  • Beginners show safer structure even when they do not score.

docs.title: Meyer Longsword Basics
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Meyer divides the body down the middle and across the belt. That gives an upper and a lower opening on each side. He uses the same four-part division for the head itself.

Both views face the fencer. Their right is on your left. The openings describe locations, not a list of permitted targets.

Arrows show blade travel. The diagonal and horizontal examples can be mirrored.

Cut English name Blade path Oberhau High Cut Straight down, like 12 to 6 on a clock. Zornhau Wrath Cut Diagonally down, like 2 to 8 or 10 to 4. Mittelhau Middle Cut Horizontally across, from either side. Underhau Low Cut Diagonally up from below, from either side.

Oberhau and Zornhau. Both descend. In Meyer’s list, Oberhau names the vertical path and Zornhau the diagonal. In broader German fencing usage, Oberhau can mean any cut from above.

A parry wards off an incoming cut. Start by asking which of your openings is threatened. Choose an action that closes the path of the incoming blade; Meyer’s four openings are not four prescribed parries.

Parry then answer. Catch or send the blade aside, then make a separate return cut if there is an opening. A cut used only to displace the blade still counts as the parry, not the answer.

Parry and strike together. The same cut closes the incoming line and reaches an opening. Meyer distinguishes this from merely parrying. If the incoming cut can still land, deal with it first.

docs.title: Meyer Longsword Basics
docs.text:
The opening tells you where a cut is aimed. The cut name tells you how the blade travels. This review covers those two ideas and how to tell a separate parry from a cut that defends as it strikes.

REFERENCE | MIXED AUDIENCE

Steel Crown | November 2026 | Version 0.1

docs.title: Three Defensive Examples
docs.text:
These are useful starting examples from Meyer’s guards and cuts, not his own numbered list of basic parries.

Example What it does Timing Hanging cover Receive a high cut on a sloping blade. Hangetort (Hanging Point) is a guard shape you can use for this cover. Parry, then answer. Cut to displace Use an Oberhau or Zornhau to send the incoming blade off its line. Look for the opening it leaves. Parry, then answer. Covering cut A Zwerchhau (Thwart Cut) can cover against a high cut while your own cut reaches an opening. Defend and strike together.

docs.title: Quick Review
docs.text:
Name the opening. Face a partner and point out their upper right and your upper right. Then identify the upper and lower openings on the head.

Show the angle. Trace the four paths with clear space and no contact. Compare the vertical Oberhau to the diagonal Zornhau at the same speed.

Check the cover. In slow partner work, distinguish a parry followed by a cut from a cut that covers as it lands. Use club-approved training swords, protective gear, and permitted targets.

docs.title: Historical Source
docs.text: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Book 1 (Sword), ch. 1 (openings), ch. 3 (guards), ch. 4 (cuts), and ch. 5 (parrying). English translation on Wiktenauer.

docs.title: Meyer Longsword Cuts and Parries
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

These are four examples from Meyer’s chapter on cuts. A named cut can still be one action. Watch how the blade turns, how it meets the other blade, and whether the reply is a separate movement.

The diagrams show features, not exact positions. Dashed gray lines represent the other blade’s line.

Cut What to look for How to tell it apart Zwerchhau Thwart Cut A crosswise cut. In the high form, the raised hilt helps cover a descending line. Mittelhau describes the horizontal path. For this Zwerchhau, also look at the hilt and the line it covers. Krumphau Crooked Cut The blade crosses the opposing blade’s line. Meyer describes a crossed-hand form. A diagonal path alone doesn’t identify it. Watch where the blades cross. Schielhau Squinting Cut A descending cut that turns to use the short edge. It can look like an Oberhau by direction. Watch which edge leads. Kronhau Crown Cut A high catch receives a descending cut, followed by a return cut in Meyer’s example. The cover and return are separate actions in this example.

Long edge and short edge. In a conventional grip, the long edge is on the knuckle side of the forward hand. The short edge is the opposite edge.

Meyer distinguishes a parry that only wards off a cut from one that wards it off and strikes in the same action. If the blades stay in contact, you can also work from that contact, called the bind.

Read each row from left to right. A separate reply doesn’t require a pause.

Parry then answer. In the Crown Cut, the catch protects first and the return comes separately. A Crooked Cut that only sends the other blade aside also counts as a parry. Any reply is a separate action.

Cover and strike. The Thwart Cut can protect and strike in the same action. If the incoming cut can still land, the motion didn’t close that line.

Work from the bind. Winden (Winding) turns the sword while the blades stay in contact, changing their angle or leverage. Meyer discusses it among the handworks, not as a third kind of parry.

docs.title: Meyer Longsword Cuts and Parries
docs.text:
The four openings stay the same. Name upper or lower and the fencer’s own left or right, on the body or on the head. For the cuts in this review, the path alone won’t always tell you which action you’re seeing.

docs.title: Quick Review
docs.text:
In a slow demonstration, name the opening first. Then compare a high Zwerchhau with a simple horizontal cut: what does the hilt position change? Finally, look at the timing. Did the reply follow the parry, arrive in the same action, or begin from blade contact?

For partner practice, use club-approved training swords, required protective gear, permitted targets, and a pace both fencers can control.

docs.text: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Book 1 (Sword), chs. 1–2 (openings and edges) and chs. 4–6 (cuts, parries, and handworks). English translation on Wiktenauer.

docs.title: Meyer Longsword Guards
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons · Guards with a Purpose I: lesson plan

A guard is an arrangement of the whole body and sword from which a fencer can act. It is not just a blade angle, a promise of protection, or a pose that must be held until the opponent attacks. Meyer describes positions for awaiting and engaging an opponent, and later explains how guards occur within cuts and other work. [S1]

For practice, ask four questions: What can I threaten? What am I offering? What answer is available? Can I move from here without rebuilding my position? Those questions are our coaching framework, not a quotation from Meyer.

A guard is not a parry. A guard is a position; a parry is an action that deals with a threat. A hanging-shaped blade that misses the incoming line has not successfully parried. An extended point that neither threatens nor constrains the opponent is not automatically controlling the center.

These are the original woodcuts from Meyer's 1570 book, reproduced from the historical hand-colored scans linked in [S3]. The complete plates retain their letter, background figures, and original body and hand positions. Captions identify the relevant foreground fencers; left and right in a caption mean the reader's view, while the formation descriptions use the fencer's own sides.

Read the pictures alongside Meyer's descriptions. A plate is not an exact technical blueprint: Meyer himself says that the arms in the Hanging Point illustration should be more extended. The book does not provide a separate labelled portrait for every guard in this catalogue, so Nebenhut and Eisenport remain explained in words rather than supplied with invented drawings. [S1]

Safety

A historical point-to-face description is not a partner-drill instruction. Use approved protection, controlled trainers and contact, and instructor-set targets. Do not let someone enter onto a rigid extended point. Learn shapes in clear solo space before adding a live partner.

In the opening of chapter 3, Meyer names Ochs, Pflug, Tag, and Olber as the four principal guards. The remaining guards arise from them in his account. Principal does not mean “the only useful four” or a four-way defensive system. [S1, fols. 5r–5v]

Figure 1. Plate B — Ochs at foreground left; Pflug at foreground right. Compare the high and low hilt positions.

Figure 2. Plate C — Tag at foreground left; Alber at foreground right. Compare the upright sword above the head with the low point in front.

Guard Formation landmarks in Meyer Do not confuse it with Ochs — Ox Right Ochs: left foot forward, hilt high beside the right side of the head, point toward the opponent's face. Left Ochs reverses those sides. Tag: Ochs presents the point forward rather than straight up. Pflug — Plow Meyer describes right Pflug with the right foot forward, hilt beside the forward knee, point rising toward the opponent's face; left Pflug uses the left foot forward. Every tradition's version of a hip-height guard. Follow this source rather than importing another author's foot rule. Tag — Day / High Guard Left foot forward, sword above the head, point upright. Meyer also uses the name Oberhut. Zornhut: Meyer's described Zornhut rests at the shoulder with the blade behind, not upright over the head. Alber — Fool Written Olber in the text: left foot forward, point extended low in front of the forward foot, short edge up and long edge down. A guarantee of a successful invitation. A low position still needs a timely answer.

These are paraphrased source landmarks, not exhaustive modern stance prescriptions. Meyer's conclusion allows work on both sides, although individual descriptions often show only one. [S1, fols. 6v–7v; 9v–10r]

These two secondary guards are especially useful for naming positions students already encounter while cutting, covering, and recovering. [S1, fols. 7v; 9r]

Figure 3. Plate A — Longpoint is shown by the foreground fencer on the left, with arms and sword extended toward the opponent.

Guard Recognition What matters in use Langort — Longpoint Arms extended before the face; point toward the opponent's face; Meyer's described example has the left foot forward. Extension needs a relationship to the opponent. Do not lock the arms and wait to be struck around or displaced. Hangetort — Hanging Point Right foot forward in the described example; arms extended forward at face height, blade hanging downward. Meyer cautions that the plate's arms are not extended enough. It is a recognizable position, not proof that the incoming cut is caught. Cover the actual line and remain able to answer or leave.

Figure 4. Plate F — Schrankhut at foreground left; Hanging Point at foreground right. Meyer explicitly corrects the Hanging Point picture: the arms should extend farther forward. [S1, fol. 9r]

You may encounter spellings such as Hängenort or Hengetort in other material. This page uses Hangetort, following the chapter heading. Naming differences do not remove the need to check the actual position and action.

The formation column summarizes chapter 3. The final column gives modern practice questions—not a claim that Meyer assigns one fixed tactical job to each guard. [S1]

Guard Formation landmarks Question to test in practice Zornhut — Wrath Guard Left foot forward; sword at the right shoulder with the blade hanging behind, prepared for a cut. Can the prepared cut arrive without an extra windup, and can I still defend a different attack? Wechsel — Change Right foot forward; point/weak extended low beside the body, short edge toward the opponent. Can I rise or change from this endpoint without first collecting the sword? Nebenhut — Side Guard Left foot forward; sword low beside the right side, point to the ground, pommel up, short edge toward the fencer. Is my rising action ready, or am I only leaving my upper opening available? Eisenport — Iron Gate Right foot forward; hands/hilt low before the knee, arms hanging down; point rises toward the opponent's face. Is the blade actually between me and the relevant threat? Schlüssel — Key Left foot forward; crossed hands and hilt before the chest; short edge lies over the left arm, point toward the opponent's face. Can I leave this chamber smoothly without trapping my wrists or gloves? Einhorn — Unicorn Left foot forward; crossed hands raised toward the right, point projecting upward and outward. Does this high position leave me a useful next action rather than an uncomfortable hold?

Wechsel is not simply Nebenhut with another name. Both can look low in a sketch; compare the side, lead foot, and short-edge orientation in the descriptions. Likewise, a familiar shoulder guard from another tradition is not automatically Meyer's described Tag.

Figure 5. Plate E — Zornhut at foreground left; Einhorn at foreground right. Compare the sword chambered behind the shoulder with the raised crossed hands and upward point.

Figure 6. Plate D — Schlüssel at foreground left; Wechsel at foreground right. Compare the crossed-hand chest position with the low side position.

Meyer explicitly separates Eisenport from Schrankhut, despite reporting that people confuse them. Iron Gate has a rising point; Schrankhut has crossed hands and a point directed to the ground. The similar names and low hands are not enough to identify them. [S1, fol. 8r]

See Figure 4 (plate F) above for Schrankhut at foreground left. Eisenport is described in the text; do not identify the point-down Schrankhut as Iron Gate.

Why the lists sometimes differ: The introductory list in the book includes Brechfenster and Schrankhut among the secondary guards. Chapter 3's opening list instead includes Nebenhut and Hangetort. Chapter 3 then discusses Schrankhut while distinguishing it from Eisenport. This sheet follows the chapter's four-plus-eight list and adds that comparison; it does not pretend every list in the book is identical. Brechfenster is noted here as a list variation, not supplied with an invented standalone posture. [S1; S2]

Use the point direction first, then the hands' height and relation to the body, then hand crossing and edge orientation. A single feature is rarely enough. These comparisons summarize the descriptions above, not a new catalogue of guard-breaking techniques. [S1]

Similar guards The useful distinction Quick check Ochs and Einhorn Both can put the hands high on a side. Ochs directs the point forward toward the face; Einhorn raises crossed hands to the right with the point up and outward. Is the point presented forward, or lifted upward? Ochs and Hangetort Ochs places the hilt high beside the head. Hangetort extends the hands forward at face height while the blade hangs down. Are the hands beside the head or reaching in front, and where is the point? Tag and Zornhut Meyer's described Tag is above the head, point upright. Zornhut is at the right shoulder, blade hanging behind. Above the head, or chambered at the shoulder? Pflug and Eisenport Both are low, rising-point positions, and their outlines can overlap. Meyer describes Pflug's hilt beside the forward knee; Eisenport's hilt before the knee with the arms hanging down. Beside or before the knee? Do not invent a large difference in point height to separate them. Pflug and Schlüssel Both can present the point forward. Pflug's hilt is low beside the knee; Key's crossed hands are before the chest, with the short edge over the left arm. Knee-height preparation, or a crossed-hand chest chamber? Alber, Wechsel, and Nebenhut Alber extends the point low in front, short edge up. Wechsel is low beside the body, short edge toward the opponent. Nebenhut's described example is beside the right side, short edge toward the fencer. Front or side, then which way is the short edge facing? Eisenport and Schrankhut Eisenport's point rises from low hands; Schrankhut's crossed hands carry the point down. Point up or down, and are the hands crossed?

Do not turn a flowing transition into an argument over the exact frame at which one name becomes another. Use the descriptions to recognize meaningful relationships, and acknowledge overlap when the source does not give a sharp boundary.

Meyer describes a descending cut passing from Tag through Langort to Alber, and a diagonal cut passing from Zornhut through Langort to Wechsel. These examples explain how named positions relate within movement. They are not orders to pause at each checkpoint or finish every tournament cut on the ground. [S1, fols. 9v–10r]

A guard can therefore be a starting position, a moment within an action, or the position from which the next decision begins. What follows depends on the opponent. If a cover is required before the illustrated endpoint, cover; if the opponent is no longer reachable, recover or leave. Do not continue a classroom path just to complete its names.

The following are Steel Crown applications to modern cut-based practice, not historical guard-breaking rules or guarantees.

Job Useful test Common failure Prepare a threat Can a credible action begin without a separate reload? Choosing a dramatic position that adds unnecessary preparation. Shape the opponent's choice Does the apparent opening produce an identifiable response? Assuming the opponent must attack the offered target. Preserve an answer Can I deal with a different attack or disengage safely? Calling a vulnerable position an invitation without having an answer. Connect actions Does the finish leave another useful threat, cover, or exit? Returning to a favorite guard automatically while the opponent attacks.

Read the guard together with measure, blade relationship, and movement. It suggests possibilities; it does not reveal a guaranteed next technique. Holding still can sometimes serve a purpose, and changing can sometimes serve a purpose. Neither stillness nor constant motion is the objective.

  • Show the four principal guards and identify the hilt and point landmarks.
  • Explain why Ochs is not Tag, and why Iron Gate is not Crossed Guard.
  • Trace a slow solo cut and name a guard it passes through without pausing there.
  • With an equipped partner at safe distance, identify one opening you appear to offer and an alternative response you must still handle.

For live practice, use the linked lesson's guard experiments and games. A cuts-only game cannot test the point's scoring threat in the same way as a ruleset that permits thrusts. This reference alone is not permission to experiment with unprotected partner attacks.

[S1] Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), longsword, chapter 3, fols. 5r–10r. Original German descriptions and guard-transition passages, consulted alongside Rebecca L. R. Garber's English translation: Chapter 3: The Guards, accessed November 18, 2026. Formation landmarks are independent concise paraphrases of the historical descriptions; no translated passage is reproduced.

[S2] Meyer, same work, longsword introduction, fol. 2r, principal/secondary guard list: Introduction and Contents, accessed November 18, 2026. Compare this list with the chapter 3 list before combining catalogues from different sections or manuscripts.

[S3] Original illustrations: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (Strasbourg, 1570), longsword plates A–F. Historical woodcuts, public domain; historical hand-colored scans from Diestro / Sprechfenster’s chapter 3 edition, accessed November 18, 2026. Direct scan links: A, B, C, D, E, F. Scans are encoded as JPEG for website delivery, with no cropping, redrawing, or recoloring. Figure numbering and identifying captions are modern Steel Crown additions outside the images. Source files, dimensions, and checksums are recorded with the website assets.

docs.text:
Recognize the positions, understand what they prepare, and connect them through actions rather than memorizing isolated poses.

docs.title: Iron Gate and Crossed Guard are different
Provoke Through Distance I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | LONGSWORD | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

How can I sell an entry, a retreat, or an attack beat so the opponent commits to the wrong answer, then take the opening cleanly?

LESSON OVERVIEW

Use movement to suggest an intention you do not fully carry out. Prepare an answer to the mistake you expect, then confirm it before finishing.

Feint Mistake you are inviting Prepared answer False step-in They attack the entry they think is arriving, but their attack falls short. Make the attack miss with a small withdrawal; answer its recovery if reachable. Half-step back They believe you are giving ground and press forward into your prepared distance. Catch an exposed advance with a covered action; defend first if they press with an attack. Stomp or footfall feint They defend on the footfall, before the real attack begins. Deliver the real attack on the following beat to the opening their early defense exposes.

Student outcomes: Students make a convincing footwork cue without losing balance or defensive options; identify the specific attack, chase, or early parry it draws; execute a prepared follow-up at usable distance; and recover or change plan when the trigger never appears. A double or an attack into a closed line does not meet the outcome.

Plan the trap before you start: Know what you are trying to make them believe and what reply you are ready to exploit. A rehearsed answer is useful. Treating the expected reply as guaranteed is the error. This is deliberate provocation, not just moving around to see what happens.

Make the signal credible: Mix genuine entries and attacks with feints. If every step is false, an opponent can simply ignore it. Use familiar attacks and defenses so the learning stays on deception, distance, and timing.

Shared practice format: Use club-required longsword equipment, permitted targets and actions, and agreed intensity. Work short phrases without points. Reset on a clear touch, double, separation, loss of control, or halt under normal club conventions. Never add a late hit after halt.

OPENING 0:00-0:05 | WARM-UP 0:05-0:15

The physical job is to start, brake, and change the timing of an action while remaining able to defend.

Say to students: "Tonight we are lying with the feet. A step can sell an entry that never quite arrives. A half-step back can invite someone to chase. A stomp can make them defend before the cut. Decide what mistake you want, be ready for it, and check that they actually make it."

Before partner work: Confirm equipment, contact level, permitted targets, stop call, and reset conditions. Leave clear stopping space. Match partners for compatible control and pace. Make it easy to request a slower version or a break.

Time Preparation What to preserve 0:05-0:10 Familiar general movement, easy forward/back steps, then brief low hops or controlled step-and-stop actions once warm. Balance and the ability to brake; short efforts with recovery. 0:10-0:15 Without swords, practise a shallow false start, a short retreat that can stop, and a small accented footfall. Partners watch which movement looks like a real entry. A believable cue with recoverable feet. An accented step is not a hard heel slam.

Coach watches: Can the fencer suggest forward commitment without pitching the head and torso into danger? Can a half-step retreat stop without needing another backward step? Can the footfall be distinct without a jump or a painful impact?

Lower demand and gear transition: Replace hops with steps and replace the stomp with a light step or body accent. Use smaller movement and more rest where needed. Begin gear transition during the end of this block; complete all checks before sword exchanges. Do not sacrifice equipment checks to the clock.

CALIBRATION 0:15-0:25

The opponent should have a reason to believe the footwork cue. Start with the same familiar setup for both possibilities.

Setup: Full club-required equipment, controlled pace, and a clear lane. Partners begin near the edge of a familiar attacking action. Confirm that the real action can reach with an appropriate step, while the false version can still stop or recover.

Initiator: Sometimes use the normal entry and a controlled cut. Sometimes show the beginning of that same entry but withhold the cut and remain recoverable. Avoid a huge blade feint: the first deceptive cue should come from the feet, body, or rhythm.

Responder: Try to prevent a clean hit and take your own appropriate opportunity. You may defend, attack, yield, or hold. Read the whole threat rather than guessing that every step is real or that every step is false.

How to run it: Demonstrate a few slow examples, then use 90-second roles and switch immediately. Change partners after a complete pair of roles where practical. No scorekeeping. Short phrases and the shared halt/reset conventions apply.

What the coach is looking for: Can the fencer make the opening cue similar while keeping the false action shorter or less committed? Does the partner react to the offered entry? Does the fencer remain able to defend if the partner attacks the feint?

Bridge to the traps: Ask: 'What did the step make you expect?' Then narrow the next block to one anticipated response: an attack aimed at the entry. Do not require the responder to be fooled every attempt.

TRAP 1 0:25-0:45

Make the opponent attack the place they expect you to occupy, then answer while they recover.

Starting problem: Begin where a normal entry would bring you into reach. Use a credible approach cue: a small forward step, a step-start, or a convincing change of rhythm. Retain enough balance and weapon readiness to withdraw or defend.

Worked example: Show the beginning of an entry. They commit an attack to meet it. Do not complete the entry: take just enough distance away for the attack to miss, then return a familiar controlled cut as their attack finishes or recovers. If their blade still threatens you, defend before answering.

The important distance: Too far away, the feint has no threat. Too large a retreat, and your answer cannot reach. Find a small distance change that makes their reach judgment wrong while leaving a usable answer. If no safe answer is reachable, recover rather than lunge after it.

First five minutes: Use a known, controlled attack response to calibrate the distance and withdrawal. Switch roles after a few attempts. The responder attacks normally within agreed control; do not ask them to lunge farther, lock a joint, or lose balance for the drill.

Remaining fifteen minutes: The initiator mixes genuine entry attacks with false entries. The responder may attack, defend, yield, or ignore the cue and tries to deny a clean finish. Use 90-second roles and partner changes after both roles. The trap must work against a choice, not only a feed.

Coach cue and success test: "Sell the entry; stay able to leave; catch the recovery." Look for the attack being drawn early or short, the fencer withdrawing in control, and a reachable protected answer. A miss by the opponent is useful evidence, but it does not automatically make your next hit available.

TRAP 2 0:45-1:05

Suggest that you are giving up ground while staying ready to stop and act as they press the apparent advantage.

Set the invitation: Begin at a distance where the opponent wants to follow if you retreat. Give a small, believable half-step back rather than a large escape. Keep a familiar guard and a stance that can stop; you are selling withdrawal, not surrendering balance or deliberately exposing your head.

Worked example: You give half a step. They step after you to maintain pressure, with the leading arm exposed and no live attack closing the line. Stop yielding and make a compact covered cut to that available forearm, using the club's permitted targets and control standard. Recover with the weapon still able to protect you.

If they press with an attack: The trap is not permission to hit through the incoming blade. Use a familiar parry and answer, or take the attack out of reach if possible. If they follow with a closed line, hold safely, or do not follow at all, the expected opening has not appeared.

First five minutes: Have the partner follow a short retreat with a normal, balanced advance while retaining defensive ability. Calibrate when the exposed target becomes reachable. Also show a following attack so the initiator can distinguish an advance from a live threat.

Remaining fifteen minutes: The responder chooses whether to hold, follow, or attack and may protect against the prepared answer. The initiator may genuinely withdraw instead of always springing the trap. Use 90-second roles; switch partners after both roles. Keep the same short-phrase stop rules.

Coach cue and success test: "Give a little ground, not the decision." Look for a believable invitation, a real forward commitment, and an answer fitted to the weapon situation. If the initiator must reverse wildly or trade hits, simplify the distance or restore the familiar defense.

COACHING AND MEYER LENS 1:05-1:15

Use one observed exchange to show the difference between a planned trap and blindly completing a sequence.

Coaching reset: Ask: 'What were you trying to make them believe? What reply were you ready for? Did that reply actually happen?' Demonstrate one response that fits the trap and one that does not. Change the finish when the trigger changes.

Historical connection in plain English: In Sword, Chapter 7, Meyer describes suggesting a broad approach while keeping the feet close, and disguising the speed of an approach. In Chapter 6's withdrawal discussion, he describes appearing to leave, drawing pursuit, letting the pursuing cut miss, and answering. Paraphrase, not quotation. [1]

Application boundary: These passages support deceptive approach and withdrawal. Today's half-step and stomp drills are modern training choices, not named Meyer sequences. The footfall feint is a preparatory cue; it is not a rule to detach every real cut from its supporting movement.

Demonstrate the next timing problem: Contrast a normal step-and-cut with an accented step followed by a withheld cut. Let the partner show an early defense on the footfall, then show the real attack on the following beat. Repeat with the partner holding a sound guard: no opening means no automatic finish.

Source: [1] Meyer, Joachim (1570), Sword, Chapters 6-7, folios I.23r.4-I.24r.2. Rebecca L. R. Garber translation (2023), Wiktenauer. Read the source text .

TRAP 3 1:15-1:35

Use the footfall and body cue to draw an early defense, then deliver the real attack on the following beat.

Setup: Use a familiar guard and a calibrated distance where a genuine step-and-cut would be believable. Start with controlled, readable actions. The initiator can actually enter and attack; the stomp is not a noise made far outside any credible threat.

First beat: Make a small, emphatic forward step or stomp with the body cue of an entry. Keep the weapon available but withhold the expected cut. The intended mistake is a defensive movement made on the footfall instead of on the real attack.

Following beat: As an early parry sweeps away from the line or opens another target, deliver the prepared controlled cut to that actual opening. The delay is a short timing offset, not a long pause. If the parry remains sound or the opponent counterattacks, change plan or defend; do not strike into a closed guard.

First five minutes: Contrast a normal entry with the footfall-first version. The partner initially gives a controlled early parry to make the timing visible, then varies its timing. Let students feel the difference before adding free choices. Switch roles after a few attempts.

Remaining fifteen minutes: Mix genuine attacks on the normal beat with footfall feints and delayed attacks. The responder may defend early, wait, yield, or attack and tries to deny a clean hit. Use 90-second roles; change partners after both roles. No points and no compulsory reaction.

Coach cue and boundaries: "Let the foot sell the cut; let their defense choose the finish." Use an accented footfall, not painful heel-pounding, jumping, or uncontrolled forward momentum. A light step or body accent is a valid lower-impact version. Check the blade and opening, not just whether the opponent flinched.

OPEN FENCING 1:35-1:55 | FINISH 1:55-2:00

Remove the drill roles. The feint must remain credible against someone who is making their own plan.

Format: Four four-minute rounds, with partner rotation and water breaks inside the twenty-minute block. Use normal Steel Crown equipment, intensity, permitted actions, and halt conventions. No bonus points for feinting and no requirement to use all three traps.

Shared objective: "Choose a trap that suits what this opponent expects: entry, retreat, or attack timing. Be ready for the reply you want. If they do something else, do not force the finish."

Watch for Evidence in normal fencing Credibility Genuine entries and attacks remain possible; the feint resembles something the opponent needs to respect. Triggered mistake A premature attack, committed chase, or early defensive action follows the cue. Prepared answer The fencer takes the specific recovery, exposed advance, or opening created by the early parry. Judgment and protection The fencer abandons the trap when necessary, deals with the blade, and avoids a double or uncontrolled finish.

Feedback between rounds: Name the cue, the response, and what made the answer available or unavailable. Give one useful adjustment rather than asking students to narrate while fencing. Compare relevant opportunities, not simply the number of hits.

Final five minutes: Allow a calm gear transition and individual feedback. If a group question helps, ask: 'What did you make them expect, and which mistake did you actually catch?' Record what should be revisited next class. One good round is not proof of lasting learning.

COACH REFERENCE

Keep one trap and one intended reply clear before adding another possibility.

If you see Useful adjustment Nobody believes the feint Check distance and whether real attacks are mixed in. Make the opening cue resemble a genuine action; do not require the partner to react. The false entry gets hit Reduce commitment, clarify the starting distance, and retain a familiar defense. Do not solve it by asking the partner to overextend. The retreat becomes an escape Reduce it to a half-step and check the reachable target. If the fencer cannot stop comfortably, slow down and simplify. Every following step gets attacked Alternate a plain advance, a covered advance, and an incoming attack. Teach the distinction before restoring freer play. The stomp produces no opening Check whether the defender actually moved early and uncovered a line. A flinch or the sound alone does not earn the attack. The delayed cut meets a counterattack Defend the live threat or recover. Shorten the pause; keep the blade ready instead of waiting helplessly for a second beat. The room needs less Use known starts, fewer choices, smaller steps, and a controlled partner. Restore choice after useful attempts are possible.

Safety and access: Use current club requirements. Stop for loss of control, collisions, equipment issues, or ignored halt calls. No forced overextension, hard heel impacts, or late hits. For odd numbers, rotate an observer who tracks one trigger. Match challenge through timing and choice, not greater impact.

After class: Which cue was believable? Which expected reply appeared? Did the prepared answer work without a trade? What needs a clearer start or more practice?

Second Intention I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

LESSON OVERVIEW | 0:00-0:05

Students use a credible first attack to invite a parry-riposte, then counter-parry the reply that actually appears and answer cleanly.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I provoke an expected response, confirm what actually happens, and defeat it without guessing?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students make a first attack that must be respected, remain ready for the expected parry-riposte, identify the actual riposte line, counter-parry it, and answer without accepting a double. If the response never appears, they recover or leave rather than completing a memorized sequence.

THE CUE: Provoke. Confirm. Answer.

SUCCESS EVIDENCE

LOOK FOR OBSERVABLE STANDARD Credible provocation The first attack can land if ignored; it is not decorative or deliberately short. Confirmation The fencer waits for a genuine parry-riposte and identifies its actual line. Correct decision Finish if open, counter-parry the reply, or leave when the expected answer never appears. Clean outcome The final action lands under cover or the fencer exits safely. A double is not success.

TIME USE: The time ranges at the top of each activity are guides, not a fixed script. Stay with a useful game longer or move on when the room has solved its current problem.

WARM-UP | 0:05-0:20

Use familiar plyometric work to prepare the feet and legs without turning the opening block into conditioning.

SECTION MOVEMENT OPTIONS COACHING FOCUS Low-box jumps Two-foot on/off; single-foot variations; lateral on/off Quiet landings; stable knees; own the box and the floor Pogo hops Quick, low contacts in place or over a short distance Tall posture; elastic ankles; stop before rhythm gets heavy Short sprints Brief accelerations followed by slow walks back Sharp start; controlled braking; the walk is recovery

PURPOSE FOR THIS LESSON: Second intention requires a credible first acceleration followed by enough balance and availability to defend and accelerate again. The warm-up prepares that repeatability without rehearsing the tactical answer in advance.

SUGGESTED RHYTHM: Move continuously through the three sections for about five minutes each. Keep demonstrations brief and let students select appropriate box and contact variations.

LOAD CONTROL: Stop before landings become noisy, posture collapses, or sprint speed meaningfully drops. Reduce box height, use step variations, shorten the lane, or replace jumping with controlled footwork when needed.

CLASS CUE: Spring. Brake. Be ready to act again.

GAME 1 | 0:20-0:30

Learn the three-part exchange without sword speed, equipment, or a complicated target map.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The attacker should expect a reply but cannot know its exact line. Soft-glove touches let both fencers see the sequence clearly before adding weapons.

STARTING STATE: No swords or protective gear. Partners wear or hold soft gloves and begin at a comfortable touch distance. Shoulders are the only targets.

FENCER A: Make one genuine touch attempt to either shoulder. If B covers it, wait for B's counter-touch, cover the shoulder B actually attacks, then answer with one final light touch.

FENCER B: Cover A's first touch and immediately counter-touch either shoulder. Change the return naturally so A cannot memorize one defensive answer.

STUDENT RULES: The first action must be able to land if ignored. A may not begin the second cover until B's counter-touch starts. Reset after the final touch, a miss, loss of balance, or a broken sequence. No scorekeeping.

ROTATION: Use 90-second fixed roles, switch immediately, then change partner after one complete A/B cycle.

SAY TO STUDENTS: Make them answer. Defend the answer that actually comes. Then take the opening.

GAME 2 | 0:30-0:45

Transfer the exchange to longsword with one known attack, parry, and riposte line.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: The decision problem is temporarily reduced so students can learn the physical sequence: credible attack, parry-riposte, counter-parry, final answer.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. A attacks one agreed upper opening. B uses one agreed parry and immediately ripostes to one agreed upper opening.

FENCER A: Make the first attack real enough to land if B fails to defend. Expect the riposte, but do not counter-parry until B actually begins it. Remove the reply and answer from the counter-parry's finish.

FENCER B: Make a genuine parry that stops the first attack, then riposte immediately and honestly. Do not freeze the sword for A or steer the reply into A's waiting defense.

RULES: One complete phrase, then reset. No simultaneous counterattack, no decorative first attack, and no extra exchange after A's final answer. Slow the phrase enough that the order remains visible.

ROTATION: Use 90-second roles. Switch immediately; change partners after the A/B cycle when time allows.

SUCCESS: A's first attack is credible, B's reply is real, A's counter-parry follows the reply rather than guessing, and the final answer does not produce a double.

GUIDED COACHING | 0:45-0:55

Use the first sword game to show how a plan can remain responsive to live information.

ASK BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN: What made the first attack worth defending? When did you know the parry had actually become a riposte? What told you which line the riposte occupied? When did expecting the answer become pre-acting against it? What should you do when the expected answer does not arrive?

SHOW THREE CONTRASTS

EXAMPLE WHAT THE FENCER DOES WHAT IT TEACHES Empty invitation A's first attack stops short or cannot land. B does not need to give a meaningful answer. Predetermined sequence A begins the counter-parry before B's riposte has a line. The plan has replaced perception. Responsive intention A attacks credibly, recognizes the reply, and counter-parries the actual line. The plan prepares attention without deciding the answer early.

FEEDBACK RHYTHM: Watch several exchanges. Name one observable event, ask what the student noticed, give one cue, and let the next exchange test it. Do not stack several technical corrections before the student can re-enter the decision.

KEY PHRASE: Expect the family of response. Believe only the response that actually happens.

MEYER SOURCE STUDY | 0:55-1:10

Meyer supplies a historical tactical model for provoking a counteraction, taking it away, and striking the opening it creates.

DIRECTLY FROM THE 1570 PRINT - CLASSROOM ENGLISH: "Sometimes the first, now the second, then the third becomes a Provoker, Taker, or Hitter." [1]

CLASSROOM ENGLISH RENDERING

MEYER: Strike in with an overcut or undercut - not because you seek to hit, but to provoke him to strike from his advantage. Take the incoming cut away with another cut; this is the Taker. By taking it away you expose him. Immediately cut to that opening; this is the Hitter. [2]

PROVOKER: A credible first action changes the opponent's problem and invites the counteraction you are prepared to manage. In this class, A's opening attack is the Provoker.

TAKER: The incoming answer is removed only after it actually appears. In this class, A's counter-parry is the Taker.

HITTER: The fencer attacks the opening produced by the taking action. The final answer is not owed; if the opening disappears, recover or leave.

MODERN TERMINOLOGY: USA Fencing describes second intention as a convincing false action used to draw a committed response. Here, 'false' describes the action's tactical purpose; it should still present a real threat that the opponent must respect. [3]

HISTORICAL BOUNDARY: Meyer does not call this sequence 'second intention.' That is the modern tactical label used to organize the class. His Provoker-Taker-Hitter description supports the underlying relationship, while the exact game structure, equipment, timing, and success test are modern coaching design.

DEMONSTRA TION: Show one clean Provoker-Taker-Hitter exchange, one guessed counter-parry, and one exchange in which no reply appears and the fencer safely declines the Hitter.

GAME 3 | 1:10-1:20

Keep the expected parry-riposte, but remove the attacker's knowledge of where the reply will arrive.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Students already know the exchange. The new problem is to let the riposte's actual line determine the counter-parry rather than replaying a memorized defense.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. A makes the same agreed first attack. B parries and may riposte to either upper opening.

FENCER A: Attack credibly, observe the riposte, counter-parry the line that appears, and answer the opening produced by that defense.

FENCER B: Parry honestly, then choose either upper opening for the immediate riposte. Vary the choice without deliberately tricking A through unsafe speed or late target changes.

RULES: A may not begin the counter-parry before B's riposte establishes a line. Reset after the final answer, a double, an early defensive guess, or a broken phrase. No preset final target and no points.

ROTATION: Use 90-second roles, then change partners after a complete A/B cycle. Preserve rapid resets so students receive many short decisions.

COACH WATCHES: Does A wait for enough information without becoming late? Does the counter-parry remain compact? Does the final answer grow directly from the defense?

GAME 4 | 1:20-1:30

The expected response may arrive, change, or never appear. The fencer must finish, counter-parry, or leave accordingly.

WHY THIS GAME NOW: Second intention becomes decision-making rather than choreography only when the opponent is permitted to withhold or change the expected response.

STARTING STATE: Full gear and swords. A initiates one credible upper-line attack. B responds naturally with one of three broad answers.

B'S ANSWER A'S DECISION No successful defense Complete the original attack if the line and measure remain valid. Parry and immediate riposte Read the actual line, counter-parry it, and answer cleanly. Parry but no riposte Recover or leave. Do not counter-parry or finish an imagined sequence.

RULES: B does not announce the answer. A receives only one deliberate resolution after the opening attack: finish, counter-parry-riposte, or recover/leave. Reset when the decision is clear, after a clean touch, or after safe separation. No extended scrambling and no points.

ROTATION: Use 90-second roles. Change partners after a complete A/B cycle so the same expectation is tested against different timing and defensive habits.

THE LESSON TEST: Know what you are trying to provoke. Believe only what actually happens.

EXAMPLES LIBRARY

The first example is today's lesson. The others show the larger tactical family and are not additional techniques to teach during this class.

FIRST ACTION EXPECTED RESPONSE PREPARED SECOND INTENTION Credible attack Parry followed by riposte Counter-parry the actual riposte and answer. Today's lesson. Recoverable attack Immediate counterattack Abandon the first finish, parry the counterattack, and riposte. Often called counter-time. Threat to a protected line Opponent searches or closes with the blade Disengage around the committed blade action and finish the newly open line. Pressure in contact Opponent presses strongly back Release or redirect around the committed resistance. Threat at the edge of measure Opponent retreats predictably Use the expected retreat to continue into the new distance without reaching after the old target.

NOT AUTOMATICALLY SECOND INTENTION: An accidental miss followed by another attack, a memorized combination performed regardless of the opponent, or a desperate continuation after being parried does not become second intention merely because it contains multiple actions.

COMPOUND ATTACK RELATIONSHIP: A compound attack describes a physical structure: feint, defensive reaction, final attack. Second intention describes the tactical plan to provoke and defeat an expected response. They can overlap, but neither label automatically proves the other.

TODAY'S BOUNDARY: Teach only the credible attack -> parry-riposte -> counter-parry-riposte family. Use the other examples to clarify the concept, not to expand the class into five unrelated techniques.

OPEN SPARRING | 1:30-2:00

Students fence normally and use second intention selectively against opponents whose defensive habits make the tactic appropriate.

FORMAT: Use normal Steel Crown fencing, intensity agreements, and pairings. Aim for five four-minute rounds with short partner changes, then use the final minutes for gear transition and individual feedback. Adapt freely to the room.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. When someone reliably parries and answers, use a real first attack to invite that response. Counter-parry only the reply that actually comes."

COACH BEHAVIOR: Watch several exchanges before speaking. Give one individual adjustment between rounds. Open sparring is the transfer test, not another constrained game.

TRANSFER EVIDENCE: The first action would land if ignored. The fencer selects second intention against a recognizable defensive habit rather than forcing it every exchange. The counter-parry responds to the actual riposte line. The final answer grows directly from the defense and survives the opponent's return. When the expected response does not appear, the fencer finishes, recovers, or leaves without inventing it.

OPTIONAL CLOSE: Ask one question if it helps: What response did you expect, and what told you it had actually happened?

STEEL CROWN STANDARD: A priority rule may explain who owns an exchange, but a double still fails this lesson. The goal is a clean tactical solution, not a technical argument after being hit.

SAFETY AND COACHING

Reduce speed, uncertainty, or movement volume while preserving the relationship between provocation, evidence, and answer.

SAFETY AND ADAPTATION

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE No-gear game Light touches to shoulders only. No face, head, throat, hard slaps, diving, or collisions. Mixed experience Keep the same decision but give newer students one known line; vary line and timing for experienced students rather than increasing impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, responder, and observer. The observer names the provocation, actual response, and final decision before rotating. Limited space or injury Shorten lanes, lower or remove jumps, reduce sword speed, or use controlled steps. Keep exchanges compact.

COACH TROUBLESHOOTING

IF YOU SEE... DO THIS Decorative first attack Let B ignore it. Require the attack to reach safely before rewarding any continuation. Counter-parry begins early Have B alternate the riposte line or withhold it. Ask A what information started the defense. Sequence becomes mechanical Shorten explanations, change partners, and return to fast resets with only one new defender choice. Huge defensive action Slow the reply and ask for the smallest counter-parry that genuinely removes it. A chases after no reply Use parry-and-hold more often. Require visible recovery or safe separation. Doubles increase Reduce speed and choice. Restore the rule that the final hit counts as learning only when A also survives.

FEEDBACK: Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Correct immediate danger at once; otherwise let the next live exchange test the smallest useful change.

Record what students actually did, where the decision broke down, and what should change in the next delivery.

SOURCES

Meyer supplies the historical tactical relationship. Modern fencing terminology and learning research support the contemporary class design.

docs.text:

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | LIECHTENAUER TRADITION LENS

The class introduces one binary information problem - hard or soft pressure - and two broad responses. It does not attempt to teach the complete winding system.

CENTRAL QUESTION: When the swords meet and remain in contact, how can I use pressure information to choose a safe continuation?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students remain calm at contact, feel whether the opponent is maintaining firm pressure or yielding, and choose a continuation that exploits that relationship without looking down or forcing a memorized technique.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: The Pseudo-Peter von Danzig gloss of Liechtenauer on Feeling, Indes, and working according to soft or hard pressure in the bind.

The target behavior counts only when all four observable conditions are present.

REQUIREMENT OBSERVABLE STANDARD Contact The student maintains useful blade contact long enough to receive information without freezing. Feeling The student distinguishes sustained firm pressure from yielding or light contact. Choice Against firm pressure, the student redirects or leaves the pressure; against soft contact, the student controls through to the opening. Protection The continuation keeps the opponent's threat contained and does not become a strength contest or double.

NO DOUBLE: A result that leaves both fencers validly hit does not satisfy the lesson, even if one blade arrived first.

C | BLOCK 1 | 0:00-0:05

Students understand the problem, success test, and class arc.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Tonight we are solving one problem: When the swords meet and remain in contact, how can I use pressure information to choose a safe continuation?"

SUCCESS DEFINITION: State the four-part success test in plain language and make clear that a double is a failed solution.

CLASS ARC: Experience the problem first; compare what worked; examine one historical lens; increase choice and pressure; test transfer in open fencing.

DO NOT: Teach the complete historical solution before the first game. Students should possess the problem before receiving the model.

C | BLOCK 2 | 0:05-0:20

Maintain postural control while receiving variable partner pressure and redirecting it without stiffening.

WHAT THIS BLOCK IS: A short movement lesson, not conditioning. Demonstrate each exercise once, keep the volume low, and stop or regress when posture or landing quality deteriorates.

TARGET QUALITY: Maintain postural control while receiving variable partner pressure and redirecting it without stiffening.

Use the checklist to distinguish learning from mere scoring.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Attention Looks at opponent while receiving blade information Stares down at crossing Contact Maintains useful, non-rigid connection Loses blade or clamps down Feeling Distinguishes sustained hard/soft pressure Reacts only to collision Choice Updates continuation from pressure Runs memorized technique Structure Point and hilt remain protective Hands collapse or point wanders Outcome Reaches opening without strength contest Pushes harder or doubles Transfer Uses feeling only when bind persists Manufactures static binds

When the swords meet and remain in contact, how can I use pressure information to choose a safe continuation?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE
