docs.title: Primary functional model
docs.text:
At the instant of contact, keep the hands functional and point threatening. If the opponent presses firmly, do not push harder; redirect or leave. If the opponent yields, maintain controlled pressure toward the nearest opening.

Preserve the sequence. If time is lost, compress explanation before removing open sparring or reflection.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival & orientation Define solve the bind i and its success test Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Athletic development Maintain postural control while receiving variable partner pressure and redirecting it without stiffening. Movement readiness 0:20-0:40 Problem exposure Game 1: Hard or Soft Experience the problem 0:40-0:55 Guided coaching Debrief; one useful intervention; variable rehearsal Small intervention 0:55-1:05 Historical integration The Pseudo-Peter von Danzig gloss of Liechtenauer on Feeling, Indes, and working according to soft or hard pressure in the bind. Historical model 1:05-1:30 Progressive constraints Game 2: Changing Pressure; Game 3: Earn the Bind More choice and pressure 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Five 4-minute rounds; normal fencing Transfer 1:55-2:00 Reflection & close Name cues, choices, failures, and next action Consolidation

TIME CHECK: 5 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 5 = 120 minutes.

TRANSITION PLAN: Students gear before the opening. Pair by compatible control and size. Keep masks and gloves on from problem exposure through sparring. Use one audible timer and announce rotations before each interval ends.

IF RUNNING LATE: Shorten the guided discussion or historical explanation by 2-3 minutes and reduce Game 2 by one role interval. Preserve at least one open-sparring round and the reflection.

docs.title: Instructor hypothesis
docs.text: Students will decide the technique before contact, stare at the blades, push against strength, or interpret any initial collision as a stable hard bind.

docs.title: Exercise sequence
docs.text:
EXERCISE DOSE COACHING FOCUS MOVEMENT PURPOSE Grip-pressure scale 2 x 20 seconds Use 2-4 of 10 grip; shoulders relaxed Separate sensitivity from excessive gripping Partner palm pressure 2 x 30 seconds each Feel changes through contact; do not anticipate Introduce hard/soft information without swords Split-stance anti-rotation hold 2 x 15 seconds each side Ribs over hips; breathe; feet quiet Maintain structure under lateral pressure Press-or-yield step reaction 3 x 20 seconds each Follow yield; redirect pressure; no tugging Connect tactile cue to an immediate directional choice

Preserve the information and decision while reducing uncertainty, speed, distance, or impact.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE First-time student Use a known attack or response, longer preparation time, controlled partner, and score safe resolution as success. Mixed experience Give beginners less uncertainty; give experienced students more choice or rhythm variation, not greater impact. Odd attendance Use attacker, defender, and observer. Observer applies the four-part success test, then roles rotate. Limited space Use narrow lanes; prohibit passing and large leaps; emphasize compact footwork and controlled stops. Injury / low impact Replace bounds with steps; reduce speed and contact; permit observer or limited-role participation. Large attendance Create lanes, assign a senior student to each cluster, and synchronize changes with one timer. Game breaks down Remove one variable, increase distance, slow the action, or return to a known starting state. Time loss Compress explanation and one role interval; preserve open transfer and reflection.

docs.title: How to perform the exercises
docs.text:
GAME CARD 3

Connect tactile decision-making to the exchange that creates contact.

STARTING STATE: Free onset; one fencer initiates a controlled cut that the other may meet, avoid, or counter.

PLAYER GOALS: If sustained contact occurs, either fencer may solve it using pressure information. No one is required to remain in a poor bind.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Normal movement; no grappling; continue to clean score, double, or safe separation.

SCORING: Clean score after correct bind decision 2; any other clean score 1; double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Change initiator every 3 minutes; final minute reset.

COACH OBSERVES: Natural contact, calm feeling, selective leaving, point control, and decisions based on present pressure.

PROGRESSION: Open fencing with no designated initiator.

REGRESSION: Require one known cut and parry to create the same bind.

docs.title: 1. GRIP-PRESSURE SCALE
docs.text:
Hold the sword only if the room is ready; otherwise use an imaginary handle. Squeeze as hard as possible for one second to identify 10 of 10, release fully to 0, then settle at 2-4. Open and close the fingers without changing wrist position. Cue: 'Secure enough to transmit information, relaxed enough to receive it.'

C | BLOCK 6 | 1:05-1:30

Increase uncertainty while preserving the lesson's central information-action relationship.

GAME CARD 2

Prevent students from treating hard and soft as fixed partner identities.

STARTING STATE: Begin from blade contact created by a controlled cut and parry. Pressure leader may remain firm, yield, or change once.

PLAYER GOALS: Solver follows current information and reaches a safe opening without losing control.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: One pressure change maximum; no grappling; halt on clean touch, double, or broken contact with safe separation.

SCORING: Correct adaptation and clean touch 2; safe disengagement 1; leader clean hit 1; double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes transition.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the solver updates after the pressure changes and whether the point remains relevant.

PROGRESSION: Remove the designated pressure leader.

REGRESSION: Hold one pressure for two seconds and announce the change.

docs.title: 2. PARTNER PALM PRESSURE
docs.text:
Partners touch one palm at chest height. The leader alternates between gently pressing forward and softening or withdrawing the hand. The follower keeps contact without leaning and takes one small step: redirect diagonally when pressure grows, follow forward when it softens. Change slowly and unpredictably. Cue: 'Do not guess; let pressure tell you.'

C | BLOCK 4 | 0:40-0:55

Use the first game's evidence to provide the smallest intervention that improves the class.

C | BLOCK 5 | 0:55-1:05

Connect the experienced tactical problem to a documented historical principle without claiming that the source prescribes the modern game.

SOURCE IDENTIFICATION: The Pseudo-Peter von Danzig gloss of Liechtenauer on Feeling, Indes, and working according to soft or hard pressure in the bind.

VERIFIED HISTORICAL CLAIM: The Pseudo-Peter von Danzig gloss instructs the fencer to feel whether the opponent is soft or hard as the swords meet and then work Indes according to that perception, toward the nearest opening. It explicitly warns against hasty winding before the pressure is perceived. [1]

MODERN TRAINING INTERPRETATION: From a right-side bind, if the partner remains firm, keep cover and redirect around or disengage to the available opening. If the partner yields, maintain controlled blade relationship and advance the point. These are introductory functional categories, not a claim that every bind has only two techniques.

DEMONSTRATION: Show three slow examples: one successful application, one common failure, and one case in which the action should be declined. Let students rehearse briefly, then return to live choice.

EVIDENCE LINE: Historical text supplies the cited principle or action. The success test, games, scoring, cues, and safety adaptations are modern coaching design.

docs.title: 3. SPLIT-STANCE ANTI-ROTATION HOLD
docs.text:
Stand in fencing stance. Partner places one open hand lightly on the student's forearm or shoulder and applies gentle sideways pressure for three seconds. Student stays tall, breathes, and resists only enough to keep posture. No sudden shoves. Switch sides. Cue: 'Structure, not stiffness.'

C | BLOCK 3 | 0:20-0:40

Make tactile information determine the continuation.

STARTING STATE: Begin in a safe crossed-blade position at medium distance, points off-line. One partner secretly chooses firm pressure or soft/yielding contact.

PLAYER GOALS: Solver identifies the pressure through contact and makes the matching controlled action: redirect around firm pressure or maintain control through soft contact.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: No initial strike; action begins on a neutral cue; slow speed; halt after one continuation.

SCORING: Correct read and protected touch 2; correct read without touch 1; wrong-direction force or double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partners and repeat from the opposite bind.

INSTRUCTOR OBSERVES: Pre-planning, staring down, grip tension, pushing harder, loss of point threat, and confusing impact with sustained pressure.

COACH POSTURE: Observe across the room before intervening. Record common patterns and let several exchanges occur before deciding what the class needs.

docs.title: 4. PRESS-OR-YIELD STEP REACTION
docs.text:
Partners connect both palms or padded forearms. Leader either increases steady pressure or softly removes it. On pressure, follower takes a short diagonal step and guides the contact past; on yield, follower takes one controlled forward step while maintaining contact. Reset after each choice. Cue: 'Pressure: redirect. Yield: follow.'

REGRESSION AND STOP RULE: Reduce speed, distance, or impact; replace jumps with controlled steps. Stop for pain, dizziness, repeated loss of balance, loud uncontrolled landings, or a student who cannot maintain the described posture.

docs.title: Representative problem exposure: Hard or Soft
Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. What did firm pressure feel like in your hands?

  2. What changed when the opponent yielded?

  3. When did you start making the decision?

  4. How did looking at the opponent rather than the blades affect your response?

PRIMARY INTERVENTION: Demonstrate equal pushing, abandoning contact blindly, and two functional responses. Cue: 'Feel first: pressure redirects you; absence lets you go through.' Clarify that hard/soft is relational and can change.

VARIABLE REHEARSAL: Partners re-test the target problem at approximately 60-70% intensity. Keep at least one meaningful variable - side, rhythm, distance, pressure, or response - rather than feeding identical repetitions.

FEEDBACK PLAN: Use one cue at a time. Correct immediate danger at once; otherwise give feedback between sets of three attempts. Ask the student to identify the information that shaped the action.

AVOID: Turning the block into a long lecture or adding several fixes before students can test the first one.

docs.title: Game 2 - Changing Pressure | 12 minutes
docs.text:
Prevent students from treating hard and soft as fixed partner identities.

  • Begin from blade contact created by a controlled cut and parry. Pressure leader may remain firm, yield, or change once.

  • Solver follows current information and reaches a safe opening without losing control.

  • One pressure change maximum; no grappling; halt on clean touch, double, or broken contact with safe separation.

  • Correct adaptation and clean touch 2; safe disengagement 1; leader clean hit 1; double 0.

  • 5 minutes each role; 2 minutes transition.

C | BLOCK 7 | 1:30-1:55

Test whether the behavior appears without forced actions or bonus scoring.

FORMAT: Five 4-minute rounds with approximately 1 minute between rounds for rotation and brief feedback. Use normal open-fencing rules and the club's usual intensity agreement.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Fence normally. If meaningful blade contact persists, resist the urge to force a favorite action: feel the present pressure, choose, and keep the opponent's threat contained."

PAIRING PLAN: Use compatible control and size, then rotate across different rhythms and preferences. Supervise novice pairings and avoid a large mismatch solely to complete the rotation.

C | BLOCK 8 | 1:55-2:00

Students consolidate one usable cue and one testable next action.

GAME CARD 1

Make tactile information determine the continuation.

STARTING STATE: Begin in a safe crossed-blade position at medium distance, points off-line. One partner secretly chooses firm pressure or soft/yielding contact.

PLAYER GOALS: Solver identifies the pressure through contact and makes the matching controlled action: redirect around firm pressure or maintain control through soft contact.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: No initial strike; action begins on a neutral cue; slow speed; halt after one continuation.

SCORING: Correct read and protected touch 2; correct read without touch 1; wrong-direction force or double 0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes each role; change partners and repeat from the opposite bind.

COACH OBSERVES: Pre-planning, staring down, grip tension, pushing harder, loss of point threat, and confusing impact with sustained pressure.

PROGRESSION: Vary pressure after contact rather than setting it in advance.

REGRESSION: Leader announces hard or soft after establishing it and holds the pressure longer.

docs.title: Game 3 - Earn the Bind | 13 minutes
docs.text:
Connect tactile decision-making to the exchange that creates contact.

  • Free onset; one fencer initiates a controlled cut that the other may meet, avoid, or counter.

  • If sustained contact occurs, either fencer may solve it using pressure information. No one is required to remain in a poor bind.

  • Normal movement; no grappling; continue to clean score, double, or safe separation.

  • Clean score after correct bind decision 2; any other clean score 1; double 0.
  • Change initiator every 3 minutes; final minute reset.

PROGRESSION TRIGGER: Open fencing with no designated initiator.

REGRESSION TRIGGER: Require one known cut and parry to create the same bind.

docs.title: Coach records
docs.text:
• Looks at opponent while receiving blade information
  • Maintains useful, non-rigid connection
  • Distinguishes sustained hard/soft pressure
  • Updates continuation from pressure
  • Point and hilt remain protective
  • Reaches opening without strength contest
  • Uses feeling only when bind persists

FEEDBACK: Observe during rounds and coach mainly between them. Open sparring is not another constrained game.

docs.title: Whole-group questions
docs.text:
1. What tactile cue separated firm from yielding contact?

  2. When did redirecting work better than pushing?

  3. When was leaving the bind safer than staying?

INDIVIDUAL NEXT ACTION: Each student states one small, observable action they will test the next time this problem appears.

INSTRUCTOR CLOSE: Restate the functional success test, not a technique name. Record any safety issue, equipment problem, or student who needs a lower-intensity follow-up.

END ON TIME: Do not let the final sparring round consume reflection. The class is incomplete until students name the information that shaped their decision.

docs.title: Plan modifications before the room forces them
What to watch without interrupting every exchange
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Name what happened, ask what information the student perceived, offer one change, and let the next round test it.

SOURCES AND FINAL GATE

Historical claims are kept narrower than the modern class design. Representative games preserve opponent information and live decisions, but no source proves that this exact lesson is uniquely optimal.

[1] Pseudo-Peter von Danzig. Cod. 44.A.8, fols. 14r.2 and 29r.2, glosses on hard/soft, Feeling, and Indes. Wiktenauer concordance and translations

[2] Liechtenauer, Johannes. Recital and gloss tradition, verses on Weak, Strong, and Indes. Wiktenauer source overview

[3] Cheney, Stephen. Ringeck, Danzig, Lew Longsword. 2020.

[4] Pinder, Ross A., Keith Davids, Ian Renshaw, and Duarte Araújo. "Representative Learning Design and Functionality of Research and Practice in Sport." Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 33, no. 1 (2011): 146-155. doi:10.1123/jsep.33.1.146. PubMed record

[5] Renshaw, Ian, Jia Yi Chow, Keith Davids, and John Hammond. "A Constraints-Led Perspective to Understanding Skill Acquisition and Game Play." Physical Education and Sport Pedagogy 24, no. 2 (2019): 103-116. doi:10.1080/17408989.2018.1552676. DOI

TERMS: Historical terminology and English renderings vary by manuscript and translation. This plan paraphrases short claims and identifies modern coaching labels as modern.

READY: Do not rush the bind: maintain useful contact, feel the present pressure, work according to it, and keep the threat contained.

docs.title: Class-level success evidence
docs.text:
• Cleaner solutions and fewer doubles from Game 1 to Game 3.
  • Students can name at least one reliable cue.
  • The target behavior appears selectively in open fencing.
  • Students can explain why an unsafe score does not satisfy the lesson.
  • Beginners show safer structure even when they do not score.

docs.title: Striking While Defending I
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

← All classes and lessons

Class context: 120 MINUTES | MEYER HISTORICAL LENS

This plan narrows the class to countering committed high cuts. It does not attempt to teach counterattacks against every possible action.

CENTRAL QUESTION: How can I strike into an incoming attack so that one continuous action both protects me and hits my opponent?

END-OF-CLASS BEHAVIOR: Students recognize a committed high cut and choose a one-action countercut that intercepts the incoming blade, lands on a valid target, moves the head or body away from the attack's path, and avoids the double.

HISTORICAL ANCHOR: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part One: Longsword, Chapter 5, especially I.16r.3-I.16v.1. The Zwerchhau is the primary historical example.

The target behavior is not simply a simultaneous hit. All four conditions must be present.

REQUIREMENT OBSERVABLE STANDARD 1. Information The response begins from information in the opponent's committed attack, not a blind guess. 2. One action One continuous sword action intercepts the attack and reaches a valid target. 3. Protection Blade, crossguard, hands, footwork, and body position remove or contain the incoming threat. 4. No double The opponent does not also land a valid hit.

NO DOUBLE: A countercut that lands but fails to remove the incoming threat is a failed attempt for this class, even if the defender's hit arrived first.

C | BLOCK 2 | 0:05-0:20

Students rehearse reactive lateral displacement and finish in a stable fencing position without accumulating unnecessary fatigue.

WHAT THIS BLOCK IS: This is a short movement lesson, not a fitness circuit. Students perform the exercises without swords, using small amounts of explosive movement and full control. Demonstrate each exercise once, let students try it, then correct one quality at a time. The goal is to rehearse moving the target out of the attack's path and arriving in a position from which the sword can work.

TARGET QUALITY: Explosive lateral or diagonal movement followed by a quiet, balanced landing and immediately usable posture. Students should finish each repetition able to move, cut, or defend immediately - not stumble, stand up, or reset their feet.

docs.title: Striking While Defending I
docs.text:
How can I strike into an incoming attack so that one action both protects me and hits my opponent?

LESSON | INSTRUCTORS AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | July 2026 | Version 1.2

docs.title: Primary technical model
docs.text:
The Zwerchhau provides a clear model: the defender receives the incoming high cut on the strong near the crossguard while the outer portion of the blade reaches the side of the opponent's mask. High hands and an offline step create the protective geometry.

C | BLOCK 1 | 0:00-0:05

Every student understands the problem, success test, contact level, and stop rules.

OPENING SENTENCE: "Tonight we are solving one problem: how to attack into an opponent's attack without simply trading hits."

READINESS SCAN: Confirm full protective equipment. Ask for injuries or low-impact needs. Identify first-time students and pair them with controlled, communicative partners.

SUCCESS DEFINITION: The counterattack succeeds only if one continuous sword action both intercepts and hits while the defender remains unhit.

CLASS ARC: Experience the timing problem first; compare what worked; examine Meyer's Zwerchhau as a historical answer; increase choice and pressure; test transfer in open fencing.

DO NOT: Demonstrate the Zwerchhau yet. Students should encounter the tactical problem before receiving the complete historical model.

docs.title: Allowed discovery
docs.text:
Students may find another safe one-action solution. The class rewards the function - perceive, intercept, hit, remain protected - rather than requiring every student to reproduce one named cut.

Preserve the sequence. If time is lost, compress explanation before removing open sparring or reflection.

TIME BLOCK PLAN FOR THIS CLASS OUTPUT 0:00-0:05 Arrival & orientation Define one action doing two jobs; set safety and scoring Clear problem 0:05-0:20 Athletic development Reactive lateral movement; bound-and-stick; stable posture Move target + establish base 0:20-0:40 Problem exposure Game 1: One Action, Two Jobs Experience the timing problem 0:40-0:55 Guided coaching Debrief; protective geometry; variable rehearsal Small useful intervention 0:55-1:05 Historical integration Meyer 1570, Ch. 5; Zwerchhau example Historical model 1:05-1:30 Progressive constraints Game 2: Two Doors; Game 3: Earn It From the Onset More choice and pressure 1:30-1:55 Open sparring Five 4-minute rounds; use only when opportunity is real Transfer without bonus scoring 1:55-2:00 Reflection & close Cue, geometry, and double analysis; next action Consolidated learning

TIME CHECK: 5 + 15 + 20 + 15 + 10 + 25 + 25 + 5 = 120 minutes. Problem exposure, progressive constraints, and open sparring provide repeated live-opponent work before the final reflection.

TRANSITION PLAN: Students gear before the five-minute opening. Pair by adjacent height and compatible intensity for Game 1. Keep masks and gloves on from 0:20 through the end of sparring. Use one audible timer and announce the next pairing before each rest interval.

IF RUNNING LATE: Shorten the guided debrief or historical explanation by 2-3 minutes and reduce Game 2 by one role interval. Do not remove the final open-sparring round or reflection.

docs.title: Instructor hypothesis
docs.text: The most common failure will be treating the counterattack as a race. Students are likely to prioritize arrival speed over blade relationship and body displacement, creating doubles. Scoring and coaching must keep protection non-negotiable.

docs.title: Exercise sequence
docs.text: EXERCISE DOSE COACHING FOCUS MOVEMENT PURPOSE Movement preparation Skipping, lateral shuffle, ankle and shoulder preparation Relaxed rhythm; usable posture Prepare the feet, ankles, shoulders, and general movement rhythm Low-level plyometrics Pogo hops 2 x 10; lateral line hops 2 x 6/side; 20-30 sec rest Short ground contact; quiet feet Rehearse elastic stiffness and quick lateral contacts Lateral bound and stick 2 x 3/side; hold 2 sec; 30-45 sec rest Knee tracks; chest controlled Displace the target and finish in a stable fencing base Reactive step and stabilize Partner visual cue; 3 x 15 sec each; ~30 sec rest Move target; establish base Connect visual reaction to a short diagonal step and usable posture

docs.title: How to perform the exercises
docs.text:
Use the checklist to distinguish learning from mere scoring.

DOMAIN LOOK FOR COMMON FAILURE Perception Waits for a committed cue; can name what initiated the response Guesses from guard or moves before commitment Timing Begins early enough to establish interception, not merely race Late panic cut or pre-emptive swing Blade Strong receives; outer blade reaches; hands stay protective Weak-to-strong collision; hands collapse Footwork Short offline or closing step supports the sword action Straight-line collision; overlarge leap Body Head and torso leave or close the incoming line Hit lands while body remains exposed Outcome One action, valid hit, no double Two actions or accepted double Transfer Action appears selectively in open fencing Forced attempts regardless of opportunity Adaptation Declines or changes solution when cue/geometry is wrong Repeats the target action as a script
  • Source link 1 (original page 20)
  • Source link 2 (original page 20)

docs.title: 1. MOVEMENT PREPARATION
docs.text:
Begin with 30-45 seconds of relaxed skipping in place or moving forward. Skipping means stepping onto one foot while the other knee rises, then switching sides in a light rhythm; it is not a high jump. Follow with 30-45 seconds of lateral shuffling: stay in a comfortable athletic stance, take short side steps, and do not let the feet cross. Finish with ankle rocks and shoulder circles: gently move the knees forward over the toes while the heels stay down, then make controlled shoulder circles. Repeat the shuffle in the other direction. The instructor should see relaxed rhythm, quiet feet, and an upright but ready posture.

The target is skilled perception and protective geometry. More speed is never the default solution to a struggling task.

CONDITION PLANNED RESPONSE First-time student Known attack side; no time limit; slow rehearsal; experienced partner; score safe defense as success. Mixed experience Beginners receive less uncertainty; experienced students receive rhythm variation and one feint, not greater impact. Odd attendance Three-person group: attacker, defender, observer. Observer applies the four-part success test, then roles rotate. Limited space Use narrow lanes; prohibit passing and large lateral leaps; emphasize short diagonal steps and stable posture. Injury / low impact Use step-and-stick instead of bounds; reduce speed/contact; permit observer or attacker- only role as needed. Large attendance Create lanes; assign a senior student to each cluster; synchronize role changes with one timer. Game breaks down Remove one variable: fix attack side, slow speed, increase distance, or remove the feint. Time loss Compress explanation and one constrained role interval; preserve at least one open round and the reflection block.

docs.title: 2. POGO HOPS
docs.text:
Stand with the feet about hip-width apart and the knees slightly soft. Bounce vertically using the ankles, as if the floor were a spring. The jumps should be small - only a few centimeters - and the heels should come up naturally. Land on the balls of the feet and let the ankles, knees, and hips soften together. Keep the torso tall and the eyes forward. Perform 10 contacts, rest, and repeat. Cue: 'Small, springy, and quiet.' Do not squat deeply or try to jump for height.

GAME CARD 3

Release the skill into a representative onset where the opportunity must be recognized rather than supplied.

STARTING STATE: Free onset. One designated initiator must launch a high-line attack within eight seconds.

PLAYER GOALS: Initiator creates a credible high-line attack using distance, guard changes, and at most one feint. Defender fences freely.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Continue to clean hit, double, or clear disengagement. Normal movement; no forced counterattack.

SCORING: Target countercut 2; any other clean score 1; double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: Change initiator every 3 minutes; use the remaining minute for reset before open sparring.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the defender waits for commitment; whether deception creates premature action; whether declining the counter is tactically correct.

PROGRESSION: Remove the designated initiator and continue directly into open sparring.

REGRESSION: Remove the feint, extend the time limit, reveal the attack side, or increase starting distance.

docs.title: 3. LATERAL LINE HOPS
docs.text:
Place a floor line, strip of tape, or imaginary line beside the feet. Keep both feet together and hop a short distance over the line to one side, then back over it. The feet should travel only a few inches; the emphasis is quick side-to-side contacts, not distance. Complete 6 hops toward one side and 6 back, or use 12 total contacts if that is easier to count. Cue: 'Stay light and keep the landing underneath you.' If the feet become noisy or the student loses balance, make the hops smaller.

C | BLOCK 6 | 1:05-1:30

Students compare the target countercut with other defenses, then re-test it from a freer onset with deception and tactical choice.

GAME CARD 2

Let students compare the target action with safer sequential defenses while preserving the value of the target skill.

STARTING STATE: Just outside measure; attacker may cut high from either side and vary timing and distance.

PLAYER GOALS: Attacker earns a clean hit. Defender chooses freely among one-action countercut, parry-riposte, or safe defense.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: No feints; no thrusts or grappling; exchange ends on clean hit, double, or clear safe disengagement.

SCORING: Target countercut 2; any other clean score 1; attacker clean hit 1; double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 5 minutes in each role; 2 minutes total for explanation and transition.

COACH OBSERVES: Whether the student selects the target action only when appropriate; whether parry-riposte becomes a useful fallback.

PROGRESSION: Add rhythm changes, a false step, or a freer starting guard.

REGRESSION: Fix the attack side, slow the action, or restore the one-action defender rule for diagnosis.

docs.title: 4. LATERAL BOUND AND STICK
docs.text:
Start balanced on the right foot with the left foot lightly off the floor. Bend the standing knee slightly, push sideways, and make a small leap to land on the left foot. Freeze the landing for two seconds. The landing foot should be under the body, the knee should point in the same direction as the toes, and the chest should remain controlled rather than falling sideways. Repeat in the opposite direction. Begin with a step instead of a leap if needed. Cue: 'Travel a little, own the landing.' Do not chase maximum distance.

C | BLOCK 3 | 0:20-0:40

Students encounter the one-action counterattack problem against an adaptive opponent before receiving a complete technical answer.

GAME: One Action, Two Jobs

STARTING STATE: Both begin just outside attacking measure. The attacker may begin from either shoulder; the defender may use any guard.

ATTACKER GOAL: Within four seconds, enter and deliver one genuine but controlled high cut from either side. Choose the side, timing, and distance. No feint yet.

DEFENDER GOAL: Respond after recognizing the attack. Use only one sword action; footwork is unrestricted. Attempt to intercept and hit without being hit.

SCORING: Attacker: 1 point for a clean hit without being hit. Defender: 2 points for a clean single-action countercut; 1 point for safely defending without scoring. Double: 0 points for both. Backing out of the lane earns no defender point.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 2 minutes to explain and establish lanes; 4 minutes in each role; change partner; repeat 4 minutes in each role; use the final 2 minutes to reset, hydrate, and collect observations.

C | BLOCK 4 | 0:40-0:55

Students name what happened, then test the smallest intervention likely to improve protection and timing.

C | BLOCK 5 | 0:55-1:05

Students connect their experienced problem to Meyer's example of counteracting and hitting in the same action.

SOURCE IDENTIFICATION: Joachim Meyer, Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (Strasbourg, 1570), Part One: Longsword, Chapter 5, sections 7-9, fols. I.16r.3-I.16v.1.

VERIFIED HISTORICAL CLAIM: Meyer distinguishes ordinary counteraction from actions that counteract and hit together. He associates this second function with inverted cuts including the Schielhau, Glützhau, Kronhau, and Zwerchhau, then gives the Zwerchhau as his example. [1]

MEYER'S EXAMPLE: From Zornhut, when a high cut arrives, step the right foot toward the opponent's side and cut a short- edge Zwerchhau inward. Receive the attack on the strong near the crossguard and strike the opponent's left ear with the outer part of the sword. [1]

MODERN TRAINING INTERPRETATION: The side of the mask replaces the historical ear target. We judge the action by whether it removes the incoming threat, not merely by whether the defender's blade arrives. 'Single-time counterattack' is used here as a modern coaching label for the function.

DEMONSTRATION: Show three slow, controlled examples. Emphasize high hands, the strong receiving near the hilt, the blade reaching beyond the contact, and the step shifting the target away from the attack.

INSTRUCTION INTO NEXT GAME: "The Zwerch is our clearest historical model. In the next task it earns the target score, but another solution may succeed if it truly intercepts, hits, protects, and avoids the double."

EVIDENCE LINE: Historical text: Meyer describes a specific action and purpose. Instructor interpretation: the protective geometry and coaching cues. Modern adaptation: mask target, safety limits, scoring, and competition transfer.

docs.title: 5. REACTIVE STEP AND STABILIZE
docs.text:
Pair students without swords. One student is the leader and the other is the mover. The leader faces the mover and gives a clear visual cue by pointing or making a small hand motion to the left, right, or a short diagonal. On seeing the cue, the mover takes one quick step in that direction, stops, and holds a balanced fencing-ready position for two seconds. The leader then gives a new cue. Switch roles after the short round. The mover should not guess before the cue. Cue: 'See it, move once, arrive ready.' Keep the step short enough that the student can stop under control.

FENCING CONNECTION: The defender must move the target while establishing a position from which the sword can intercept and hit. The landing should support the cut rather than occur as a separate preliminary movement. The athletic block is not teaching the Zwerchhau yet; it is preparing the movement qualities the later fencing task will require.

REGRESSION: Replace every jump with a fast step-and-stick. Reduce distance and remove the partner reaction cue.

STOP RULE: Regress or stop if landings become loud, balance deteriorates, the knee collapses inward, speed falls sharply, or anyone experiences pain.

AVOID: Turning this block into conditioning. Preserve speed, landing quality, and enough energy for the fencing problem.

docs.title: Coach observes
docs.text:
• Guessing before the attack supplies usable information.
  • Countercuts that land but fail to close the incoming line.
  • Passive blocks followed by a second attacking motion.
  • Hands dropping below the incoming blade.
  • Straight-line entries that leave the head in the attack's path.
  • Successful use of the strong to receive while the outer blade reaches the target.

COACH ROLE: Observe patterns across the room. Correct immediate safety issues, but do not stop every failed attempt.

docs.title: Debrief questions
docs.text:
1. What told you the attack was genuinely beginning?

  2. Where did the blades meet when the counter worked?

  3. What caused a successful-looking attempt to become a double?

  4. What happened when you moved straight backward or stayed directly on the attack's path?

PRIMARY INTERVENTION: "Move your head behind your sword as your strong takes their cut." Show the relationship among high hands, crossguard, strong of the blade, target displacement, and the outer blade reaching the opponent.

THREE-WAY COMPARISON: Briefly demonstrate: (1) hitting into the attack and trading; (2) blocking first and attacking afterward; and (3) one continuous action whose geometry both intercepts and hits.

VARIABLE REHEARSAL: For approximately eight minutes, the attacker delivers controlled high cuts from either side at 60-70% intensity and varies timing and distance. The defender tests the intervention. Pause only between sets of three attempts.

FEEDBACK PLAN: Use one cue at a time. Give safety-critical corrections immediately. Otherwise, ask the student what changed and provide feedback between sets rather than during the action.

AVOID: Adding several technical fixes at once or converting the block into a long Zwerchhau lecture.

docs.title: Game 2 - Two Doors | 12 minutes
docs.text:
The attacker may make a high cut from either side and vary distance and rhythm. The defender may use any defense and is no longer limited to one sword action.

  • Clean single-action countercut: 2 points.
  • Any other clean hit, including parry-riposte: 1 point.
  • Clean attacker hit: 1 point.
  • Double: 0 points.
  • Fence five minutes in each role, with two minutes total for explanation and transition.

C | BLOCK 7 | 1:30-1:55

Students transfer the behavior into the least constrained environment and abandon it when the opportunity is wrong.

FORMAT: Five 4-minute rounds with approximately 1 minute between rounds to rotate, breathe, and receive brief feedback. Use normal open-fencing rules and the club's usual intensity agreements.

PAIRING PLAN: Start with compatible size and control. Rotate so students encounter different rhythms and attack preferences. Keep novice pairings supervised; do not use a large skill mismatch merely to complete the rotation.

SHARED OBJECTIVE: "Do not manufacture the countercut. Fence normally and use it only when you perceive a committed attack that gives you the opportunity."

INDIVIDUAL OBJECTIVES: Defenders: recognize commitment, attempt the action only with a real cue, and reduce doubles. Attackers: continue building credible attacks rather than feeding the lesson. Advanced students: notice when the opportunity should be declined.

C | BLOCK 8 | 1:55-2:00

Students consolidate one usable cue and choose one small action for their next training exposure.

GAME CARD 1

Expose the difference between interception and doubling before formal instruction.

STARTING STATE: Just outside attacking measure. Attacker may start from either shoulder; defender from any guard.

PLAYER GOALS: Attacker lands one controlled high cut. Defender recognizes it and attempts one sword action that intercepts and hits.

RULES AND CONSTRAINTS: Attack within four seconds; no feints; defender gets one sword action; footwork is free; halt after hit or double.

SCORING: Attacker clean hit 1; defender target action 2; safe defense only 1; double 0-0.

DOSE AND ROTATION: 4 minutes in each role; change partner; repeat. Explain and reset within the 20-minute block.

COACH OBSERVES: Guessing, low hands, late passive blocks, straight-line collision, contact on defender's weak, clean strong-to-weak relationship.

PROGRESSION: Allow variable rhythm or begin from a freer onset.

REGRESSION: Use one known attack side, slower speed, and greater starting distance.

docs.title: Game 3 - Earn It From the Onset | 13 minutes
docs.text:
Both begin in a free onset. One fencer is designated the initiator and must launch a high-line attack within eight seconds. The initiator may change guards, manipulate distance, and use one feint. The defender fences freely; continue until a clean hit, double, or clear disengagement.

  • Target single-action countercut: 2 points.
  • Any other clean score: 1 point.
  • Double: 0 points.
  • Change roles every three minutes; use the remaining minute for reset and transition.

PROGRESSION TRIGGER: Increase speed, side choice, or deception only when the defender consistently receives the attack on the strong, lands, and remains protected.

REGRESSION TRIGGER: If students guess, close their eyes, collide, or accept doubles, remove the feint, increase starting distance, lower speed, or return to one known attack side.

MIXED-EXPERIENCE CHALLENGE: Beginners receive a known attack side and longer preparation time. Experienced fencers face either side, variable rhythm, and one feint, but not additional power.

docs.title: Coach records
docs.text:
• Was the response based on a real attacking cue or a guess?
  • Did one continuous action both protect and threaten?
  • Did the strong receive the incoming blade?
  • Did the body leave or close the attack's line?
  • Did the behavior appear without bonus scoring?
  • Did the fencer abandon the attempt when the timing or geometry was wrong?

FEEDBACK: Observe during rounds; coach primarily between rounds. Open sparring is not another constrained game.

docs.title: Whole-group questions
docs.text:
1. What was the earliest reliable cue that the attack was committed?

  2. What blade-and-foot relationship produced your cleanest result?

  3. What caused the action to become a double?

INDIVIDUAL NEXT ACTION: Each student states one testable action. Example: 'Next time I will wait for commitment instead of guessing,' or 'I will keep my hands above the incoming blade as I move offline.'

INSTRUCTOR CLOSE: Reinforce that the lesson is selective interception, not cutting simultaneously into every attack. Record any safety issue, gear problem, or student who needs a lower-intensity follow-up.

NATURAL FOLLOW-UP CLASS: How do we create or invite the committed high attack that makes a single-action countercut available?

END ON TIME: Do not let the final sparring round consume reflection. The class is incomplete until students name what informed the decision.

docs.title: Plan modifications before the room forces them
What to watch without interrupting every exchange
Between-round feedback formula
docs.text:
Observation -> question -> one cue -> re-test. Example: 'Your cut landed, but their blade also reached you. Where did the blades meet? On the next attempt, keep your hands high enough that your strong takes their cut.'

SOURCES AND FINAL GATE

The class design is a modern coaching application. The cited historical claim is narrower: Meyer explicitly describes cuts that counteract and hit together and gives the Zwerchhau as an example.

[1] Meyer, Joachim. Gründtliche Beschreibung der Kunst des Fechtens (1570), Part One: Longsword, Chapter 5, sections 7-9, fols. I.16r.3-I.16v.1. Wiktenauer transcription and Garber-Chidester translation

[2] Meyer, Joachim. The Art of Combat: A German Martial Arts Treatise of 1570, 2nd ed., translated by Jeffrey L. Forgeng. Frontline Books, 2015. Part One, Chapter 5.

[3] Meyer, Joachim. Foundational Description of the Art of Fencing: The 1570 Treatise of Joachim Meyer, translated by Rebecca L. R. Garber and edited by Michael Chidester. HEMA Bookshelf, 2023; revised 2025. Publisher information

TERMS: Terminology varies by translation: Zwerchhau may appear as Crosswise Cut, Thwart Cut, or related spellings. This plan retains the familiar German term and paraphrases rather than presenting a long quotation.

READY: Teach the function, not the name: perceive the committed attack, intercept and hit in one continuous action, remain protected, and do not double.

docs.text:

  • Students can identify at least one reliable cue of commitment.
  • Students use the action selectively during open sparring.
  • Students can explain why a landed double does not satisfy the target.
  • Beginners show safer structure even if they do not yet score.

docs.title: Fencing Concepts
docs.text:
← Back to Materials

Techniques are specific. Principles are general.

This section covers foundational concepts that apply across weapon systems and historical traditions. Understanding these principles gives you a framework for reading exchanges, diagnosing why something failed, and making better decisions under pressure, regardless of what you are holding.

The concepts here are not alternatives to the weapon-specific curricula. They are the underlying logic that makes those curricula coherent. A student who understands lines, openings, opposition, and structure will learn specific techniques faster and retain them better.

docs.title: What's Inside
docs.text:
The Four Openings — How the body is divided into targets, and why that vocabulary matters for every exchange.

Inside and Outside Line — The most practically useful spatial concept in fencing. Where your weapon is relative to your opponent's determines what options are available to both of you.

Opposition and Cover — The difference between deflecting an attack and controlling the line. Why some defenses hold and others don't.

Structure — What makes a position strong. The difference between a blade that looks threatening and one that actually is.

docs.title: Inside and Outside Line
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

Core principle

Where your weapon is relative to your opponent's weapon determines what both of you can do.

This is not a subtle point. It is probably the single most practically useful spatial concept in fencing. Students who understand it make better decisions in sparring immediately. Students who do not understand it repeat the same errors indefinitely without knowing why.

Main point

Your position relative to your opponent's weapon is the first thing to read in any exchange.

Foundations

Line Definition Inside The inside line is the space between your opponent's weapon and their centerline. If your blade is on the inside line, it is positioned between their guard and the center of their body. Outside The outside line is the space on the far side of their weapon arm. If your blade is on the outside line, it is positioned away from their centerline, on the side of their weapon hand or beyond it.

A simpler way to feel the distinction: on the inside line, your blade and their blade are in the same general space. On the outside line, your blade has cleared their weapon entirely and is approaching from a direction they cannot easily address with it.

Decision-making

From the inside line, both weapons are competing for the same space. Your attack and their parry are likely to meet. Your thrust goes toward the center of their body, but their blade can reach it. You can threaten directly, but so can they.

From the outside line, their weapon cannot easily reach your blade without a significant change of position. You are attacking from an angle their guard does not naturally cover. This is why gaining the outside line is a central goal in most fencing systems — not because it is safe, but because it limits what the opponent can do in response.

The Exchange of Thrusts works precisely because the offline step moves your body to the outside line while your blade returns on the inside. Your target is exposed. Theirs is not.

Movement and adaptation

Lines are not fixed. They shift constantly as the exchange develops.

A step offline can move you from the inside to the outside line in a single motion. A crossing of the blades can reverse which fencer holds which line. A beat or deflection that moves the opponent's blade past center puts them on the outside line.

The goal is not to be on the outside line once. It is to understand which line you currently hold and make decisions accordingly.

Coaching observations

Attacking from the inside line without controlling the opponent's weapon. This is the most common beginner error. The attack is direct and the target is real, but the opponent's weapon can reach you just as directly. Both fencers hit each other. The solution is either to move to the outside line first, or to control the opponent's weapon before committing.

Gaining the outside line and then not committing. A student steps offline, has a clear outside line, and then hesitates or reverts to a technique that works from the inside. The advantage evaporates because it was not used.

Confusing outside line with wide measure. The outside line is about the angle of your weapon relative to theirs, not about how far away you are. You can be on the outside line at stretto distance. A disarm from Fiore's stretto section often requires being on the outside line of the weapon arm at extremely close range.

Historical connection

Every largo play in the Fiore curriculum involves a line decision.

Breaking the Thrust gains the outside line by stepping left while beating the blade to that side. The Peasant's Blow exits the inside line when the opponent's strike carries past center, leaving the Scholar on the effective outside of a now-committed attack.

In stretto, the joint locks require an outside position on the weapon arm specifically. The Lower Bind, Middle Bind, and Upper Bind all fail if applied from the inside. The outside position is not a preference, it is a mechanical requirement.

Reading the plays with this concept in mind makes the spatial logic of each technique clear.

docs.title: Opposition and Cover
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

Not all defenses are equal.

A parry that deflects an attack has stopped one threat. A parry that controls the line has stopped all threats from that direction while creating an immediate counter-opportunity. These are different actions with different outcomes, and the distinction between them matters every time blades meet.

Opposition closes a line with your blade while your point threatens. Cover only closes the line.

Cover is a defensive action that moves an incoming weapon off its target. The attack is deflected. The line is cleared for that moment. But nothing else is established. The opponent can recover their blade, change lines, and attack again. Cover buys time.

Opposition is a defensive action that controls the incoming weapon by maintaining contact and pressure while your own point angles toward the opponent's target. The attack is not just deflected — it is held. The opponent cannot recover their blade freely because yours is against it and your weight is behind it. Opposition closes one threat and creates another simultaneously.

The Exchange of Thrusts is the clearest example in the curriculum. The offline step takes your body away from the incoming thrust. The crossing of the blades is not a deflection — your arms extend low and outward to collect the incoming blade while your point rises toward the opponent's face. Both happen in one motion. The attack is opposed, not just parried. You are threatening before their attack has finished.

Opposition requires three things to be present at the same time:

Contact with the incoming weapon. Your blade must be against theirs with enough pressure to control its path. Light contact deflects. Maintained contact controls.

Weight behind the blade. Opposition is not an arm movement. The force that holds the opponent's blade in check comes from body alignment and weight transfer, not from grip strength. A fencer who opposes with the arms alone will be pushed off by a stronger opponent. A fencer who opposes with their structure behind the blade will hold the line regardless of size difference.

Point threatening a target. If your blade controls theirs but your point is aimed at the ceiling, you have cover, not opposition. The point must be on a line that forces the opponent to respond to it. This is what makes opposition a simultaneous action — defense and offense exist at the same moment.

Cover is not wrong. There are situations where deflection is the correct choice.

Breaking the Thrust uses a beat, which is closer to a forceful cover than a true opposition. The blade is knocked aside and the body moves to exploit the moment before it recovers. This is two-time: cover, then counter. It works because the body movement is fast enough that the gap between the two actions is negligible.

The distinction is that opposition collapses the two actions into one. When one-time action is available, it is preferable. When the geometry or timing makes it unavailable, two-time cover and counter is the correct response.

Training to prefer opposition when possible builds the habit of simultaneous action. Training to accept cover when necessary builds tactical flexibility.

Opposition continues to matter at close range, though it changes form.

In stretto, the weapons are no longer crossing near the tips. The contact is mid-blade or at the hilt. The mechanical principle is the same: pressure against the opponent's weapon arm or blade while your own action continues toward its target.

The pommel strike is an opposition in this sense. The bind is the contact. The roll under the bind and the strike of the pommel happen together. The blade controls the line while the pommel acts.

When reviewing a defensive action that failed, ask whether it was cover or opposition.

If the opponent hit you after your parry, the parry may have been cover that deflected without controlling. Their blade recovered before yours returned to threaten. The fix is not a harder parry. It is an earlier point — threatening before they can recover.

If your opposition failed, the cause is almost always weight. The arms held the line but the body was not behind them. The fix is to feel where your mass is when you make contact with the blade, and make sure it is moving toward the opponent, not away.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

What Makes a Position Strong

A blade can be pointed at the opponent and still be no threat.

A guard can look correct and still fold under the first pressure. A thrust can reach its target and still be pushed aside. The difference in each case is structure: whether the body position behind the technique supports it or undermines it.

A line without structure is a suggestion. A line with structure is a fact.

Structure is the alignment of your body behind your weapon.

When your blade is extended and your shoulder, hip, and foot are aligned to support it, force applied against your blade travels into your skeleton rather than collapsing your arm. Your position is load-bearing. An opponent who pushes against it is pushing against your weight.

When your blade is extended but your elbow is bent outward, your shoulder is dropped, or your weight is on the wrong foot, force applied against your blade bypasses your skeleton and goes directly into your muscles. Muscles fatigue and fail. Structure holds.

This is why Fiore's guards look the way they do. They are not aesthetic choices. Each guard positions the body so that the weapon is backed by weight and alignment. The guard is strong not because the fencer grips harder, but because the geometry makes it load-bearing.

Line describes where your weapon is pointed. Structure describes whether your body supports it.

You can have line without structure: blade aimed at the opponent, weight on the back foot, shoulder floating. The line exists but collapses on contact.

You can have structure without a threatening line: weight forward, body aligned, blade pointed at the ground. The position is stable but not dangerous.

What you want is both: a blade on a threatening line with your weight and alignment behind it. This is what Fiore's master figures demonstrate. The guard is positioned so that extending from it naturally produces both.

Weight on the wrong foot. A thrust with your weight on the rear foot has no mass behind it. The blade reaches but the body does not follow. Against any resistance, the thrust deflects. The fix is to feel whether your weight is moving toward your target as the blade extends.

Collapsed shoulder. When the sword shoulder drops or rotates inward, the alignment from hand to shoulder to torso breaks. Force against the blade now levers against a bent joint rather than traveling into the skeleton. Shoulder alignment is one of the most common structural errors in both guards and extended positions.

Elbow lifted or floating. In a guard or extended position, an elbow that is not supported by the structure underneath it creates a weak point. The blade may be on the correct line, but pressure against it bends the arm at the elbow rather than transmitting into the body.

Over-reaching. Extending further than your structure can support. The blade reaches the target but the body is stretched beyond stability. The position looks like it has line but has sacrificed the structural support that makes the line meaningful.

The clearest test of structure is contact.

In a static drill, almost any position looks reasonable. Under pressure — a partner pushing against your blade, applying a bind, or trying to displace your guard — structural weaknesses become immediately apparent. A guard that folds when pushed was never a guard; it was a shape.

This is why pressure testing is part of learning any technique. The drill teaches the position. The pressure reveals whether the structure is present. If the position collapses, the feedback is not that the technique is wrong. It is that the structure is missing.

The three joint locks demonstrate structure most clearly from the receiving end.

When the ligadura mezana is applied correctly, the structural failure is not in the arm being grabbed. It is in the elbow joint reaching its mechanical limit. No amount of grip strength or muscle tension overcomes a joint at its limit. The lock exploits a structural vulnerability.

Conversely, the scholar who applies the lock must have structure behind the pressing motion. The lock fails when the scholar's own alignment breaks: arm without body weight, weight on the back foot, shoulder not supporting the press.

The same principle applies in every largo exchange. A guard that holds when the opponent's blade makes contact is structurally sound. One that deflects or collapses is not, regardless of how correct it looked before contact was made.

When a technique fails under pressure, structure is usually the first place to look.

Ask: was my weight moving toward the target, or away from it? Was my shoulder aligned, or floating? Was the contact point of the technique load-bearing, or was I relying on muscle tension to hold the position?

Structure is built slowly through deliberate practice with feedback. Drilling in front of a mirror, working with a partner who provides controlled resistance, and reviewing video of sparring are all useful. The goal is to build positions that hold under contact automatically, without conscious attention to alignment, so that attention is free for reading the exchange.

docs.title: The Relationship Between Line and Structure
The Four Openings
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

Quattro Partimenti

Every attack lands somewhere. Every defense covers something.

Fencing vocabulary without a system for describing the body quickly becomes imprecise. "He hit me" tells you nothing useful. "He took the upper left opening after I crossed wide" tells you exactly what happened and why.

The four openings give you that system.

The body has four targets. Every technique either threatens one or closes one.

The body is divided into four quadrants by two lines: one horizontal at the waist, one vertical through the centerline.

Upper right — Above the waist, on your opponent's right side (your left as you face them). Includes the right shoulder, neck, and head.

Upper left — Above the waist, on your opponent's left side. Includes the left shoulder and the same targets from the other angle.

Lower right — Below the waist, on your opponent's right side. Legs, hip, and flank.

Lower left — Below the waist, on your opponent's left side.

Fiore explicitly numbers these in the Getty manuscript. The master figure in several plays calls out which opening is being taken or covered. This is not an abstraction imposed on the system — it is the system's own vocabulary.

A guard covers certain openings and leaves others accessible.

Posta di Donna Destra is positioned to threaten the upper openings with a diagonal cut. It naturally covers the upper right while the cut travels. What it leaves open depends on how the opponent responds.

Tutta Porta di Ferro covers the lower openings strongly. The low blade position makes it difficult to target the legs and lower body effectively. But the high openings are more exposed than from an elevated guard.

Understanding this lets you read a guard as information rather than just a posture. If your opponent is in a low guard, the lower openings are covered and the upper ones are available. Your technique choice follows from that read.

An opening that exists at the start of an exchange may close as the technique develops, and a new one may appear.

When the opponent raises their guard to cover the upper right, the lower openings open. When they extend for a thrust, their arm and shoulder are exposed in ways they were not before. When they step offline, the opening that was directly in front of them shifts.

Training to read openings means training to read them as they change, not just at the start of the exchange.

In the plays section, the four openings appear constantly without being named explicitly.

The Exchange of Thrusts takes the upper opening opposite to the incoming thrust. The Peasant's Blow exploits the opening created when the opponent's strike carries past center. The pommel strike in stretto targets the face — the upper opening — before the blade wraps to close behind the neck.

Reading those plays through the lens of the four openings makes the logic visible. The plays are not a collection of tricks. They are a set of answers to specific opening-and-cover problems.

When reviewing a sparring exchange, use the openings as a diagnostic:

  • What opening did the attack target?
  • Was that opening actually available, or did the attacker misread the guard?
  • What opened up as a result of the attack?
  • Did the defender's response close the targeted opening, or did it close a different one while leaving the first exposed?

Most fencing errors reduce to one of two problems: attacking a closed opening, or failing to close the opening being attacked. The four openings make those errors visible and nameable.

docs.title: Guards of the Sword in Two Hands
Bicorno
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

Getty MS Ludwig XV 13, c. 1409 - J. Paul Getty Museum (Open Content)

Flos Duellatorum (Pisani-Dossi MS), c. 1409 - Novati facsimile edition, 1902

The Two-Horned Guard

Classification: Instabile — Mutable Guard

Bicorno is unlike any other guard in Fiore's longsword system. Where every other guard uses a conventional placement of both hands on the handle, Bicorno introduces a reversed grip: both hands remain on the handle, but the front hand grips near the pommel with the palm rotated outward, while both elbows press inward toward each other. The sword is raised overhead, the elbows form the guard's characteristic horned silhouette, and the guard presents two simultaneous threats: the point projecting forward from above, and the pommel ready at close quarters.

For the modern fencer, Bicorno teaches a principle that no other guard addresses so directly: the sword in close combat is not only a blade: it is a lever, a hook, a bludgeon, and a handle. When measure collapses and the blade is too long to swing freely, Bicorno transforms the weapon from a distance tool into a close-quarters control instrument.

Fiore calls it "perfect defense." That precision of language is worth noting. Not strong, not stable, but perfect.

Bicorno introduces a grip configuration found nowhere else in Fiore's longsword system.

In the standard grip, both hands hold the handle with the palms facing the same direction. In Bicorno, the front hand is reversed: it grips near the pommel with the palm rotated outward and the elbow pressed inward toward the body's centerline.

This reversed configuration accomplishes several things.

It creates the horned silhouette. The elbows, pressed inward and raised overhead, form the characteristic shape that gives the guard its name. The inward pressure of both elbows produces a strong triangular structure that resists displacement from multiple directions.

It positions the pommel as an active weapon. With the front hand reversed near the pommel, that end of the sword is oriented toward the opponent and can be struck forward or used to hook at close distance.

It locks the overhead structure. The combination of elbows inward and reversed front hand creates a position that is genuinely difficult to press through or displace. This is the "perfect defense" Fiore describes — not because the guard covers every line passively, but because its structure resists interference.

It enables immediate transitions. As an Instabile guard, Bicorno is not meant to be held statically. The reversed grip can release quickly into descending cuts or thrusts as the tactical moment demands.

Understanding both horns of Bicorno as active and simultaneous threats is essential to understanding the guard correctly.

The blade point: Projecting forward from the overhead position, the point threatens the opponent's face, throat, and upper chest. A thrust from this position arrives at an unusual downward angle, which makes it difficult to read and hard to parry with a standard guard response.

The pommel: The reversed front hand near the pommel positions that end of the sword toward the opponent for hooking, striking, or controlling actions. In close quarters where the blade cannot swing freely, the pommel can impact with significant force.

An opponent who tries to close against Bicorno discovers that both ends of the weapon are dangerous. There is no safe angle of approach.

In modern fencing, Bicorno is most relevant in two contexts.

As a close-quarters guard: When sparring has closed to bind distance and neither fencer can freely swing, Bicorno provides a structured response rather than scrambling. The locked overhead structure allows the fencer to maintain control, continue threatening with both the point from above and the pommel at close range, and seek the decisive thrust that ends the exchange.

As a pedagogical tool: The reversed grip teaches students that the sword can be held in configurations beyond the standard grip, and that both ends of the weapon can be threatening simultaneously. Practicing Bicorno develops a more complete understanding of the weapon's versatility at close distance.

Bicorno most strongly expresses the Elephant.

The reversed grip structure creates a guard that is genuinely very difficult to displace or overwhelm. The inward elbows, the overhead position, and the locked geometry all contribute to a structural solidity that can receive pressure from multiple directions without collapsing. Like the elephant with its castle, Bicorno holds its ground through structural superiority rather than agility.

The Tiger governs the speed of the close-quarters thrust. At narrow play distance, the thrust from Bicorno must arrive before the opponent can reset to a more advantageous position.

The Lynx reads which horn is appropriate — the point thrust or the pommel strike — based on what the opponent is doing and where the opening exists.

The Lion commits to the close-quarters range that Bicorno requires. Maintaining the guard at narrow play distance, with the opponent immediately present, demands courage and willingness to engage at the most demanding measure.

Bicorno is most vulnerable before close distance is established.

At standard measure, where full cutting arcs are available, the overhead grip sacrifices the flexibility that a standard grip provides. An opponent who can maintain or create distance prevents the guard from reaching its optimal range.

The guard is also less effective against opponents with superior physical strength who can use grappling or wrestling actions to overwhelm the overhead structure before the point or pommel can be brought to bear.

Finally, the overhead structure leaves the lower body and legs more exposed than most guards. An opponent who directs attacks low, while staying outside the immediate threat of the two horns, can find lines that Bicorno does not naturally cover.

Bicorno is not a guard for middle or long measure. Its design is explicitly for close quarters — the narrow play where other guards have lost their primary function.

It is also not a guard for wide cutting actions. The reversed grip and locked elbow structure limit the available cutting arcs. The guard favors controlled thrusting and close-quarters control over large rotational cuts.

Finally, the guard requires familiarity with the reversed grip before it can be used confidently. Students should practice the grip structure and locked elbow position in isolation before attempting to apply it in dynamic exchanges.

docs.title: Bicorno
docs.text:
A reference on Bicorno, the Two-Horned Guard, in Fiore's longsword system.

REFERENCE | MIXED AUDIENCE

Chris Mineweaser | November 2026 | Version 0.1

docs.title: Getty Manuscript Text
docs.text:
"Bicorno son chiamado, per nome si perfecta, che cum doe punte e cum doe tagli, facio mia defesa perfecta. E posso ferir e defender cum li agudissimi mei corni. E per tal cason io son contra le altre prese ad ogne homo adorni."

Bicorno means Two-Horned, from the Italian bi (two) and corno (horn).

The name refers to the dual-threat structure of the guard. The first horn is the sword's point, projecting forward from the overhead position. The second horn is the pommel, positioned toward the opponent by the reversed front hand and ready to strike or hook at close distance.

The shape of the guard itself expresses the name: the elbows pressed inward and raised overhead form the arcing silhouette of two horns rising from the body's center. The image is immediate and physical. This is a guard that looks like what it is.

docs.title: Translation
docs.text:
"I am called Two-Horned, by name so perfect, for with two points and two edges I make my defense perfect. And I can strike and defend with my very sharp horns. And for this reason I am against the other grips, adorned for every man."

Fiore's description has a different quality from the other guards. He does not describe physical positioning or tactical movement — he declares perfection. Two points and two edges. Perfect defense. Against the other grips.

The language of "horns" is deliberate and precise. The guard does not simply have one threatening point; it has two. And both horns are sharp.

docs.title: Body Position
docs.text:
The stance is forward-weighted, reflecting the guard's commitment to close-quarters engagement.

The body leans slightly into the overhead structure. Where Posta Corona and Posta Frontale hold the elevated position from a neutral stance, Bicorno's forward weight reflects its role as an entering guard — it is built for the moment when distance has already collapsed and the fencer is in close contact.

Bicorno's tactical identity is built around one specific context: gioco stretto, the narrow play at close distance where the opponent's blade is no longer free to swing.

When two fencers have closed to bind distance and the full cutting arcs of the longsword are no longer available, most guards become difficult to deploy. Bicorno is designed for exactly this range.

Perfect defense through dual threats: With the point projecting from above and the pommel available at close range, the guard covers two lines simultaneously. An opponent trying to find an opening must account for both threats, and the angle of the overhead position makes many attacking lines converge directly on one or the other.

Precision thrusting from above: The overhead position angles the point downward at an unusual approach, arriving from above rather than straight ahead, which makes it difficult to read and hard to parry with a standard guard response. Against armored opponents, this downward angle was critical for finding gaps in the armor around the neck and shoulders.

Against grips and grappling: Fiore says the guard is "against the other grips." When an opponent attempts to grab or control the sword or the fencer's body, the pommel provides immediate counter-options, and the locked structure of the reversed grip makes the fencer's weapon more secure against attempts to disarm.

docs.title: Hand and Sword Position
docs.text:
Both hands grip the handle: the rear hand in a standard grip, the front hand reversed near the pommel with the palm facing outward.

The sword is raised overhead with both elbows pressed inward toward the centerline. The point projects forward and slightly downward from the overhead position, threatening at roughly the opponent's face height from above.

The elbows form the "horns" of the guard. Their inward pressure creates a compact structural triangle — body, rear arm, front arm — that is very difficult to displace.

The pommel, held by the reversed front hand, remains available for striking or hooking actions at close distance.

docs.title: What This Guard Is Not For
Drill 1 — Establishing the Reversed Grip
docs.text:
Begin by establishing the reversed grip: rear hand on the handle with a standard grip, front hand reversed near the pommel with the palm facing outward.

Raise the sword overhead, pressing both elbows inward toward the centerline. The point projects forward from the overhead position.

A partner applies gentle downward pressure on the blade from above. Maintain the structure without the elbows collapsing outward or the reversed front hand losing its connection.

Hold for ten seconds, then rest. Repeat five times. Focus on the structural triangle formed by the elbows and sword, and the feeling of the locked overhead position.

Bicorno is the guard of the narrow space.

It carries two threats simultaneously — the point projecting from above, the pommel ready below — and holds them both through the locked structure of the reversed grip. Against attempts to control, grab, or overwhelm at close distance, it presents a problem with two sharp answers.

Perfect defense does not mean perfect coverage of every line. It means that wherever the opponent reaches, one horn is already there.

docs.title: Drill 2 — The Overhead Thrust
docs.text:
From Bicorno, step forward and deliver a controlled thrust downward and forward from the overhead position.

The point drops toward a specific target — a partner holds their fist at face height as a reference point.

The overhead starting position gives the thrust an unusual downward angle. Repeat ten times, adjusting the target height: face, throat, chest.

The goal is to experience the distinctive angle of the overhead thrust and the way the locked structure guides the point forward.

The most common mistake is allowing the elbows to collapse outward rather than pressing them inward. The elbows-in position is what creates the structural lock and the characteristic "horned" shape. Elbows pointing outward convert Bicorno into an unstable overhead position with no structural advantage.

Another frequent error is reversing the wrong hand or gripping too loosely with the front hand. The front hand should be near the pommel, fully reversed with the palm facing outward, and with enough grip to maintain control under pressure.

Some students also treat Bicorno as a purely defensive guard and fail to use both horns actively. The point must remain threatening forward, and the pommel must remain available as a striking or hooking option. Focusing only on one horn misses the guard's defining characteristic.

Finally, hunched or collapsed shoulders reduce the structural integrity of the overhead position. The shoulders should be relaxed and the structure open — tension in the upper body creates rigidity that slows response.

docs.title: Drill 3 — Defending the Overhead
docs.text:
One fencer assumes Bicorno. The partner delivers a slow descending Fendente toward the Bicorno fencer's head.

The Bicorno fencer uses the overhead structure — the elevated blade and locked elbows — to receive the descending strike, allowing it to contact the blade and be deflected.

After the deflection, the Bicorno fencer immediately delivers a controlled thrust downward from the overhead position.

Repeat ten times, then switch roles. The lesson: the overhead structure in Bicorno is not passive — it catches the incoming strike and immediately creates the opportunity for a counter-thrust.

docs.title: Coda Longa
docs.text:
Print / Save as PDF

Flos Duellatorum (Pisani-Dossi MS), c. 1409 - Novati facsimile edition, 1902

The Long Tail

Classification: Stabile — Stable Guard

Coda Longa is one of the most deceptive guards in the Getty manuscript of Fiore dei Liberi. The sword trails behind the body like the tail of an animal, appearing withdrawn, passive, or even vulnerable.

But this appearance is intentional.

Fiore describes Coda Longa as a false guard, a position designed to mislead the opponent about your true intentions. Although the posture appears defensive, the guard is built for sudden offense, explosive upward strikes, and aggressive entry.

For the modern fencer, Coda Longa teaches an essential tactical principle:

What appears weak may actually be preparing to attack.

This guard is not about waiting safely behind structure. It is about baiting the opponent into overcommitting before launching forward with explosive motion.

This chapter treats Coda Longa Destra and Coda Longa Sinestra together, since both versions express the same tactical idea through mirrored body mechanics.

Like many guards in Fiore’s system, Coda Longa exists on both the right and left sides of the body.

Although the tactical purpose remains the same, the angle of acceleration and entry changes significantly between the two versions.

One of the primary tactical purposes of Coda Longa is to provoke commitment from the opponent.

Because the guard appears defensive or withdrawn, opponents are often tempted to:

  • rush forward
  • overextend
  • attempt to seize initiative
  • attack aggressively into perceived weakness

Coda Longa exploits this reaction.

As the opponent commits, the guard launches upward into the opening created by their forward motion.

This is why Fiore describes the guard as both deceptive and aggressive simultaneously.

In modern fencing, Coda Longa is often underestimated because it appears unconventional and vulnerable.

In practice, however, it can be extremely effective for:

  • baiting aggressive opponents
  • disguising upward attacks
  • creating explosive acceleration
  • forcing reactions through deceptive posture

The guard is especially useful against opponents who:

  • overcommit aggressively
  • chase perceived openings
  • attack recklessly into withdrawn positions

For modern practitioners, the greatest value of Coda Longa lies in understanding how posture and intention influence an opponent’s decisions.

Coda Longa strongly expresses the Lynx.

The guard depends on observation, timing, and deception. The fencer studies the opponent and invites a reaction before striking.

The Tiger appears in the explosive acceleration of the release. The Elephant appears in the stable rear-weighted structure. The Lion appears in the courage required to stand in an apparently vulnerable position.

Coda Longa is strongest when opponents attack impulsively into its invitation.

The guard becomes less effective when the opponent:

  • refuses to overcommit
  • controls distance carefully
  • pressures safely from above
  • forces the guard to act first

Because the sword begins deeply chambered behind the body, interrupting the rising action early can limit the guard’s effectiveness.

Maintaining measured pressure while denying explosive entry is often more effective than rushing aggressively into the trap.

Coda Longa is not designed for passive retreating.

Although the posture appears defensive, the guard functions through aggressive offensive intent.

It is also not intended for static point control or prolonged centerline dominance. The sword begins withdrawn rather than extended.
